beginner.content:
What is the History of HTML?

• HTML was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 at CERN, Switzerland.
• He needed a way for scientists to share documents that linked to one another.
• The idea of a clickable link joining two documents is called hypertext.
• That is where the name comes from: Hyper Text Markup Language.

Why it Matters

• HTML was designed to describe documents, not to design pages.
• This is why HTML handles structure and CSS handles appearance.
• Understanding this split makes every later topic easier.

The Journey in Short

• 1991 - First version, only 18 tags existed.
• 1995 - HTML 2.0, the first official standard.
• 1997 - HTML 3.2 and HTML 4.0, tables and scripting arrived.
• 1999 - HTML 4.01, used for nearly a decade.
• 2000 - XHTML 1.0, strict XML-style rules.
• 2014 - HTML5 became an official W3C Recommendation.
• Today - HTML is a Living Standard, updated continuously by WHATWG.
codeExamples:
Welcome

This is a paragraph of text.

Go to another document

intermediate.content:
Who Controls HTML?

• W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) - published the numbered versions.
• WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group) - formed in 2004 by browser makers.
• WHATWG was created because developers felt W3C was moving toward XHTML 2.0, which broke old pages.
• In 2019 W3C and WHATWG agreed that WHATWG maintains the single Living Standard.

What is a Living Standard?

• There are no more version numbers after HTML5.
• Features are added continuously as browsers implement them.
• So writing HTML6 on a resume is incorrect - it does not exist.

expert.content:
The XHTML Detour - An Interview Favourite

• XHTML forced HTML to obey strict XML rules.
• Every tag had to be closed, every attribute quoted, everything lowercase.
• One tiny error meant the browser showed a yellow screen of death instead of the page.
• That strictness was unforgiving for real websites, so the industry moved back to HTML5.

The Lesson HTML5 Learned

• HTML5 defines exactly how a browser should recover from bad markup.
• Before HTML5, every browser guessed differently - the main cause of old cross-browser bugs.
• This is why HTML5 pages render consistently even when the markup is imperfect.
codeExamples: Modern

beginner.content:
HTML Versions

• Each version added new tags and removed old ones.
• You only write HTML5 today, but interviews still ask about the history.

Version Table

• HTML 1.0 (1991) - 18 tags, text and links only.
• HTML 2.0 (1995) - forms introduced.
• HTML 3.2 (1997) - tables, applets, text flow around images.
• HTML 4.01 (1999) - CSS support, frames, scripting.
• XHTML 1.0 (2000) - HTML rewritten with strict XML rules.
• HTML5 (2014) - semantic tags, audio, video, canvas, new form inputs.

intermediate.content:
How the Browser Knows the Version

• The DOCTYPE on the first line tells the browser which rules to use.
• Old versions needed a long, unmemorable DOCTYPE with a DTD URL.
• HTML5 shortened it to a single line that anyone can type from memory.

Quirks Mode - Why the Short DOCTYPE Matters

• If the DOCTYPE is missing or wrong, the browser enters quirks mode.
• In quirks mode the browser imitates 1990s bugs on purpose for old sites.
• The box model changes, and your CSS widths silently become wrong.
• Always include the DOCTYPE - it is one line and prevents a whole class of layout bugs.
codeExamples:
<!-- HTML 4.01 Strict -->
<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 4.01//EN"
  "http://www.w3.org/TR/html4/strict.dtd">

<!-- XHTML 1.0 Transitional -->
<!DOCTYPE html PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD XHTML 1.0 Transitional//EN"
  "http://www.w3.org/TR/xhtml1/DTD/xhtml1-transitional.dtd">

<!-- HTML5 - this is all you ever need now -->
<!DOCTYPE html>

expert.content:
Deprecated Tags - Removed in HTML5

• These existed for styling, which is now entirely CSS's job.
• <font> - set colour and size. Use CSS color and font-size.
• <center> - centred content. Use CSS text-align or margin auto.
• <big>, <strike>, <tt> - use CSS, or <del> for struck text.
• <frame>, <frameset> - broke bookmarking and accessibility.
• <marquee>, <blink> - never standard, badly hurt accessibility.

Why They Were Removed

• Presentation mixed into markup makes a site impossible to restyle.
• Screen readers and search engines could not tell content from decoration.
• A browser may still render them, but they are invalid and must not be used.
codeExamples:
Important Notice

Important Notice

What is HTML5?

• HTML5 is the current version of HTML, and the one you will always use.
• It made web pages able to do things that previously needed Flash plugins.

Main Additions

• Semantic tags - header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer.
• Media tags - audio and video play natively, no plugin needed.
• Graphics - canvas and inline SVG.
• New form inputs - email, date, number, color, range.
• Built-in validation - required and pattern work without JavaScript.
• Storage APIs - localStorage and sessionStorage.
• Simplified DOCTYPE and charset declaration.

intermediate.content:
HTML5 vs HTML4 - Quick Comparison

• DOCTYPE - HTML4 needed a long DTD line, HTML5 needs one short line.
• Charset - HTML4 used a long meta http-equiv, HTML5 uses meta charset.
• Structure - HTML4 used div id="header", HTML5 uses <header>.
• Media - HTML4 needed Flash, HTML5 has audio and video.
• Validation - HTML4 needed JavaScript, HTML5 has required and pattern.
• Storage - HTML4 had cookies only, HTML5 adds localStorage.

Why Semantic Tags Beat Divs

• A page full of divs tells the browser nothing about meaning.
• Screen readers use semantic tags to offer landmark navigation.
• Search engines use them to understand which part is the real content.
• Other developers read the structure instantly.

expert.content:
Feature Detection, Not Browser Detection

• Never check which browser is running - check whether the feature exists.
• Browser sniffing breaks the moment a new version or browser appears.
• Feature detection keeps working forever.

Progressive Enhancement

• Build a page that works with plain HTML first.
• Then add HTML5 and JavaScript features on top for browsers that support them.
• Users on old or limited devices still get a working page instead of a blank one.
• This is why <video> allows fallback content between its tags.

beginner.content:
HTML Syntax Rules

• HTML is written as elements made of tags.
• A normal element has an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.
• The closing tag repeats the name with a forward slash.

Anatomy of an Element

• <p class="note">Hello</p>
• p is the tag name.
• class="note" is an attribute: a name, an equals sign, and a quoted value.
• Hello is the content.
• </p> closes the element.
codeExamples:
This is a heading

This is a paragraph.

Visit Example

intermediate.content:
Rules Worth Memorising

• Tag names are case-insensitive, but always write them lowercase.
• Attribute values should always be in quotes - single or double both work.
• Elements must be properly nested - close in the reverse order you opened.
• Void elements such as br, img and input never get a closing tag.
• Boolean attributes need no value - the presence alone means true.

Boolean Attributes

• required, disabled, checked, readonly, multiple, autofocus.
• Writing disabled="false" still disables the element - the value is ignored.
• To turn it off, remove the attribute entirely.
codeExamples: This is correctly nested text.

expert.content:
Error Recovery

• HTML5 specifies exactly how browsers must fix broken markup.
• A missing </p> is auto-closed when the next block element starts.
• Overlapping tags are silently reordered into a valid tree.
• This is convenient, but the DOM you get may not be the DOM you expected.

Why You Should Still Write Valid HTML

• Your CSS selectors target the fixed DOM, not the text you wrote.
• A stray unclosed tag can move an element into a different parent, and your styles stop matching.
• Use the W3C validator, and inspect the Elements panel in DevTools to see the real tree.

beginner.content:
Structure of Every HTML Page

• Every page follows the same skeleton, in this exact order.
• <!DOCTYPE html> - tells the browser this is HTML5.
• <html> - the root element, wraps everything.
• <head> - information about the page. Not visible.
• <body> - everything the user actually sees.

Remember the Rule

• head = information for the browser and search engines.
• body = information for the human.
codeExamples:
Visible Heading

Visible paragraph the user reads.

intermediate.content:
A Production-Ready Skeleton

• lang on <html> - helps screen readers pronounce words correctly.
• charset must be the first thing in head, within the first 1024 bytes.
• viewport is mandatory for the page to work on mobile.
• title is required and appears in search results and browser tabs.
• description is the grey text shown under your link on Google.

Script Placement

• A plain <script> in head blocks page rendering while it downloads.
• Put scripts at the end of body, or use defer in the head.
• defer downloads in parallel and runs after the HTML is parsed - the best default.

expert.content:
The DOM Tree

• The browser turns your markup into a tree of objects called the DOM.
• document is the root, then html, then head and body as its two children.
• JavaScript and CSS both work on this tree, not on your text file.

Implied Tags

• html, head and body are technically optional in the source.
• The browser inserts them automatically if missing.
• So a file containing only <p>Hi</p> still produces a full DOM tree.
• Never rely on this - always write them, because tooling and lang attributes depend on them.
codeExamples: Hi

beginner.content:
What is the DOCTYPE?

• It is the very first line of every HTML page.
• It tells the browser: render this page using modern standards.
• In HTML5 it is short and easy to remember.

Key Points

• It is not an HTML tag - it is an instruction to the browser.
• It has no closing tag.
• It is case-insensitive, so DOCTYPE and doctype both work.
• It must come before the <html> tag, with nothing above it.
codeExamples: The DOCTYPE is the first line, above everything else.

intermediate.content:
Standards Mode vs Quirks Mode

• With a correct DOCTYPE the browser uses standards mode - the modern, correct rules.
• With a missing or wrong DOCTYPE it drops into quirks mode.
• Quirks mode deliberately reproduces 1990s Internet Explorer bugs so old sites still work.

What Actually Breaks in Quirks Mode

• The box model changes: width starts including padding and border.
• So a 200px box with 20px padding becomes 200px wide instead of 240px.
• Every measurement in your CSS is then subtly wrong.
• Line heights, table font inheritance and image spacing also change.

How to Check

• Type document.compatMode in the console.
• CSS1Compat means standards mode - correct.
• BackCompat means quirks mode - your DOCTYPE is missing.
codeExamples: Measure me

expert.content:
Why HTML5's DOCTYPE is So Short

• Older DOCTYPEs pointed at a DTD - a Document Type Definition file.
• The DTD described every legal tag, for XML-style validation.
• HTML5 is not defined by a DTD, so no URL is needed.
• <!DOCTYPE html> is the shortest string that reliably triggers standards mode in every browser, including very old ones. That is its only job.

Almost Standards Mode

• A third, rarely mentioned mode exists.
• It matches standards mode except for one rule about image spacing inside table cells.
• Some transitional DOCTYPEs trigger it.
• Another good reason to use only the HTML5 DOCTYPE.
codeExamples:
<!-- All of these are VALID and trigger standards mode -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<!doctype html>
<!DocType HTML>


<!-- BROKEN: a comment above the DOCTYPE pushes it out of first position
     in old browsers, causing quirks mode -->
<!-- My website, 2025 -->
<!DOCTYPE html>


<!-- BROKEN: even a blank line or a space before it can matter -->

<!DOCTYPE html>


<!-- CORRECT: DOCTYPE is byte number one of the file -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

beginner.content:
The <html> Element

• It is the root element - every other element lives inside it.
• It comes directly after the DOCTYPE.
• It has exactly two children: <head> and <body>, in that order.

The lang Attribute

• Always add lang to the html tag.
• It tells screen readers which language to pronounce.
• It helps browsers offer the correct translation.
• It helps search engines serve your page to the right audience.
• Examples: lang="en" English, lang="hi" Hindi, lang="mr" Marathi.
codeExamples: Everything visible sits inside body, which sits inside html.

intermediate.content:
Regional Language Codes

• You may add a region after the language: en-US, en-GB, en-IN.
• This affects pronunciation and date or spelling expectations.
• en-IN tells a screen reader to use an Indian English voice.

Mixed Languages on One Page

• Set the main language on <html>.
• Override it on any element that uses a different language.
• Without this, a screen reader reads Hindi text using English pronunciation rules, which is unintelligible.

The dir Attribute

• dir="ltr" is left to right, the default.
• dir="rtl" is right to left, for Arabic, Hebrew and Urdu.
• Setting dir on <html> flips the entire layout direction.
codeExamples:
This paragraph is in Indian English.

HTML shikane sope aahe.

Arabic text flows from the right.

expert.content:
document.documentElement

• In JavaScript the <html> element is document.documentElement.
• It is not document.body - a very common mistake.
• It is the usual place to store a theme, because CSS can then style the whole page from one attribute.

Why Themes Go on <html>

• It is the highest element, so every descendant can be targeted from it.
• It exists before body is parsed, so a theme can be applied with no flash of the wrong colour.
• Setting it on body instead means the page background flashes white first.
• This is exactly how the dark mode on this website works.
codeExamples: Toggle the theme and the whole page follows.

beginner.content:
The <head> Element

• Holds information about the page, not content of the page.
• Nothing inside head is displayed to the user.
• The one exception is <title>, which appears in the browser tab.

What Goes Inside head

• <title> - page title. Required on every page.
• <meta> - charset, viewport, description, keywords.
• <link> - stylesheets, favicon, fonts.
• <style> - CSS written directly in the page.
• <script> - JavaScript files.
• <base> - a base URL for all relative links.
codeExamples: Only this part is visible.

intermediate.content:
Order Matters in head

• charset first - it must appear within the first 1024 bytes, or the browser has to restart parsing.
• viewport next - needed before layout begins.
• title and description - for SEO and sharing.
• stylesheets - CSS blocks rendering, so load it early and keep it small.
• scripts last, with defer.

Render Blocking

• CSS is render blocking by design - the browser refuses to paint until it knows the styles, otherwise you would see unstyled text flash.
• A plain script is parser blocking - HTML parsing stops completely while it downloads and runs.
• That is why script placement is a real performance topic, not a style preference.
codeExamples: Content

expert.content:
Social Sharing Tags

• Open Graph tags control how your link looks on WhatsApp, LinkedIn and Facebook.
• Twitter Card tags do the same for X.
• Without them your shared link shows no image and no description - it looks untrustworthy and gets far fewer clicks.

Performance Hints

• preconnect - open the connection to a domain early.
• dns-prefetch - resolve the DNS early.
• preload - fetch a critical file at high priority.
• These save real milliseconds on fonts and hero images.

The canonical Link

• Tells search engines which URL is the real one.
• Prevents duplicate content penalties when the same page is reachable at several URLs.
codeExamples: Spring Boot

beginner.content:
The <body> Element

• Contains everything the user sees.
• Text, headings, images, links, tables, forms, videos - all live here.
• There is exactly one body per page.
• It is the second child of <html>, after <head>.

Simple Rule

• If the user should see it, it goes in body.
• If it only describes the page, it goes in head.
codeExamples:

intermediate.content:
Structuring the Body Properly

• Do not fill body with plain <div> elements.
• Use the HTML5 landmark elements so the page has meaning.
• <header> - logo and site title.
• <nav> - the main navigation links.
• <main> - the unique content of this page. Only one per page.
• <aside> - sidebar content.
• <footer> - copyright and contact.

Why This Helps Real Users

• Screen reader users can jump directly between landmarks.
• They do not have to listen to the whole navigation on every page.
• A skip link plus a <main> element saves them dozens of keystrokes per page.

expert.content:
Old body Attributes - All Removed

• bgcolor, text, link, vlink, alink, background were used in the 1990s.
• All are deprecated in HTML5 - use CSS instead.

body vs html in CSS

• Setting a background on body does not confine it to the body box.
• If html has no background, the body background is propagated to the whole canvas.
• This special rule exists so short pages do not show a white strip below the content.
• If you set a background on both html and body, the propagation stops and body behaves like a normal box.

Practical Consequence

• A gradient on body stretches to fill the viewport.
• The same gradient, once html also has a background, only covers the content height.
codeExamples: Short page. The gradient still covers the entire window.

beginner.content:
• HTML comments are used to write notes inside the code.
• Comments are not displayed in the browser.
• They help developers understand the code.

Syntax of Comment

<!-- This is a comment -->

beginner.content:
What is an Element?

• An element is a complete unit: opening tag + content + closing tag.
• <p>Hello</p> is one element.
• The element is the thing; the tags are just the markers around it.

Element vs Tag

• Tag - <p> or </p>, just the marker.
• Element - the whole thing including content.
• This exact difference is asked in interviews very often.

Types of Element

• Normal - has content and a closing tag, like p and div.
• Void - no content, no closing tag, like br, img and input.
codeExamples:

intermediate.content:
Content Categories

• HTML5 groups elements by what they may contain, which decides what is legal where.
• Metadata - title, meta, link, style. Belong in head.
• Flow - almost anything that goes in body.
• Sectioning - article, section, nav, aside.
• Heading - h1 to h6.
• Phrasing - text-level content such as span, strong, em, a.
• Embedded - img, video, audio, canvas, iframe.
• Interactive - a, button, input, select.

The Rule That Catches Everyone

• A <p> may only contain phrasing content.
• So a <div> inside a <p> is invalid, and the browser silently closes the p.
• Your CSS then fails to match, and the bug looks mysterious.

expert.content:
Replaced vs Non-Replaced Elements

• A replaced element's content comes from outside the document: img, video, iframe, input.
• The browser replaces the tag with an external resource.
• A non-replaced element's content is the markup itself: p, div, span.

Why the Difference Matters in CSS

• Replaced elements have intrinsic dimensions - a real natural width and height.
• So width and height work on an <img> even though it is inline.
• On a non-replaced inline element such as <span>, width and height are ignored entirely.
• This is the real answer to the classic question: why can I size an img but not a span?

Also Unique to Replaced Elements

• object-fit and object-position only work on replaced elements.
• vertical-align behaves differently, which causes the famous gap under images.

beginner.content:
What is a Tag?

• A tag is the marker written between angle brackets.
• <p> is an opening tag. </p> is a closing tag.
• Tags are instructions to the browser, and are never shown to the user.

Rules for Tags

• Always write tags in lowercase - it is the universal convention.
• Most tags come in pairs.
• Void tags such as <br> and <img> have no pair.
• Close tags in the reverse order you opened them.

Common Tags to Know First

• h1 to h6 - headings.
• p - paragraph.
• a - link.
• img - image.
• ul, ol, li - lists.
• div - generic block container.
• span - generic inline container.

Tags You Do Not Have to Close

• HTML5 allows some closing tags to be omitted because the browser infers them.
• </p> is implied by the next block element.
• </li> is implied by the next <li>.
• </td> and </tr> are implied by the next cell or row.

But Always Close Them Anyway

• Omitted tags make code harder to read and to review.
• Linters and formatters expect them.
• A missing tag in the wrong place silently changes your DOM tree.
• The cost of typing four characters is far lower than the cost of one confusing bug.

Self-Closing Syntax

• <br /> with a slash is XHTML style.
• In HTML5 the slash is allowed but ignored on void elements.
• On a normal element such as <div /> it is meaningless - the div stays open.

Custom Elements

• You may invent your own tags, but the name must contain a hyphen.
• The hyphen guarantees your tag can never clash with a future standard tag.
• <user-card> is valid. <usercard> is not a valid custom element name.

Unknown Tags

• A browser does not reject a tag it has never seen.
• It creates an HTMLUnknownElement and styles it as inline by default.
• That is why an unstyled custom tag appears to do nothing.
• Give it display: block in CSS and it behaves normally.

Why This Matters

• This forgiving behaviour is how new HTML tags can be introduced safely.
• Old browsers simply treat <main> as an unknown inline element rather than crashing.

What are Global Attributes?

• Attributes that can be used on any HTML element.
• You do not have to memorise which tags accept them - they all do.

The Ones You Will Use Daily

• id - a unique name for one element.
• class - a group name, reusable on many elements.
• style - inline CSS for that one element.
• title - tooltip text shown on hover.
• hidden - hides the element completely.
• lang - the language of that element's text.
• dir - text direction, ltr or rtl.
• data-* - your own custom data.

data-* Attributes

• Let you attach your own data to any element, legally.
• The name must start with data- and be lowercase.
• Read them in JavaScript through the dataset property.
• data-user-id becomes dataset.userId - the dashes become camelCase.

Why Not Just Invent an Attribute?

• A non-standard attribute such as userid makes the page invalid.
• It may clash with a future HTML feature.
• data-* is guaranteed safe forever.

Accessibility Globals

• tabindex - controls keyboard focus order.
• role - tells assistive technology what an element is.
• aria-label - gives an accessible name when there is no visible text.
• contenteditable - makes any element editable by the user.

expert.content:
tabindex - Use With Care

• tabindex="0" - put the element in the natural tab order. This is what you usually want.
• tabindex="-1" - focusable by JavaScript only, not by Tab. Useful for dialogs.
• tabindex="1" or higher - avoid. It jumps ahead of every natural element and destroys the keyboard order for the whole page.

hidden vs display none

• The hidden attribute is equivalent to display: none.
• But any CSS display rule overrides it, because the attribute is only a default style.
• So a rule like div { display: block } makes hidden divs visible again - a subtle and confusing bug.

Best Practice

• Prefer a real element over role plus tabindex.
• A <button> is focusable, clickable by Enter and Space, and announced correctly, all for free.
• A div with role="button" needs tabindex, keydown handlers and ARIA to match it.

beginner.content:
What are Inline Elements?

• They flow within a line of text.
• They do not start on a new line.
• They take only as much width as their content needs.

Common Inline Elements

• span - generic inline container.
• a - link.
• strong and b - bold.
• em and i - italic.
• img - image.
• label, input, button - form controls.
• code, small, sub, sup, mark.
codeExamples:

intermediate.content:
The CSS Rules That Trip Everyone Up

• width and height are ignored on inline elements.
• Top and bottom margin are ignored.
• Left and right margin do work.
• Top and bottom padding is applied but does not push other lines away - it overlaps them.

The Fix: inline-block

• display: inline-block keeps the element on the same line.
• But it now accepts width, height and vertical margin like a block.
• This is the usual solution for buttons, badges and navigation items.

Three Display Values Compared

• inline - flows in text, ignores size.
• block - new line, full width, accepts size.
• inline-block - stays in the line, accepts size.

expert.content:
The Mysterious Gap Between Inline Elements

• Put two inline-block elements on separate source lines and a small gap appears.
• The gap is not margin - it is the whitespace (newline) in your HTML.
• Inline elements honour whitespace, and a newline collapses to one space character.

Ways to Remove It

• Put the tags on one line with no space between them.
• End the line with a comment so the newline is inside the comment.
• Set font-size: 0 on the parent and restore it on the children.
• Best modern answer: use flexbox or grid on the parent, which ignores whitespace entirely.

The Gap Under an Image

• An <img> sits on the text baseline, leaving room for descenders such as g and y.
• That leaves a few pixels of space below it inside its container.
• Fix with display: block, or vertical-align: bottom.

beginner.content:
What are Void Elements?

• Elements that have no content and therefore no closing tag.
• They are also called empty elements or self-closing elements.
• Everything they do is expressed through their attributes.

The Complete List

• br - line break.
• hr - horizontal rule.
• img - image.
• input - form field.
• meta - page metadata.
• link - stylesheet or icon.
• source, track - media sources.
• area, base, col, embed, param, wbr.

• There are only 14 of them, so they are worth memorising.
codeExamples:
Line one
Line two

intermediate.content:
Common Mistakes

• Writing </br> or </img> - these closing tags do not exist and are invalid.
• Trying to put content inside: <img>caption</img> is wrong. Use <figcaption>.
• Using <br> to create spacing between paragraphs - use CSS margin instead.

The Trailing Slash

• <br /> is valid HTML5 but the slash is completely ignored.
• It is a leftover from XHTML.
• React and JSX require it, because JSX follows XML rules - this is why you see it in React code.
• In plain HTML files, either style is fine. Be consistent.

Empty vs Void - Not the Same

• A void element can never have content: <br>.
• An empty element is a normal element that simply has no content right now: <div></div>.
• The CSS :empty selector matches the second, never the first.

expert.content:
Why You Cannot Style Void Elements With ::before

• ::before and ::after insert content inside the element.
• A void element has no inside, so the pseudo-elements are simply never generated.
• This is why the classic trick of adding an icon with ::after fails on <img> and <input>.

The Workarounds

• Wrap the void element in a span or div, and style the wrapper.
• For inputs, style the associated <label> instead.
• For images, use a <figure> wrapper.

The One Exception

• A broken image can be styled, because the browser then renders the alt text as normal content.
• Some browsers do generate pseudo-elements in that failed state - useful for showing a fallback.

beginner.content:
What is Nesting?

• Putting one element inside another.
• This is how every web page is built - a tree of elements.
• The outer element is the parent, the inner one is the child.

The Golden Rule

• Close tags in the reverse order you opened them.
• Opened p, then strong? Close strong first, then p.
• Think of it like brackets in mathematics - they must not cross.

Indentation

• Indent each level by 2 or 4 spaces.
• The browser ignores indentation, but humans do not.
codeExamples:
This is bold text inside a paragraph.

Course Title

  • Module one
  • Module two

intermediate.content:
Nesting Rules You Must Not Break

• A <p> cannot contain a div, another p, or any block element.
• An <a> cannot contain another a, or a button.
• A <button> cannot contain an a or another button.
• A <ul> or <ol> may only have <li> as a direct child.
• A <form> cannot contain another form.

What Happens If You Break Them

• The browser does not show an error.
• It silently repairs the tree into something valid.
• The DOM you get is not the markup you wrote, so your CSS and JavaScript stop matching.
• Always check the Elements panel in DevTools, not your source file.

Nesting Lists Correctly

• A nested list goes inside an <li>, never directly inside the ul.
codeExamples:

    • Advanced Java
  • Spring Boot

expert.content:
Parent, Child, Descendant, Sibling

• Parent - the element directly containing another.
• Child - directly inside the parent, one level down.
• Descendant - inside at any depth.
• Sibling - shares the same parent.
• Ancestor - any element further up the tree.

Why the Vocabulary Matters

• CSS selectors map exactly onto these words.
• div p - any p descendant, at any depth.
• div > p - only a direct child p.
• h2 + p - the p immediately after an h2.
• h2 ~ p - every p sibling after an h2.

Nesting Depth and Performance

• Very deep nesting makes CSS slower to match and code harder to read.
• Aim to keep the tree under roughly 10 to 15 levels.
• Flexbox and grid usually let you delete several wrapper divs.

beginner.content:
Is HTML Case Sensitive?

• Tag names - not case sensitive. <P> and <p> are the same.
• Attribute names - not case sensitive. HREF and href are the same.
• Attribute values - it depends. Some are case sensitive, some are not.

The Convention

• Always write tags and attribute names in lowercase.
• Every style guide, linter and formatter expects lowercase.
• Uppercase HTML looks like it was written in 1998.
codeExamples:
Uppercase tag

Lowercase tag

Mixed case tag

Works Preferred

Clean, lowercase, conventional.

intermediate.content:
Where Case DOES Matter

• id and class values - fully case sensitive. myBox and mybox are different.
• CSS selectors matching those values are case sensitive too.
• File paths in src and href - case sensitive on Linux servers.
• URLs - the path part is case sensitive.
• JavaScript - always case sensitive.

The Classic Deployment Bug

• Windows treats Logo.PNG and logo.png as the same file.
• Linux does not.
• So a site works perfectly on your laptop and every image breaks on the server.
• Rule: name all files in lowercase, and reference them exactly.

Attribute Values That Ignore Case

• type="TEXT" and type="text" are the same.
• Predefined keyword values are generally case insensitive.
codeExamples:
Green - matches .myBox only

Red - matches .mybox only

expert.content:
Why HTML is Case Insensitive but XHTML is Not

• XHTML is XML, and XML is strictly case sensitive by definition.
• In XHTML, <P> and <p> are genuinely different elements.
• HTML5 kept case insensitivity for backward compatibility with millions of old pages.

The DOM Normalises Case

• Whatever case you write, the DOM stores tag names in uppercase.
• So element.tagName returns "P", never "p".
• Compare with toLowerCase() or use localName, which returns lowercase for HTML documents.

SVG is the Exception Inside HTML

• Inline SVG follows XML rules even inside an HTML page.
• So viewBox must be written with a capital B - viewbox silently fails.
• Same for preserveAspectRatio and linearGradient.
• This catches almost everyone the first time they hand-write SVG.
codeExamples: Check the console

beginner.content:
How HTML Treats Whitespace

• Spaces, tabs and newlines are all whitespace.
• HTML collapses any run of whitespace into a single space.
• Ten spaces, a tab, or five newlines all display as one space.

Why This is Useful

• You can indent your code neatly without changing the output.
• You can break a long line in the source for readability.

What This Means Practically

• Pressing Enter in your editor does not create a line break on the page.
• To force a line break use <br>.
• To create space use CSS margin and padding, never repeated spaces.
codeExamples:
Hello World

Hello World

Hello World

Line one
Line two

intermediate.content:
Preserving Whitespace

• <pre> keeps every space and newline exactly as typed.
• It also renders in a monospace font by default.
• Perfect for code, ASCII art and poems.

The CSS white-space Property

• normal - collapse whitespace, wrap lines. The default.
• nowrap - collapse whitespace, never wrap. Text runs off the edge.
• pre - preserve whitespace, do not wrap.
• pre-wrap - preserve whitespace and wrap. Usually the best choice.
• pre-line - collapse spaces but keep newlines.

The Non-Breaking Space

•   is a space that does not collapse and does not break to a new line.
• Correct use: keeping "Rs. 500" or "Dr. Sharma" together.
• Wrong use: pressing it repeatedly to indent. Use CSS padding instead.

expert.content:
Whitespace Creates Text Nodes

• Every run of whitespace between tags becomes a text node in the DOM.
• So a formatted, indented list has text nodes between the <li> elements.
• This is why childNodes.length is larger than you expect.

The Safe Properties

• childNodes - includes whitespace text nodes. Usually not what you want.
• children - elements only. Use this.
• firstChild - may be a whitespace text node.
• firstElementChild - always an element. Use this.

The Layout Consequence

• Those same whitespace text nodes produce the gap between inline-block elements.
• Flexbox and grid containers discard whitespace-only children, which is why the gap disappears there.

beginner.content:
What is Character Encoding?

• Computers store text as numbers.
• An encoding is the agreed table saying which number means which character.
• If the browser guesses the wrong table, you see boxes and question marks instead of text.

Always Use UTF-8

• UTF-8 can represent every character in every language.
• English, Hindi, Marathi, Chinese, Arabic, emoji - all of it.
• It is the default and correct choice for every modern web page.

How to Declare It

• Put <meta charset="UTF-8"> as the first line inside <head>.
• It must appear within the first 1024 bytes of the file.
codeExamples:
English text works everywhere.

Hindi: नमस्ते दुनिया

Marathi: नमस्कार जग

Symbols: © ® ™ € £

Emoji: 🎓 📚 💻

intermediate.content:
Why It Must Come First

• The browser starts parsing immediately, guessing an encoding.
• If it finds a charset declaration later, it must throw away its work and re-parse the whole page.
• That wastes time and can briefly show broken characters.
• Within the first 1024 bytes is the rule; first line in head is the safe habit.

Two Places Encoding is Set

• The HTTP header Content-Type sent by the server.
• The meta charset tag in the document.
• The HTTP header wins if the two disagree.
• So if your page still shows broken characters despite a correct meta tag, check what the server is sending.

Also Save the File as UTF-8

• Declaring UTF-8 while saving the file as ANSI still produces broken text.
• The declaration and the actual file bytes must agree.
• In VS Code the current encoding is shown in the bottom status bar.
codeExamples: नमस्ते - renders correctly

expert.content:
ASCII, ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8

• ASCII - 128 characters, English only.
• ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) - 256 characters, Western European. The old web default.
• UTF-8 - all 1.1 million Unicode code points.

Why UTF-8 Won

• It is variable width: 1 byte for English, 2 to 4 bytes for other scripts.
• So an English page costs exactly the same as it did in ASCII.
• It is fully backward compatible with ASCII - the first 128 characters are identical bytes.
• UTF-16 has no such compatibility and wastes space on English.

Mojibake

• The garbled text you get when UTF-8 bytes are read as Latin-1.
• A classic sign: an accented character showing as two strange characters.
• The data is not lost - it is being decoded with the wrong table.

The Byte Order Mark

• Some editors add an invisible BOM at the start of the file.
• It can push the DOCTYPE out of first position and cause odd blank lines.
• Save as UTF-8 without BOM for web files.

beginner.content:
What are HTML Entities?

• Special codes used to display characters that HTML would otherwise misread.
• They start with & and end with ;.

Why They Are Needed

• If you type a < character, the browser thinks a tag is starting.
• So to display a less-than sign you must write <

The Five You Must Know

• < - less than, the < sign.
• > - greater than, the > sign.
• & - ampersand, the & sign.
• " - double quote.
•   - non-breaking space.

• © is ©, ® is ®, ™ is ™.
• &rupee; is not standard - use ₹ for the ₹ symbol.

• Decimal - © Works for every Unicode character.
• Hexadecimal - © Same, written in hex.

When You MUST Escape

• & - always, otherwise it may be read as the start of an entity.
• < - always in text content.
• " - inside a double-quoted attribute value.
• ' - inside a single-quoted attribute value.

The URL Trap

• A query string joins parameters with &.
• In an href you must write & to be valid HTML.
• Browsers usually forgive this, but validators do not, and some parameters can genuinely break.

expert.content:
Entities and Security - XSS

• This is the most important reason entities exist.
• If user input is inserted into a page without escaping, a user can submit a <script> tag that then runs.
• That is Cross-Site Scripting, one of the most common web vulnerabilities.

The Rule

• Never put untrusted input into innerHTML.
• Use textContent instead - it escapes automatically and cannot execute anything.
• On the server, escape < > & " and ' before rendering.

When You Still Need Entities With UTF-8

• For the five reserved characters - always.
• For invisible characters such as   and ­, where the source would otherwise be ambiguous.
• For characters your editor or font cannot display reliably.
• Everything else can be typed directly.

Heading Tags

• HTML gives you six levels of heading: h1 to h6.
• h1 is the most important, h6 the least.
• Headings create the outline of your page, like chapters in a book.

Key Rules

• Use one h1 per page - the main title.
• Do not skip levels: h1 then h2, never h1 then h4.
• Choose a heading by its meaning, not by how big it looks.
• If you only want bigger text, use CSS font-size instead.

Why the Outline Matters

• Screen reader users can list all headings and jump straight to a section.
• Around 70 percent of screen reader users navigate a page this way.
• A broken heading order makes that navigation useless.

SEO Impact

• Search engines use the h1 to understand the page topic.
• Headings give structure to long content, which improves ranking.
• Keyword-stuffed headings do the opposite.

Styling Without Breaking Meaning

• Never pick h4 because you want smaller text.
• Pick the correct level for the structure, then set the size in CSS.
• A visually hidden heading is a legitimate technique for labelling a section that has no visible title.

The Document Outline Algorithm - A Common Myth

• HTML5 once proposed that each <section> would restart heading levels automatically.
• So an h1 inside a section would behave like an h2.
• No browser ever implemented this, and it has been removed from the specification.
• Therefore an h1 inside a section is still an h1 to every screen reader.

What This Means in Practice

• You must still manage heading levels manually.
• Do not put multiple h1 elements in different sections and assume they nest.
• Component-based frameworks make this hard, because a component does not know its depth.
• The usual solution is to pass the heading level in as a prop.

Spacing Without Hacks

• Control the gap between paragraphs with margin on the p element.
• Use p + p to indent or space only the paragraphs that follow another paragraph.
• Never use empty paragraphs or   to push content down.

Common Mistakes

• Putting block elements such as lists inside a p. The browser closes the paragraph early.
• Using br to fake paragraphs, which removes the structure assistive technology relies on.

The <p> Tag

• Defines a paragraph of text.
• It is a block element, so it starts on a new line.
• Browsers add a default margin above and below.

Important Behaviour

• Multiple spaces and newlines inside a p collapse to one space.
• The closing </p> can be omitted, but always write it.
• A p can only contain inline content - never a div or another p.

The Nesting Trap

• A <div> inside a <p> is invalid.
• The browser silently closes the p before the div, then opens an empty p after it.
• You end up with three elements instead of one, and an unexpected empty paragraph.
• This is one of the most common causes of mysterious extra spacing.

Do Not Use <br> for Spacing

• Two <br> tags between paragraphs is a beginner habit.
• It creates no structure, so screen readers hear one long run-on paragraph.
• Use separate <p> elements and control the gap with margin.

Useful CSS for Paragraphs

• line-height around 1.5 to 1.7 for comfortable reading.
• max-width around 65 characters - long lines are hard to read.
• text-align: justify can create awkward rivers of space; left align usually reads better.

Where br Belongs

• Lines that are part of the content: poems, song lyrics and postal addresses.
• A forced break inside a short label or table cell where wrapping would look wrong.

Where It Does Not

• Spacing between blocks. Use paragraphs and margin instead.
• Separating form fields. Wrap each field in a div or use CSS grid or flex.
• Layout in general. Stacked br tags are fragile and read badly with a screen reader.

Useful Detail

• br is a void element, so it has no closing tag. Both <br> and <br /> are valid.
• The CSS white-space: pre-line keeps line breaks from the source text without any br tags.

When to Use It

• Poems and song lyrics.
• Any text where the line break is part of the content.

When NOT to Use It

Why Overusing br Hurts

• A screen reader pauses between paragraphs but not at a <br>.
• So text broken with br is announced as one continuous block.

Responsive Problem

• A br is a fixed break at a fixed point in the text.
• On a narrow phone that break may land in an ugly place.
• Real paragraphs re-wrap naturally at any width.

Better Alternatives

• white-space: pre-line in CSS keeps newlines from the source without any br tags.
• <wbr> marks an optional break point, used only if needed.
• Flexbox or grid for laying out separate items.

cite Tag vs cite Attribute - The Classic Confusion

• The <cite> tag is the visible title of a work.
• The cite attribute on blockquote or q is a hidden URL.
• They share a name but are completely unrelated. This is a favourite interview question.

An Important Restriction

• <cite> is for the title of the work, not for a person's name.
• So marking up an author's name with cite is incorrect according to the specification.
• Put the name as plain text, and only the work's title inside cite.

• Add a subtle background and padding so it stands out from body text.
• Do not use code for text that merely looks technical. It should be real code or a literal value.

Escaping

Escaping is Mandatory

Related Semantic Tags

• <samp> - program output.

Real-World Use

• Show the keys a reader should press: Ctrl + S to save or Ctrl + Shift + P for a command palette.

Nesting for Combinations

• Wrap each key in its own kbd and join them with a plus sign. This lets you style every key as a keycap.

Do Not Confuse

• kbd is what the user types. samp is what the computer prints. code is program source.

beginner.content:
The <kbd> Tag

• Marks keyboard input - keys the user should press.
• Rendered in monospace by default.
• Very useful in tutorials and documentation.

intermediate.content:
Nesting Rules for Key Combinations

• Each individual key gets its own <kbd>.
• The plus sign between them stays outside, as plain text.
• A whole combination may be wrapped in an outer <kbd> if you want to style it as a unit.

kbd Inside samp

• <kbd> inside <samp> means input echoed back by the system.
• <samp> inside <kbd> means the user selects a displayed menu item.
• These nested meanings are rarely needed but are asked about in interviews.

Styling as Real Keys

• A border, small radius and a bottom shadow make it look like a physical key.
codeExamples:
Press Ctrl + Shift + P.

Press Alt + F4 to close.

Choose File from the menu.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Sample output from a program: console messages, error text and results of a command.
• Typical in tutorials: show what the learner types with kbd, then what appears with samp.

Putting It Together

• Use pre with samp for multi-line output so the line breaks stay intact.
• Keep the output exact. If the real program prints three lines, the sample should too.

Common Mistakes

• Using samp for input the user types. That is kbd.
• Dropping the monospace look. Output looks wrong in a proportional font.
codeExamples:
Run java Hello and you will see:

Hello, JavaSchoolLab!
Done in 0.12s

If the file is missing, Java prints Error: Could not find or load main class Hello.

beginner.content:
The <samp> Tag

• Short for sample output.
• Marks text that a program or system produced.
• Error messages, console output, status text.
• Rendered in monospace by default.

The Easy Way to Remember

• kbd - what the user types in.
• samp - what the computer prints out.
codeExamples:
Type java Main and the program prints Hello, World!

If the file is missing you will see Error: file not found

Compiling...
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 2s
3 actionable tasks

intermediate.content:
Why Not Just Use a span?

• A span carries no meaning at all.
• samp tells a screen reader, a search engine and the next developer that this is machine output.
• It also gives you a clean styling hook with no extra class.

Typical Real Use

• Documentation showing a command and its result.
• Tutorials describing what the student should expect to see.
• Error message references in support articles.

Combining With pre

• For multi-line output, wrap samp in <pre> to keep the line structure.
codeExamples:
npm run build
vite v6.3.5 building for production...
1442 modules transformed.
built in 17.69s

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Variables in a formula or a code explanation: the area is w × h, where each letter is a var.
• Documentation for APIs uses it for placeholders such as /users/{id}.

Styling

• Browsers show italics. Keep this for maths-style text.
• Combine it with code or math markup when the surrounding text is code.

Common Mistakes

• Using var for emphasis. Use em for stress.
• Mixing it with the JavaScript keyword var. The HTML element has nothing to do with it.
codeExamples: The area of a rectangle is w × h, where w is the width and h is the height.

beginner.content:
The <var> Tag

• Marks a variable - in programming or in mathematics.
• Rendered in italic by default.
• Use it for a name that stands for a value.
codeExamples:
The area is l × w.

If x = 5 and y = 3, then x + y = 8.

Store the result in the total variable.

intermediate.content:
var Tag vs the JavaScript var Keyword

• Completely unrelated - they only share the name.
• The HTML <var> tag marks up a variable name in text.
• The JavaScript var keyword declares a variable in code.
• Do not use the <var> tag inside a code block just because the code contains variables - <code> already covers that.

Where var Really Shines

• Mathematical formulas in prose.
• Explaining an algorithm in words.
• Documentation describing a placeholder the reader must replace.

Styling

• The default italic can be confusing next to <em>, which is also italic.
• Many sites give var a monospace font instead, to group it visually with code.
codeExamples:
Simple interest is calculated as SI = (P × R × T) / 100, where P is the principal, R the rate and T the time in years.

Replace your-api-key with the key from your dashboard.

int total = price * quantity;

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Highlight the term a visitor searched for in a results page.
• Draw attention to a key phrase in a quotation, because it is relevant now and not because it is generally important.

mark or strong?

• strong says the text is important in its own right.
• mark says the text is relevant in the current context, such as a search match.

Styling and Accessibility

• The default yellow background is a good starting point. Keep enough contrast with the text colour.
• Do not rely on colour alone to communicate meaning.
codeExamples:
Search results for "flexbox"

Use flexbox to align items in one dimension.

The flexbox layout model replaced many float hacks.

beginner.content:
The <mark> Tag

• Highlights text, like a yellow marker pen.
• Default styling is black text on a yellow background.
• Introduced in HTML5.

Its Meaning

• Text marked because it is relevant right now, in the current context.
• The classic use is highlighting search terms in results.
codeExamples:
Search results for Spring:

Learn Spring Boot with real examples. Spring is a Java framework.

Please note the deadline is 30 September.

intermediate.content:
mark vs strong vs em

• mark - relevant in the current context. Its importance is temporary.
• strong - genuinely important, always.
• em - stressed when read aloud.
• A search term is a perfect mark. A safety warning is strong.

Accessibility Warning

• Most screen readers do not announce mark by default.
• So a purely visual highlight is invisible to those users.
• If the highlight carries essential meaning, add hidden text with ::before and ::after.

Contrast

• The default yellow with black text has good contrast.
• Custom highlight colours often fail contrast checks - always verify.
codeExamples:
Results: Learn Java today.

Warning: this action cannot be undone.

The exam covers chapters 4 to 7.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Side comments and fine print: copyright lines, legal notes, licences and disclaimers.
• Price footnotes such as *inclusive of taxes.

What It Is Not

• Not a way to make any text smaller. Use font-size in CSS for pure appearance.
• Not for important warnings. Small text is harder to read.

Readability

• Keep small text above about 12px, with good contrast.
• Avoid wrapping whole paragraphs in small.
codeExamples:
Course price: Rs. 999 (inclusive of all taxes)

© 2026 JavaSchoolLab. All rights reserved.

beginner.content:
The <small> Tag

• Represents side comments and small print.
• Copyright notices, legal disclaimers, terms and conditions.
• Renders one font size smaller by default.

Meaning, Not Size

• In HTML5 small is semantic, not presentational.
• It means "this is fine print", not simply "make this smaller".
• To only reduce size, use CSS font-size.
codeExamples:
Buy now for Rs. 4,999. Prices include GST. Terms and conditions apply.

© 2025 DHIPAN Software Technologies Private Limited. All rights reserved.

Just smaller text.

intermediate.content:
Nesting Compounds the Size

• Each nested <small> shrinks again, because the default is a relative size.
• Two levels deep the text quickly becomes unreadable.
• The specification advises against nesting more than once.

Accessibility Concern

• Small print is genuinely harder to read for users with low vision.
• Never go below roughly 12px, and keep good contrast.
• Legal text that a user must read should not be visually hidden away.

small vs sub and sup

• small is about the nature of the content.
• sub and sup are about mathematical or chemical position.
• They are not interchangeable.
codeExamples:
Level one level two unreadable

Total: Rs. 999 (inclusive of all taxes)

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• A warning that must not be missed: Do not share your password.
• A key term the reader needs to remember in a lesson.

Semantics Matter

• strong means strong importance, and screen readers can announce it differently.
• Nested strong tags raise the level of importance.
• For bold appearance with no extra meaning, use CSS font-weight or the b element.

Common Mistakes

• Making whole paragraphs strong, which makes nothing stand out.
• Using it to style headings. Use a heading element.
codeExamples: Warning: never share your password, even with support staff.

beginner.content:
The <strong> Tag

• Marks text of strong importance, seriousness or urgency.
• Displayed in bold by default.
• It is an inline element.

Use It For

• Warnings and safety notices.
• Critical instructions.
• Words a reader must not miss.
codeExamples:
Warning: deleting your account is permanent.

The deadline is 30 September. Late submissions are not accepted.

Before you begin, back up your database.

intermediate.content:
strong vs b - The Interview Question

• <strong> - carries meaning: this is important.
• <b> - purely visual: draw attention with bold, no added importance.
• Both look identical on screen. The difference is what they communicate.

How Screen Readers Treat Them

• Many screen readers change tone or emphasis for strong.
• <b> is announced as ordinary text.
• So a warning wrapped in <b> loses its urgency for a blind user.

The Rule of Thumb

• Ask: if this were read aloud, should it sound more urgent?
• Yes, use strong. No, use b or CSS font-weight.
• Nesting strong inside strong increases the level of importance further.
codeExamples:
Danger: high voltage.

You must submit before midnight.

The Spring Framework is widely used in enterprise Java.

Ingredients: rice, dal, ghee.

Important: do not share your password.

Purely a design choice.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Product names in a review, or the first words of a paragraph styled as a lead-in.
• Keywords in a summary where the bold has no extra importance.

b or strong?

• b draws attention without adding importance.
• strong marks real importance.
• When unsure, ask whether a screen reader should stress it. If yes, use strong.

Better Alternatives

• A CSS class such as .lead-in gives you full control and keeps the HTML meaningful.
codeExamples: Spring Boot makes it easy to build production-ready services, while Hibernate handles database mapping.

beginner.content:
The <b> Tag

• Makes text bold.
• Carries no extra importance - it is visual only.
• In HTML5 it means: draw attention, without implying urgency.

Legitimate Uses

• Keywords in a summary.
• Product names in a review.
• The opening words of an article.
• Names in a list of ingredients.
codeExamples:
Java is a popular programming language used for enterprise applications.

Ingredients: rice, lentils, turmeric.

Note: this is a stylistic lead-in, not a warning.

intermediate.content:
Is <b> Deprecated?

• No. This is a very common misconception in interviews.
• <b> and <i> were redefined in HTML5, not removed.
• They now have semantic definitions of their own - stylistically offset text.
• <font> and <center> were removed. <b> and <i> were not.

When to Prefer CSS Instead

• If the boldness is purely a design decision that might change, use a class.
• A class can be restyled site-wide; a <b> tag cannot.
• Use <b> when the offset is part of the content itself.

Choosing Between the Three

• Important content, must be noticed - strong.
• Content that is set apart by convention - b.
• Purely a visual style choice - CSS class.
codeExamples:
Do not refresh during payment.

We compared Redmi Note 13 with Realme 12.

This opening line is bold by design choice.

Buy the Spring Boot Course today.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Stress that changes the meaning of a sentence: I did not say that, versus I did not say that.
• Emphasis on a word the reader should read with a different tone.

Nesting

• Nested em elements add more emphasis, but use that rarely.

em or i?

• em is about stress emphasis.
• i is about an alternative voice, such as a foreign term, thought or ship name.
• Both look italic by default, but they mean different things.
codeExamples:
I did not say that.

I did not say that.

Cats are cute. Dogs are really cute.

beginner.content:
The <em> Tag

• Marks emphasis - a word you would stress when speaking.
• Displayed in italic by default.
• Short for emphasis.

Emphasis Changes Meaning

• "I never said she stole the money" has a different meaning depending on which word you stress.
• <em> marks which word carries that stress.
codeExamples:
I never said she took it. (someone else did)

I never said she took it. (someone else took it)

I never said she took it. (she borrowed it)

Please submit the form before Friday.

intermediate.content:
em vs i

• <em> - stress emphasis. Changes how the sentence is spoken.
• <i> - italic for a different reason: a foreign phrase, a technical term, a thought, a ship's name.
• Both render italic; only em changes the meaning.

Screen Reader Behaviour

• Some screen readers alter pitch or pace for em.
• <i> is read normally.
• So the choice genuinely affects how the sentence is heard.

Nesting

• <em> inside <em> increases the degree of emphasis.
• Browsers often flip back to upright text for the inner one, which is correct typography.
codeExamples:
You must submit it today, not tomorrow.

The concept of carpe diem means seize the day.

A closure is a function that remembers its scope.

She wondered, will this even work?

Please do not refresh this page.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Foreign words and technical terms: the Latin phrase in situ.
• Thoughts of a character in fiction and titles of ships.
• Icon fonts, where an empty i is a common (though debated) hook.

Do Not Use It For

• Stress emphasis, which belongs to em.
• Titles of works, which belong to cite.

Accessibility Note

• An empty i used as an icon should be hidden from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true", and the button needs real text.
codeExamples:
The bug was fixed in situ, without restarting the server.

This will never work, she thought.

beginner.content:
The <i> Tag

• Displays text in italic.
• In HTML5 it means text in an alternate voice or mood.
• It does not add spoken emphasis - that is <em>.

Correct Uses

• Foreign words and phrases.
• Technical terms being introduced.
• Thoughts of a character.
• Names of ships, and taxonomic names.
• Icon fonts, by long-standing convention.
codeExamples:
The Latin phrase et cetera means and so on.

In Java, a lambda expression is an anonymous function.

He thought, this cannot be happening.

The Titanic sank in 1912.

Species: Panthera tigris

intermediate.content:
Always Add lang to Foreign Text

• Italic alone does not tell a screen reader the language has changed.
• Without lang, a French phrase is pronounced with English rules and becomes unintelligible.
• <i lang="fr"> solves this completely.

The Icon Font Convention

• Font Awesome and Bootstrap use <i> for icons.
• This is convention, not semantics - the tag was simply short.
• A decorative icon must have aria-hidden="true", or a screen reader announces nothing useful.
• A meaningful icon needs an accessible label.

Modern Alternative

• <span> with a class is arguably cleaner for icons.
• But <i> is so established that both are accepted.
codeExamples:
She said bonjour as she entered.

The term namaste is a respectful greeting.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Mark text with an unarticulated annotation, such as a misspelled word flagged by a spell checker.
• Chinese proper name marks.

The Big Warning

• Readers associate underline with links. Underlined plain text looks clickable and confuses people.
• For a simple style change, use text-decoration in CSS instead.

Styling

• Use text-decoration-style: wavy and a colour to mimic a spelling error mark.
codeExamples: This sentance has a mispelled word.

beginner.content:
The <u> Tag

• Draws an underline under text.
• In HTML5 it means an unarticulated annotation.
• The main real use is marking a spelling mistake, the way a word processor does.

Use It Carefully

• On the web, underlined text looks like a link.
• Users will try to click it and be confused when nothing happens.
• For this reason <u> is rarely the right choice.
codeExamples:
The word recieve is misspelled. It should be receive.

Names are sometimes marked this way.

intermediate.content:
Better Alternatives

• For emphasis - use <em> or <strong>.
• For a spelling error - <u> with a wavy red underline in CSS.
• For any decorative underline - text-decoration in CSS on the element you actually mean.

The Modern text-decoration Properties

• text-decoration-line - underline, overline, line-through.
• text-decoration-style - solid, double, dotted, dashed, wavy.
• text-decoration-color - any colour.
• text-decoration-thickness - the line weight.
• text-underline-offset - distance from the text.

Distinguishing From Links

• If you must underline non-link text, use a different colour or a dotted style.
• Conversely, never remove the underline from links in body text - it is the main visual cue that they are clickable.
codeExamples:
The word recieve is misspelled.

This phrase is annotated, not clickable.

This is a real link.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Old prices on a sale: Rs. 1999 Rs. 999.
• A list item that is no longer accurate or relevant, such as a sold-out size.

s or del?

• s shows content that is no longer correct or relevant.
• del shows content that was removed from a document, usually in an edit history.

Accessibility

• Screen readers often ignore the strike. Add text such as was or visually hidden labels for important prices.
codeExamples:
Rs. 1999 Rs. 999

Size M sold out

beginner.content:
The <s> Tag

• Draws a line through the text.
• Means content that is no longer accurate or relevant.
• The classic use is showing an old price next to a new one.

s vs del

• <s> - no longer correct, but not an edit to the document.
• <del> - content that was actually removed in an edit.
codeExamples:
Price: Rs. 4,999 Rs. 2,999

Offer valid until 30 August Offer extended to 30 September.

Only 5 seats left Sold out.

intermediate.content:
The Accessibility Gap

• Most screen readers do not announce the strikethrough.
• So a blind user hears "Price: 4,999 rupees 2,999 rupees" and hears two prices with no indication that one is void.
• This is a genuine problem on e-commerce sites.

The Fix

• Add visually hidden text that states the meaning.
• Or use ::before and ::after with clipped positioning.
• Screen reader users then hear "was 4,999 rupees, now 2,999 rupees".

The Old <strike> Tag

• <strike> was removed in HTML5.
• Use <s> for stale content or <del> for a deletion.
codeExamples:
Price: Rs. 4,999 Rs. 2,999

Original price: Rs. 4,999 Discounted price: Rs. 2,999

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Show a revision: text that was removed from a document, usually together with ins for what replaced it.
• Change logs, legal drafts and edited articles.

Attributes

• cite points to a page that explains the change.
• datetime records when the deletion was made in a machine readable format.

Common Mistakes

• Using del for a price that was reduced. That is s.
• Forgetting to keep a visual difference. Browsers draw a line through the text, so do not turn that off.
codeExamples: The meeting is on Monday Tuesday at 10 AM.

beginner.content:
The <del> Tag

• Marks text that has been deleted from the document.
• Shown with a line through it.
• Almost always used together with <ins> for the replacement.

Its Attributes

• cite - URL explaining why the change was made.
• datetime - when the deletion happened.
codeExamples:
The meeting is on Monday Tuesday.

Course fee: Rs. 9,999 Rs. 6,999

Status: Draft Published

intermediate.content:
del vs s - The Precise Difference

• <del> - an edit. This text was removed from the document at some point.
• <s> - the content is simply no longer accurate, with no editing history implied.
• A discounted price is <s>. A corrected sentence in a published article is <del>.

Block or Inline

• <del> is unusual - it can wrap either inline text or entire blocks.
• So you may delete a whole paragraph or a single word with the same tag.

The datetime Format

• Must be a valid ISO 8601 string: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm.
• Not displayed by default, but readable by tools building a change history.
codeExamples:
Submit by Friday Monday.

This whole paragraph was removed from the article.

This paragraph replaced it.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Show text added during an edit, shown beside the del text it replaced.
• Document history views, contract markups and wiki changes.

Attributes

• datetime gives the date of the insertion.
• cite links to an explanation.

Styling

• Browsers underline ins by default. Add a soft green background so insertions are easy to find.
• Because both ins and del are inline, wrap whole blocks of changes in a block element when needed.
codeExamples: The course covers HTML4 HTML5 and CSS.

beginner.content:
The <ins> Tag

• Marks text that has been inserted into the document.
• Underlined by default.
• The natural partner of <del>.

Attributes

• cite - a URL explaining the change.
• datetime - when the insertion was made.
codeExamples:
Venue: Room 101 Room 205

The syllabus now also covers Spring Security.

intermediate.content:
The Underline Problem

• <ins> is underlined by default, so it looks exactly like a link.
• Almost every real site restyles it - usually a green background instead.
• This is the same confusion problem that affects <u>.

Accessibility

• Like del and s, insertions are usually not announced by screen readers.
• For a genuine change log, add visually hidden labels such as "inserted" and "deleted".
• Do not rely on colour alone either - a red and green diff is invisible to colour-blind users.

Where This Really Gets Used

• Wikis and documentation change history.
• Legal documents showing amendments.
• Terms and conditions updates.
codeExamples:
Amendment to the syllabus

The course covers deleted: Struts inserted: Spring Boot.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Chemical formulas: H2O and CO2.
• Mathematical indices such as x1 and x2.
• Footnote markers when the style requires lowered text.

Layout Tip

• sub and sup can change line spacing and make a line taller. Set line-height: 0 on them to keep the lines even.

When Not to Use

• Do not use sub just to push text lower for design. Use CSS vertical-align for that.
codeExamples:
Water is H2O and carbon dioxide is CO2.

The sequence is x1, x2, x3.

beginner.content:
The <sub> Tag

• Displays text below the normal baseline, in a smaller size.
• Short for subscript.

Where It Is Used

• Chemical formulas - H2O, CO2.
• Mathematical indices - x1, an.
• Footnote markers in some styles.
codeExamples:
Water is H2O.

Carbon dioxide is CO2.

Glucose: C6H12O6

The sequence is x1, x2, x3.

intermediate.content:
Semantics, Not Styling

• Only use sub when lowering the text changes the meaning.
• H2O and H2O mean different things - the subscript is essential.
• If you only want smaller, lower text for design, use CSS.

The Line-Height Problem

• sub and sup use vertical-align, which can increase the line height of that line.
• In a paragraph this makes one line taller than the rest, which looks uneven.
• The standard fix sets font-size and line-height to zero-effect values and positions with relative offsets.

Accessibility

• Screen readers usually read the characters without indicating the subscript.
• For critical formulas, consider MathML or an aria-label.
codeExamples:
Without the fix, the line containing H2O would be taller than its neighbours, making the paragraph look uneven.

With the fix, H2SO4 sits neatly on the same line height as ordinary text.

H2SO4

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Powers and exponents: x2 and 106.
• Ordinal suffixes: 1st, 2nd.
• Footnote references that link to a note at the bottom.

Footnotes Done Right

• Wrap the number in a link that points to the note id, and give the note a link back.
• Screen reader users then jump to and from the footnote easily.

Tip

• Set line-height: 0 on sup so it does not stretch the line.
codeExamples:
The area is r2 times pi.

He finished 1st in the contest.[1]

1. Results announced on 19 October. Back

beginner.content:
The <sup> Tag

• Displays text above the normal baseline, in a smaller size.
• Short for superscript.

Where It Is Used

• Exponents - x2, 106.
• Ordinal suffixes - 1st, 2nd.
• Footnote references.
• Trademark and registered symbols.
codeExamples:
The area of a square is a2.

E = mc2

This is the 1st lesson and that was the 2nd.

See the reference[1] for details.

JavaSchoolLab™

intermediate.content:
Building Real Footnotes

• A superscript number alone is not a footnote - it is just small text.
• Wrap it in a link that jumps to the note, and link back again.
• Add aria-label so a screen reader announces "footnote 1" rather than just "1".

Trademark Symbols

• ™ and ® already contain their raised appearance.
• Wrapping them in sup raises them twice, which looks wrong.
• Use the entity on its own.

Same Line-Height Caution

• sup stretches the line height exactly as sub does.
• Apply the same CSS fix.
codeExamples:
Spring Boot simplifies configuration1 and speeds up development2.

Notes

  1. Auto-configuration removes most XML. back
  2. Starters bundle common dependencies. back

Brand™

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Lists of user generated names where some may be written right-to-left, such as Arabic or Hebrew.
• Search results, comments and leaderboards.

The Problem It Solves

• Without isolation, right-to-left text can reorder the punctuation and numbers next to it, producing a confusing line.
• bdi isolates the name, so the surrounding text stays in order.

Compare

• bdi lets the browser detect the direction.
• bdo forces a direction you choose.
codeExamples:
• User Alice: 12 points
  • User إيان: 7 points
  • User Bob: 5 points

beginner.content:
The <bdi> Tag

• Bi-Directional Isolate.
• Keeps a piece of text from affecting the direction of the text around it.
• Added in HTML5.

When You Need It

• When you display user-generated names that might be in Arabic, Hebrew or Urdu.
• Without bdi, a right-to-left name can scramble the layout of your entire sentence.
codeExamples:
Leaderboard

  • Pankaj - 90 points
  • Ramchandra - 85 points
  • مستخدم - 80 points

intermediate.content:
Why the Scrambling Happens

• Browsers use the Unicode bidirectional algorithm to decide display order.
• A strongly right-to-left character can pull neighbouring neutral characters - spaces, dashes, digits - into its own direction.
• So "- 80 points" can jump to the wrong side of the name.

bdi vs bdo

• bdi - isolates. It says: whatever direction this text is, do not let it affect the rest.
• bdo - overrides. It says: force this text to render in the direction I specify.
• bdi is automatic and safe; bdo is manual and forceful.

The Practical Rule

• Wrap every piece of user-supplied text in bdi when it appears next to your own text.
• Usernames, comment authors, search terms, file names.
• It costs nothing when the text is left-to-right.
codeExamples:
Without bdi - order can break

  • مستخدم - 80 points

With bdi - the name is isolated

  • مستخدم - 80 points

bdo forces a direction (different purpose)

This English text is forced right to left

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Force a direction when the text is a code or a label that must read in a fixed order.
• Demos and tests for right-to-left layouts.

How It Works

• The required dir attribute is ltr or rtl.
• It overrides the default Unicode bidirectional algorithm for the text inside.

Handle with Care

• Reversed real text is hard to read. Use it sparingly, and never for body content.
• For user supplied text, prefer bdi so the browser decides.
codeExamples:
Normal: JavaSchoolLab

Forced right to left: JavaSchoolLab

beginner.content:
The <bdo> Tag

• Bi-Directional Override.
• Forces text to display in a chosen direction.
• The dir attribute is required.

The dir Values

• dir="ltr" - left to right.
• dir="rtl" - right to left.
codeExamples:
Normal: This text reads left to right.

This text is forced right to left.

This stays left to right.

intermediate.content:
Override Means Override

• bdo does not ask the bidirectional algorithm - it replaces it.
• Every character inside is laid out in the direction you specify, regardless of its natural direction.
• That is powerful and easy to misuse.

Legitimate Uses

• Demonstrating or teaching text direction, as on this page.
• Displaying text where the stored order is known to be wrong and must be corrected.
• Certain database or legacy-system outputs.

What NOT to Do

• Do not use bdo to reverse text as a visual trick - CSS transform is the right tool.
• Do not wrap real Arabic or Hebrew content in bdo. The browser already handles it correctly, and overriding breaks it.
• For user content, you almost always want bdi instead.

The CSS Equivalent

• unicode-bidi: bidi-override together with direction does the same job in CSS.
codeExamples:
Forced RTL: abcdef

Same effect via CSS

مرحبا بالعالم

Mirrored by CSS, not by bdo

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Long URLs, file paths and identifiers inside narrow columns or table cells.
• Mobile layouts where a long word would force sideways scrolling.

How It Works

• wbr marks a place where the browser may break the line if it needs to.
• It adds no visible character and does not force a break, unlike br.

CSS Alternatives

• overflow-wrap: anywhere breaks long strings automatically with no markup.
• hyphens: auto adds hyphens in natural language text.
• Use wbr when you want control over where the break happens.
codeExamples: https://example.com/courses/html-and-css/text-elements

beginner.content:
The <wbr> Tag

• Word Break opportunity.
• Marks a place where the browser may break a long word if it needs to.
• It is a void element.

How It Differs From br

• <br> - always breaks the line.
• <wbr> - breaks only if necessary. If the word fits, nothing happens.

intermediate.content:
The Problem It Solves

• A long unbroken string - a URL, a hash, a file path - overflows its container.
• That causes horizontal scrolling on mobile and breaks the layout.
• wbr lets you choose sensible break points instead of leaving it to chance.

The CSS Alternatives

• overflow-wrap: break-word - breaks only when the word would overflow. Usually the best general rule.
• word-break: break-all - breaks anywhere, even mid-syllable. Often ugly.
• hyphens: auto - adds real hyphens, but needs a lang attribute.

When wbr Still Wins

• CSS breaks wherever it must; wbr breaks where you decide is readable.
• Breaking a URL after each slash is far more readable than breaking mid-word.
• wbr adds no visible character - unlike a hyphen, nothing is added to the text.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• The <a> tag is called the anchor element.
• It creates a hyperlink - clickable text or an image that takes the user somewhere else.
• It is an inline element and needs both an opening and a closing tag.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To connect one page to another page.
• To let a user move around a website without typing URLs.
• Links are what turn separate documents into a connected web.

3. Need of This Topic

• Without links, every page would be an island.
• A user would have to type the full address of every page manually.
• Search engines discover new pages by following links - no links means no indexing.
codeExamples: About Us View Courses Contact Us

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Easy navigation - one click moves the user anywhere.
• SEO benefit - search engines follow links to find and rank pages.
• Works everywhere - no JavaScript required at all.
• Keyboard accessible for free - Tab focuses it, Enter activates it.
• Shareable - the user can right-click and copy the address.
• Browser history works - Back and Forward behave correctly.

5. Disadvantages

• Broken links - if the target page is deleted, the user gets a 404 error.
• Security risk - target="_blank" without rel="noopener" can be exploited.
• Vague text - "click here" tells a screen reader user nothing.
• Page reload - a normal link reloads the whole page, which feels slower than an app.
• Maintenance cost - moving a file means fixing every link that pointed at it.
codeExamples: Fully keyboard accessible Read the Spring Boot tutorial Safe

beginner.content:
6. Real Time Examples

• Amazon - every product image and title is an anchor to the product page.
• Wikipedia - the blue words inside articles are anchors; this is how the whole encyclopedia connects.
• Any website menu - Home, About, Contact are all anchor tags.
• Google search results - each blue heading is an anchor to that website.
• JavaSchoolLab - the course list in the sidebar is a set of anchors.
codeExamples:
Home Courses About Contact

Spring Boot Course

Rs. 2,999

Java is an object oriented language. Learn about inheritance and polymorphism next.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• In the DOM the anchor is an HTMLAnchorElement.
• It exposes the URL in parts: protocol, hostname, port, pathname, search, hash.
• An anchor without href is only a placeholder - it is not focusable and not a link.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To act as the browser's built-in navigation control, complete with history, focus and context menu.
• To give assistive technology a recognisable link role automatically.

3. Need (Advanced)

• Developers often replace links with div plus onclick, and lose every built-in behaviour.
• You then have to rebuild focus, Enter key handling, middle-click, Ctrl+click and the context menu by hand - and almost nobody does it correctly.
• Knowing what the anchor gives you for free is what prevents that mistake.
codeExamples:

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Free behaviours you would otherwise hand-code: focus ring, Enter activation, middle-click to open in a new tab, Ctrl+click, right-click menu, drag to bookmark bar, status bar preview.
• Announced correctly - screen readers can list every link on the page.
• Prefetchable - browsers can pre-load a likely next page.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Reverse tabnabbing - a target="_blank" link lets the new page rewrite your original tab through window.opener. Modern browsers default to noopener, but older ones do not.
• Referrer leakage - the destination sees the full URL you came from, which may contain private data.
• Link rot - external sites disappear over time.
• Full page reload - which is why single page apps intercept clicks.
• href="#" jumps to the top of the page, a classic annoyance.
codeExamples: Safe No referrer sent Dashboard

expert.content:
6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Gmail - every external link in an email gets rel="noopener noreferrer" added automatically, to protect the mailbox tab.
• News websites - use rel="nofollow" on advertiser links so their SEO ranking is not passed on.
• React and Angular apps - the Link component renders a real <a> and intercepts the click, so the URL is still copyable and Ctrl+click still opens a new tab.
• Banking sites - use rel="noreferrer" so the session URL never leaks to third parties.
• E-commerce - preloads the product page on hover, so the click feels instant.
