expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• height is a presentational hint, easily overridden by CSS, but it survives long enough to shape the first layout.
• Together with width it fills the internal aspect-ratio property, written as width divided by height.
• img.height gives the current layout height, img.naturalHeight gives the intrinsic pixel height of the decoded file.
• With object-fit a fixed height crops rather than distorts, which is how catalogue tiles keep a uniform grid.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To eliminate Cumulative Layout Shift from images, ads and embeds in server rendered pages.
• To make virtualized lists and infinite scroll predictable, since the row height is known before paint.
• To keep art directed crops consistent by pairing declared height with object-fit and object-position.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• A CLS above 0.1 fails Core Web Vitals, and images without height are the usual cause.
• Print stylesheets for marksheets and invoices need deterministic image heights.
• Interview question: how do width and height create an implicit aspect ratio, and what breaks it.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Deterministic first paint. Server rendered HTML lays out correctly before any script runs.
• Build time automation. Image plugins read the file header and inject height, so it is never wrong.
• Better scrolling. Known heights avoid repeated relayout in long product lists.
• Composable with object-fit for grids that must look uniform even with mixed source ratios.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Stale after a redesign. New artwork with a different ratio silently distorts or mis reserves the box.
• Conflicts with srcset variants that do not share one ratio.
• Cropping loses content. object-fit cover can cut a face or a price tag if object-position is not tuned.
• CSS height in percent needs a sized parent, so a naive fix collapses the image to zero height.
• No payload benefit. Height never reduces bytes, only srcset and a CDN do that.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Myntra and Ajio: portrait product photos are cropped to a fixed tile height with object-position tuned so the garment stays centred.
• Flipkart home page: the banner carousel declares a single ratio, so rotating slides never move the category row below.
• News portals: both ad slots and article images reserve height, which is the standard fix for a poor CLS score.
• Next.js and Astro image components: read the image header at build time and emit width and height into the HTML automatically.
• Invoice and marksheet PDFs: generated from HTML where every logo and photo has a fixed height, so pagination is stable.
• GitHub timeline: avatars are fixed at 40 by 40, keeping thousands of scrolled rows at a constant height.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• <figure> is a container for content that is referred to from the main text, such as a photo, a chart, a code block or a table.
• It is a semantic tag. It tells the browser and the screen reader that this content is one unit.
• It usually holds an image plus a <figcaption> that describes it.
• The figure can be moved to another place on the page without breaking the meaning of the article.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To group a picture with its caption so they always travel together.
• To make articles and documentation easier to read and to style.
• To give screen readers a clear boundary, so the user knows where the figure starts and ends.

3. Need of This Topic

• A plain <div> carries no meaning, while <figure> tells everyone what the block is.
• Blogs, news sites, Wikipedia and documentation all use this pattern.
• Interviewers ask the difference between <figure> and a normal <div>.
codeExamples: As shown above, the metro connects Hinjewadi to Shivajinagar.

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Meaningful. Search engines and screen readers understand the block.
• Self contained. You can move the figure anywhere without losing the caption.
• Easy to style. One CSS rule for figure styles every picture with its caption.
• Works with any content. Images, videos, code and tables can all sit inside.

5. Disadvantages

• Extra markup. For a simple decorative logo it is unnecessary.
• Default margin. Browsers add left and right margin to figure, which surprises beginners.
• Misuse. Students wrap every image in a figure even when there is no caption and no reference from the text.
• Only one figcaption is allowed, so two separate captions are not possible.

6. Real Time Examples

• Wikipedia: every article photo sits in a figure with a caption below it.
• News websites: a photo with the photographer credit written in the caption.
• College portal: a lab experiment diagram with a caption naming the experiment number.
• Documentation sites: a screenshot with a caption like Figure 2, the login screen.
• GitHub README: an architecture diagram with a caption explaining the flow.
• Flipkart blog: a product photo with a caption showing the price in rupees.
codeExamples: Pune City Report

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <figure> maps to the ARIA role figure. When it has a figcaption, the caption becomes the accessible name of the whole group.
• The content model is flow content with an optional figcaption as the first or last child, and at most one.
• It is a sectioning neutral element, so headings inside it do not create a new outline section.
• It pairs naturally with schema.org ImageObject markup for rich results in search.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To give complex images an accessible grouping plus a programmatic caption, which alt alone cannot express.
• To build reusable content components in CMS driven sites, where editors insert a figure block.
• To keep print and PDF pipelines correct, since a figure and its caption should not break across pages.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Accessibility audits distinguish an image with alt from a properly labelled figure group.
• Content pipelines like markdown to HTML emit figures, so developers must style and validate them.
• Interview question: when does figcaption replace alt, and when must both exist.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Programmatic caption. Assistive technology announces the group with its caption, which is stronger than alt alone.
• Print safe. break-inside avoid on a figure keeps the picture and caption on the same page in generated PDFs.
• Component friendly. CMS blocks, MDX components and markdown pipelines map cleanly to a figure.
• SEO ready. Search engines associate the caption text with the image, improving image search relevance.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Redundant announcements. If alt repeats the caption word for word, screen reader users hear the same sentence twice.
• Wrapper inflation. Automatically wrapping every markdown image in a figure creates empty captions across the site.
• Layout traps. The default margin and the block display often need resetting in a design system.
• Not a section. A heading inside a figure does not appear in the document outline, which surprises teams.
• Nested figures are legal but confusing for assistive technology and are best avoided.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Wikipedia thumbnails: a figure holds the image, a magnify link and the caption, and the whole group is announced as one unit.
• Technical documentation: MDX or markdown pipelines auto convert an image with a title into a figure with a numbered caption.
• Newsrooms: the CMS figure block stores photographer credit, licence and caption as separate fields, then renders one figure.
• Invoice and report PDFs: break-inside avoid on figures keeps a chart together with its caption on one printed page.
• Research portals: figures carry a stable id so a paper can link directly to Figure 3.
• E commerce blogs: figures include schema.org ImageObject data so the photo can appear as a rich result in Google.
codeExamples: See Figure 3 for the flooding on Marine Drive.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

<figcaption> is the caption or title of a <figure>.
• It must be written inside a figure, as the first child or the last child.
• Only one figcaption is allowed inside one figure.
• It is normal readable text on the page, unlike alt which is only for screen readers and broken images.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To explain the picture to every user, not only to blind users.
• To write the photo credit, the source or the date under a news photo.
• To number figures in a report, for example Figure 2, Circuit diagram.

3. Need of This Topic

• A picture without a caption often confuses the reader, especially charts and diagrams.
• News, Wikipedia and college documents all need visible captions.
• Interviewers ask the difference between alt text and figcaption.

4. Advantages

• Visible to everyone. Sighted users also get the explanation, unlike alt.
• Real HTML text. It can be searched, copied, translated and styled.
• Links allowed. A caption can hold a link to the source or to a full report.
• Accessible grouping. It names the whole figure for a screen reader.

5. Disadvantages

• Takes space. On a small mobile screen a long caption pushes content down.
• Only one per figure. Credit and caption must be combined into a single element.
• Duplication. Copying the caption into alt makes screen readers repeat the same sentence.
• Wrong placement in the middle of a figure is invalid HTML and is easy to do by mistake.

6. Real Time Examples

• Wikipedia: the caption under a photo names the person, place and year.
• News sites: caption plus photographer credit under every article photo.
• College lab manual: Figure 2, circuit diagram for experiment 2.
• Documentation: a screenshot with a caption telling the user what to click.
• GitHub README: a diagram with a caption explaining the request flow.
• Recipe blogs: a dish photo with a caption giving the cooking time.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• When present, figcaption provides the accessible name of the figure element in the accessibility tree.
• It is defined as flow content, so it can hold links, emphasis, lists and even a table.
• It must be the first or last child of the figure. Any other position is a content model error that validators flag.
• The naming order matters: aria-label or aria-labelledby on the figure will override the figcaption.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To give complex images such as charts a visible long description, which alt cannot carry well.
• To store editorial metadata such as credit, licence and source in structured, styleable markup.
• To support numbered cross references in generated documentation and print output.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Accessibility guidance for data images requires both a short alt and a longer visible explanation.
• CMS and markdown pipelines generate captions automatically, so validation is needed to avoid invalid markup.
• Interview question: how does figcaption interact with alt, aria-labelledby and aria-describedby.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Dual purpose. One element serves both the visual reader and the accessibility tree.
• Rich content allowed. Links, lists and a full data table can live inside the caption for complex charts.
• Structured metadata. Works cleanly with schema.org caption and creditText properties.
• Print and PDF ready. Numbered captions plus break-inside avoid give professional documents.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Verbose announcements. A very long caption is read as the figure name, which is tiring for screen reader users.
• Duplicate content risk. Repeating the caption in alt doubles the announcement.
• Auto generated empty captions from a CMS pollute the page and confuse audits.
• Override confusion. aria-labelledby on the figure quietly replaces the caption as the name.
• Layout cost. Long captions in a tight grid break the visual rhythm on mobile.
codeExamples: West led every quarter, peaking at Rs 7.9 crore in Q4. South grew fastest, up 41 percent.

expert.content:
6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Wikipedia: captions carry inline links to related articles, licences and the file page, all inside one figcaption.
• Newsroom CMS: caption, credit and licence are separate database fields rendered into a single caption with spans.
• Documentation builds: a build step numbers every caption and generates a list of figures, exactly like a printed book.
• Financial reports: the chart figure caption contains the full data table so the numbers are machine readable.
• Research portals: figure ids plus captions let a paper deep link to Figure 3 with a working anchor.
• Accessibility audits at banks: captions are checked to make sure they add information rather than repeat alt text.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• Responsive images means showing a picture that fits the user screen and downloads only the bytes that are needed.
• A mobile phone should get a small file and a desktop should get a big file, from the same HTML.
• The main tools are CSS max-width, the srcset and sizes attributes, and the <picture> element.
• The browser picks the best file. We only give it the choices and the rules.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To save mobile data for users on 3G and 4G in small towns.
• To stop a big desktop banner from overflowing a phone screen.
• To make pages open fast, which keeps shoppers on Flipkart or Amazon instead of leaving.

3. Need of This Topic

• In India most traffic is from mobile, so a 2 MB desktop photo is a real cost to the user.
• Slow pages lose sales and rank lower on Google.
• It is a standard interview topic for any front end job.
codeExamples: Price: Rs 14999

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Saves data. A phone may download 60 KB instead of 900 KB.
• Faster pages. Less data means the picture appears sooner.
• Sharper on big screens. Retina and 4K screens get a higher resolution file.
• One HTML for all devices. No separate mobile website is needed.
• Better SEO. Google rewards fast mobile pages.

5. Disadvantages

• More files to make. Every picture must be exported in three or four sizes.
• Harder syntax. srcset and sizes confuse beginners, and a wrong sizes value can make things worse.
• Storage and build time grow when a catalogue has lakhs of products.
• Testing effort. You must check the result on many screen widths.
• Cache spread. Many variants mean the CDN cache is split across files.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart: the same product card sends a 200 pixel file to a phone and an 800 pixel file to a desktop.
• Amazon: the home banner uses a different crop on mobile so the offer text stays readable.
• Wikipedia: thumbnails are generated at the exact needed width by the image server.
• College portal: the campus photo on the home page loads small on a phone during admission rush.
• News apps: article photos are served in webp at three widths to save data on 4G.
• GitHub: avatars use a size parameter so a 40 pixel avatar never downloads a 460 pixel file.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• Responsive images cover two different problems. Resolution switching serves the same picture at different pixel sizes using srcset with w descriptors plus sizes. Art direction serves a different crop or a different format using <picture> with media or type.
• The browser selects a candidate using the device pixel ratio and the computed value from sizes, and it may keep a larger cached variant instead of downloading a smaller one.
• Selection happens in the preload scanner, before CSS is applied, which is why sizes must be written by hand and cannot be inferred from the layout.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To reduce the LCP image transfer size, which is usually the single biggest performance win on an e commerce page.
• To adopt modern formats such as webp and avif safely, with a jpeg fallback.
• To feed an image CDN pipeline where each candidate is a query on the same master file.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Core Web Vitals are measured on real Indian 4G devices, where image bytes dominate.
• A wrong sizes value silently causes over downloading, and no error is ever shown.
• Interview question: what is the difference between w descriptors with sizes and x descriptors.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Large transfer savings. Correct sizes plus webp often cuts image bytes by 60 to 80 percent.
• Native and free. No JavaScript library and no extra runtime cost.
• Preload scanner friendly. The right file starts downloading before CSS is parsed.
• Format future proofing. New formats can be added as extra source elements without touching the fallback.
• CDN friendly. Candidates map to a fixed, cacheable set of widths.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• sizes drifts from CSS. A layout change silently breaks the selection and nobody notices.
• Cache split. Too many widths lower the CDN hit rate and raise origin cost.
• Browser may over select. A cached larger variant is reused, so measured savings vary.
• Art direction is verbose. Each breakpoint and format combination adds another source element.
• Testing burden. You need device pixel ratio and width matrices in automated tests.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Flipkart and Myntra: a fixed ladder of widths such as 200, 400 and 800 keeps the CDN hit rate high while still serving phones a small file.
• Amazon: art direction changes the hero crop on mobile so the offer text is never cut, which plain resolution switching cannot do.
• Wikipedia: the thumbnail service generates any requested width once, then caches it globally for years.
• News apps: avif first with a webp and jpeg fallback chain, giving about 30 percent smaller files than webp alone.
• Next.js image component: generates srcset and sizes automatically from a layout prop, which is exactly this topic packaged as a component.
• Performance budgets in CI: a Lighthouse check fails the build when image transfer on the product page crosses the agreed KB limit.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• <picture> is a wrapper that gives the browser several choices of an image and lets it pick one.
• Inside it we write one or more <source> tags and exactly one <img> at the end.
• The browser checks each source from top to bottom and uses the first one that matches.
• If no source matches, or the browser is very old, the <img> is used. So the <img> is compulsory.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To show a different crop of the picture on mobile and on desktop. This is called art direction.
• To offer a modern format like webp, with jpg as a backup for old browsers.
• To change the picture in dark mode or for printing.

3. Need of This Topic

• A wide desktop banner looks tiny and unreadable when squeezed into a phone screen.
• srcset alone can change the size but it cannot change the crop, only <picture> can.
• It is a common interview question, picture versus srcset.

4. Advantages

• Art direction. A tall crop on mobile and a wide crop on desktop, from one HTML.
• Safe format upgrade. New formats can be used without breaking old browsers.
• No JavaScript needed. Everything is handled by the browser.
• Full control. You decide exactly which file is used at which screen width.

5. Disadvantages

• Long markup. Four sources plus an img is a lot of code for one picture.
• More files. Each crop and each format must be prepared and stored.
• Easy mistakes. Forgetting the img, or writing sources in the wrong order, breaks it.
• alt lives on the img only. Beginners try to put alt on source, where it does nothing.
• Hard to maintain when a designer changes the breakpoints later.

6. Real Time Examples

• Amazon home page: a wide banner on desktop and a square banner on mobile so the offer text stays readable.
• Flipkart: webp for modern browsers and jpg for old ones, using the type attribute.
• News sites: a close crop of the person on mobile and the full scene on desktop.
• College portal: a wide campus photo on desktop and only the main building on a phone.
• Wikipedia: svg for diagrams with a png backup.
• Dark mode sites: a light logo in dark mode using a prefers-color-scheme media query.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <picture> is not a rendered element. It is a selection wrapper. The <img> inside it is the element that actually paints, and it keeps all styling, alt and dimensions.
• The browser evaluates each <source> in document order against media and type, then applies srcset and sizes on the winning source.
• Selection happens in the preload scanner, so it is decided before CSS and before JavaScript run.
• Unknown type values are skipped silently, which is exactly what makes progressive format adoption safe.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To combine art direction with resolution switching, since each source can also carry its own srcset and sizes.
• To roll out avif and webp with a guaranteed jpeg fallback and no user agent sniffing on the server.
• To support theme aware and print aware imagery through media queries.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Server side format negotiation using the Accept header splits CDN caches, while picture keeps caching simple.
• LCP images often need a different crop on mobile, which srcset alone cannot deliver.
• Interview question: why must alt, width, height and loading stay on the img and not on the source.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Cache friendly format adoption. No Vary on Accept, so each url is a single stable CDN object.
• Deterministic. You control the exact file per breakpoint, unlike the browser heuristics in a bare srcset.
• Progressive enhancement built in. A browser that does not know avif simply skips that source.
• Composable. Media, type, srcset and sizes can all be combined on one source.
• Works with preload. imagesrcset and imagesizes on a link preload can match the same candidate.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Markup explosion. Three breakpoints times three formats becomes nine source elements.
• Breakpoint drift. The media queries duplicate CSS breakpoints and silently go stale after a redesign.
• Asset pipeline cost. Each crop and format multiplies build time and storage for a large catalogue.
• Preload mismatch. A preload that does not exactly mirror the picture rules causes a double download.
• No CSS selection. Sources cannot react to container size, only to viewport media queries.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Amazon and Flipkart home banners: a square mobile crop and a wide desktop crop, both preloaded with matching media rules so LCP fires on the first paint.
• Avif rollout at news portals: avif first, webp second, jpeg last, which cut image bytes by about 30 percent with zero server sniffing.
• Design systems: a Picture component takes crops and formats as props and generates the source ladder, so no developer writes it by hand.
• Dark mode products: prefers-color-scheme sources swap logos and illustrations without any JavaScript flash.
• Print pipelines: a print media source supplies a high contrast version for generated PDFs.
• Build tooling: an image plugin generates every crop at build time and fails the build if a source file is missing.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• srcset is a list of image files that the browser can choose from.
• Each item is written as file name, a space, then a descriptor, and items are separated by commas.
• A w descriptor like 800w tells the real pixel width of that file.
• An x descriptor like 2x tells the screen density it is meant for.
• The plain src stays as the backup for very old browsers.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To send a small file to a phone and a big file to a desktop.
• To send a sharp 2x file to a retina laptop and a normal file to an old monitor.
• To save mobile data for users on limited 4G packs.

3. Need of This Topic

• Downloading a 1600 pixel picture on a 360 pixel phone wastes data and time.
• A page that opens fast on mobile keeps customers on the site.
• It is asked in almost every front end interview about performance.
codeExamples: Price: Rs 14999

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Big data saving. A phone may load 60 KB instead of 700 KB.
• Sharp on retina screens. High density screens get a 2x file automatically.
• No JavaScript. The browser does all the work.
• Safe. Old browsers fall back to src, so nothing breaks.
• Works with picture. Each source can have its own srcset.

5. Disadvantages

• Needs sizes. With w descriptors, a missing sizes makes the browser assume 100vw and download too much.
• Many files. Every image must be exported in several widths.
• No crop change. srcset can only change the size, not the shape, that needs <picture>.
• Hard to verify. The wrong choice causes no error, only a slow page.
• Mixing w and x in the same srcset is invalid and is a common mistake.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart: product tiles offer 200, 400 and 800 pixel files so a phone downloads the smallest one.
• Amazon: the main product photo has several widths for the zoom feature.
• Wikipedia: thumbnails are listed with 1.5x and 2x versions for sharp screens.
• GitHub avatars: a size parameter builds a 1x and 2x pair.
• College portal: the campus banner is served small during admission season when traffic is high.
• News apps: article thumbnails at three widths to keep 4G data usage low.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• srcset declares a candidate set. With w descriptors the browser computes an effective density for each candidate as the candidate width divided by the value computed from sizes, then picks the smallest candidate whose density is at or above the device pixel ratio.
• w and x descriptors cannot be mixed in one attribute, and w descriptors are ignored unless sizes is present.
• The chosen candidate is exposed as currentSrc, which is the only reliable way to test the selection.
• Browsers may deliberately choose a larger cached candidate or, under data saver mode, a smaller one.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To minimise LCP transfer bytes without any server side device detection.
• To integrate with an image CDN, where every candidate is the same master file with a width query.
• To let a design system component generate a fixed width ladder that keeps CDN cache hit rates high.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Image bytes dominate page weight on Indian e commerce, so this attribute is a direct business lever.
• Wrong sizes causes silent over downloading that no error log will ever reveal.
• Interview question: how exactly does the browser choose a candidate, and why is sizes mandatory with w.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• No server negotiation. Each url is a stable CDN object, so no Vary header and no cache fragmentation by user agent.
• Preload scanner aware. The right candidate begins downloading before CSS is parsed.
• Measurable. currentSrc plus the Resource Timing API gives a hard number for image bytes in CI.
• Automatable. A component generates the ladder from one master asset, removing human error.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• sizes duplicates CSS and drifts silently after any layout change.
• Cache dilution. A ladder with too many widths lowers CDN hit ratio and raises origin cost.
• Selection is a heuristic. Browsers may keep a cached larger file, so lab numbers differ from field numbers.
• No art direction. A different crop still requires <picture>.
• Attribute bloat. Long srcset strings noticeably increase HTML size on a hundred item listing page.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Flipkart and Myntra: a fixed ladder of 200, 400 and 800 keeps the CDN hit ratio above 95 percent while still serving phones the smallest file.
• Wikimedia: the thumbnail service creates any requested width on first use, then caches it globally, so srcset can list exact pixel widths.
• Framework image components: Next.js and Astro generate srcset and sizes from a layout prop, which removes the classic stale sizes bug.
• Performance budgets: a CI job loads the listing page at 360 and 1440 pixel widths and fails the build if image bytes exceed the budget.
• Data saver users: some browsers pick a smaller candidate under Save Data, which is free extra saving for low end Indian devices.
• Ad networks: creative images ship 1x and 2x pairs since ad slot sizes are fixed and w descriptors add no value there.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• sizes tells the browser how wide the image box will be on the page, at different screen widths.
• It is written as a list of media condition and length pairs, with a final length that has no condition.
• Example: sizes equal to (max-width: 600px) 100vw, 400px means full screen width on phones and 400 pixels otherwise.
• It is used together with srcset w descriptors. Without sizes, those w values are almost useless.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To help the browser choose the right file before the CSS is applied.
• To avoid downloading a 1200 pixel file for a 200 pixel thumbnail.
• To make one image tag work correctly in a one column mobile layout and a four column desktop grid.

3. Need of This Topic

• The browser starts downloading images very early, before it knows the CSS layout, so we must tell it the width.
• A missing sizes means the browser assumes 100vw and downloads a file that is far too big.
• It is the part of responsive images that beginners get wrong most often.
codeExamples: Price: Rs 14999

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Correct file choice. The browser picks the smallest file that still looks sharp.
• Big data saving. A wrong sizes can waste hundreds of KB on every image.
• Very early decision. It works even before CSS is downloaded.
• Flexible. Any number of breakpoints can be described.
• Percentage units. Values like 50vw and calc are allowed, which suits fluid grids.

5. Disadvantages

• Duplicates the CSS. The same breakpoints are written twice, in CSS and in sizes.
• Goes stale. When the designer changes the layout, sizes is usually forgotten.
• No error shown. A wrong value only makes the page slower, never broken, so nobody notices.
• Confusing syntax. The last value must have no condition, which students often miss.
• Ignored with x descriptors, so it only helps when srcset uses w.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart grid: sizes says 50vw on a phone and 200px on desktop, matching the two column and six column grids.
• Amazon cart: sizes is a fixed 60px for the small thumbnails.
• News site article: sizes says 100vw on mobile and 700px inside the desktop article column.
• College portal banner: sizes is 100vw because the banner is always full width.
• Wikipedia info box: a fixed 220px sizes value on desktop.
• Blog sidebar: sizes uses calc so the gap between columns is taken into account.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• sizes is a list of source size entries. Each entry is an optional media condition plus a source size value, and the last entry must be a bare length that acts as the default.
• The first matching entry wins. The resulting length is the CSS pixel width that the browser assumes for the image box.
• That length, multiplied by the device pixel ratio, becomes the target the srcset candidates are compared against.
• It supports vw, px, em and calc, but not percent, because there is no parent box at selection time.
• sizes is ignored when srcset uses x descriptors, and it is evaluated in the preload scanner before CSS exists.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To make the resolution switching maths correct, which is where nearly all real byte savings come from.
• To describe complex responsive grids, including gaps, using calc.
• To let a design system compute sizes automatically from the same tokens that generate the CSS.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• A stale sizes is the single most common silent performance regression in responsive image work.
• Lighthouse reports oversized images but does not tell you that sizes is the cause, so engineers must understand it.
• Interview question: why can sizes not use percent, and why must it be authored by hand.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Precise byte control. Correct sizes is usually worth more saving than switching image format.
• Runs before CSS. The preload scanner can start the right download immediately.
• calc support lets you express gutters, padding and multi column grids exactly.
• Generatable. A component that owns both the grid CSS and the sizes string can never drift.
• Testable. Comparing clientWidth against the authored value catches drift automatically.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Duplication of layout knowledge in two places, CSS and HTML.
• Silent failure mode. Wrong values produce no warning, only wasted bytes.
• No container awareness. sizes cannot react to a container query, only to the viewport.
• Percent is invalid, which surprises developers who copy CSS values directly.
• Verbose. A three breakpoint calc string adds real weight to a hundred item listing page.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Flipkart listing: sizes uses calc with the grid gap so a six column desktop grid never over downloads by even one step of the ladder.
• Framework components: Next.js and Astro accept a sizes prop and warn in development when it is missing, because the default of 100vw is almost always wrong.
• News CMS: the article template hard codes sizes for the fixed reading column, since that width never changes.
• CI performance tests: Puppeteer loads the page at 360, 768 and 1440 pixels and asserts currentSrc, which catches sizes drift on every pull request.
• Wikipedia: info box images use a fixed pixel sizes value that matches the fixed info box width.
• Design systems: the same design tokens generate both the grid CSS and the sizes string, so the two can never disagree.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• An image format is the way picture data is stored in a file, shown by the extension like jpg, png, gif, webp, avif or svg.
• JPG is best for photographs. It loses a little quality to become small.
• PNG keeps perfect quality and supports transparency, good for logos and screenshots.
• GIF is old, only 256 colours, used for simple animations.
• WebP and AVIF are modern formats, much smaller than jpg at the same quality.
• SVG is not pixels at all, it is drawing instructions, so it never becomes blurry.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To pick the right format so pages load fast and still look good.
• To use transparency correctly for logos placed on coloured backgrounds.
• To keep icons sharp on every screen size using svg.

3. Need of This Topic

• Choosing png for a photograph can make a 200 KB file into 2 MB, which wastes mobile data.
• Choosing jpg for a logo gives ugly grey edges because jpg has no transparency.
• Interviewers ask when to use png, when jpg, and why webp is preferred today.

4. Advantages

• JPG: very small files for photographs, supported everywhere.
• PNG: perfect quality and transparency, ideal for logos and screenshots.
• WebP: about 25 to 35 percent smaller than jpg, and it supports transparency and animation.
• AVIF: even smaller than webp, very good for large banner photos.
• SVG: tiny file, infinitely sharp, and its colour can be changed with CSS.

5. Disadvantages

• JPG: no transparency, and text inside becomes blurry after compression.
• PNG: photographs become very heavy files.
• GIF: only 256 colours and large file size, mostly replaced by webp and video.
• AVIF: slower to encode, and very old browsers do not support it.
• SVG: not suitable for photographs, and it can carry scripts, so files from outside must be sanitised.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart and Amazon: product photos in webp, with jpg as the fallback.
• Company logos: png or svg so the transparent background works on any colour.
• College portal: student passport photos as jpg since they are photographs.
• Wikipedia: diagrams and flags as svg so they stay sharp when zoomed.
• GitHub: build badges are svg, screenshots in issues are png.
• News apps: avif for big article photos to save 4G data.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• Formats differ on compression model, colour depth, alpha support and animation. JPEG uses lossy DCT, PNG uses lossless DEFLATE, WebP offers both lossy and lossless, AVIF uses AV1 intra frame coding, SVG is XML vector text.
• Progressive JPEG paints in passes, which improves perceived speed on slow links even at equal bytes.
• AVIF supports wide colour gamut and HDR and typically beats WebP by 20 to 30 percent at equal visual quality.
• Encoding cost matters. AVIF encoding is significantly slower, which affects build and upload pipelines.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To design a format ladder per asset class: photos, UI icons, screenshots and animations each get a different rule.
• To decide between client side selection using <picture> and server side negotiation using the Accept header, with their different caching consequences.
• To set quality targets objectively using a metric such as SSIM or Butteraugli rather than by eye.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Image bytes are the largest part of most pages, so format policy is a real infrastructure decision.
• SVG from user uploads is an XSS vector, so a sanitisation policy is mandatory.
• Interview question: compare webp, avif and progressive jpeg on compression, support and encode cost.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• AVIF and WebP cut real transfer bytes, often 30 to 60 percent versus baseline JPEG, which directly improves LCP.
• Picture based selection keeps CDN caching simple, since there is no Vary on Accept.
• SVG is styleable and animatable, and inline SVG can be recoloured by CSS custom properties for theming.
• Progressive JPEG improves the perceived load even when the byte count is unchanged.
• Lossless WebP replaces PNG for UI assets with roughly 25 percent smaller files.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Encoding cost. AVIF encoding can be an order of magnitude slower, which is painful for user uploads at scale.
• Storage multiplication. Three formats times four widths is twelve derivatives per master asset.
• Vary on Accept fragments CDN caches and can be mishandled by intermediate proxies.
• SVG security. Uploaded SVG can contain script or external references, so it must be sanitised or served from a sandboxed origin.
• Colour management. Stripping ICC profiles to save bytes can visibly shift product colours, which causes returns on fashion sites.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Flipkart and Myntra: a webp first policy with jpeg fallback, plus preserved colour profiles in fashion categories to reduce colour based returns.
• News portals: avif rollout behind a picture ladder cut article image bytes by about 30 percent with no server sniffing and no cache fragmentation.
• Wikimedia Commons: stores lossless masters and generates jpeg and webp derivatives on demand, caching each derivative url separately.
• GitHub: badges are svg for sharpness and tiny size, while user uploaded screenshots are stored as png on a separate user content domain.
• Marketplaces with seller uploads: every uploaded svg is sanitised server side and re served from a cookie free domain to contain XSS risk.
• Build pipelines: a CI step generates avif, webp and jpeg derivatives and fails the build when any master asset exceeds the byte budget.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• SVG means Scalable Vector Graphics. It stores drawing instructions, not pixels.
• The file is plain text written in XML, so you can open it in Notepad and read it.
• Because it is drawn by maths, it stays perfectly sharp at any size, even when zoomed a lot.
• It can be used in two ways: as a file inside <img>, or written inline directly in the HTML.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To draw logos, icons, charts and diagrams that never become blurry.
• To keep icon files very small, often under 1 KB.
• To change the colour of an icon with CSS instead of exporting a new file.

3. Need of This Topic

• Indian users have screens from 360 pixels to 4K, and svg looks correct on all of them.
• Every modern icon system, including Bootstrap and Material icons, is svg based.
• Interviewers ask the difference between svg and png, and when to use inline svg.

4. Advantages

• Never blurry. One file works for a 16 pixel icon and a 1000 pixel poster.
• Very small. A simple icon is often less than 1 KB.
• Styleable. Inline svg can be coloured, animated and hovered using CSS.
• Searchable text. Text inside svg is real text, so it can be read and translated.
• Editable. You can open it in a text editor and change a colour by hand.

5. Disadvantages

• Not for photographs. A photo saved as svg becomes huge and looks wrong.
• Complex drawings are slow. Thousands of paths make the browser struggle.
• Security risk. An svg file can contain scripts, so files uploaded by users must be cleaned.
• Inline svg makes HTML long and is repeated on every page unless a sprite is used.
• CSS cannot style an svg loaded through <img>, only inline svg can be styled.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart and Amazon: the cart, search and menu icons are svg so they look sharp on every phone.
• Company logos: almost every modern logo is shipped as svg.
• GitHub: the whole icon set is svg, and build badges are svg too.
• Wikipedia: country flags and scientific diagrams are svg.
• College portal: attendance and marks charts drawn as svg.
• Payment apps: bank logos as svg so they stay sharp inside a small list.
codeExamples: Pay Rs 14999 using HDFC net banking

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• SVG is an XML based vector format with its own DOM. Inline SVG nodes are real DOM elements, so they can be selected, styled and animated like HTML.
• The viewBox defines the user coordinate system, and preserveAspectRatio controls how it maps into the element box. This is what makes svg truly resolution independent.
• Delivery mode changes the capabilities. <img> with an svg file is an isolated document: no external CSS, no script, no external resources. Inline SVG shares the page CSS and JavaScript. <use> with a sprite sits in the middle and has its own CORS rules.
• currentColor is the standard bridge that lets one sprite icon inherit theme colours.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To build a themeable, cacheable icon system with a single sprite request instead of dozens.
• To render data visualisations that stay accessible, since svg text remains real text.
• To ship logos and illustrations that respond to dark mode and to prefers-reduced-motion.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• User uploaded SVG is a known XSS vector, so a sanitisation and serving policy is mandatory.
• Inline sprites versus separate files is a real performance trade off that teams must reason about.
• Interview question: why can CSS not style an svg loaded through <img>.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Advanced points 1, 2 and 3 - SVG delivery modes</title>
  <style>
    :root { --icon: #0a58ca; }
    @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --icon: #74c0fc; } }
    .icon { width: 28px; height: 28px; color: var(--icon); fill: currentColor; }
    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
      .spin { animation: turn 1.2s linear infinite; }
      @keyframes turn { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- RIGHT: advanced point 1, sprite plus use, one cached request for all icons -->
  <svg class="icon"><use href="/icons/sprite.svg#cart"></use></svg>
  <svg class="icon"><use href="/icons/sprite.svg#user"></use></svg>

  <!-- RIGHT: advanced point 1, inline svg that reacts to theme and to motion settings -->
  <svg class="icon spin" viewBox="0 0 24 24" role="img" aria-label="Loading your order">
    <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"
            stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="40 20"></circle>
  </svg>

  <!-- RIGHT: advanced point 1, viewBox plus preserveAspectRatio control the mapping -->
  <svg viewBox="0 0 100 50" width="300" height="150"
       preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Sales trend line">
    <polyline points="0,45 25,30 50,35 75,12 100,5"
              fill="none" stroke="#2f9e44" stroke-width="3"></polyline>
  </svg>

  <script>
    // Advanced point 1: inline svg nodes are ordinary DOM elements
    document.querySelectorAll('svg polyline').forEach(function (p) {
      console.log('points attribute:', p.getAttribute('points'));
      console.log('total length:', Math.round(p.getTotalLength()));
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Single sprite request. One cached sprite plus <use> replaces dozens of icon requests.
• Theming for free. currentColor plus CSS custom properties gives dark mode with no extra assets.
• Accessible data graphics. Titles, roles and real text make charts readable by assistive technology.
• Animation without JavaScript. CSS transitions and SMIL like effects run on the compositor.
• Tiny after optimisation. SVGO plus gzip usually brings icons well under 1 KB each.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• XSS through uploads. SVG can carry script, foreignObject and external references, so it must be sanitised and ideally served from a separate origin.
• Rendering cost. Thousands of path nodes cause main thread jank, where canvas would be faster.
• Sprite CORS rules. Cross origin <use> is blocked in modern browsers, so sprites must be same origin.
• HTML bloat. Repeating inline svg on every page prevents caching of that markup.
• Font and text pitfalls. Text in svg depends on fonts that may not be present, so paths are safer for logos.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Design systems at scale: a build step runs SVGO, generates one sprite and exposes icons as components, cutting dozens of requests to one cached file.
• GitHub: its whole icon set is svg with currentColor, which is how dark mode works with no extra asset downloads.
• Marketplaces with seller uploads: uploaded svg is sanitised server side and served from a cookie free domain, so an injected script has no useful origin.
• Dashboards: svg is used up to a few thousand points, then teams switch to canvas because svg node count becomes the bottleneck.
• Indian payment apps: bank logos as svg keep a long list of banks sharp on every device with a tiny total payload.
• Wikipedia: stores diagrams as svg masters and generates png thumbnails for clients that need them, keeping both worlds available.
codeExamples:
Cart has 3 items, total Rs 24998

Order delivered on 12 August

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• An image map is a single picture where different areas are different links.
• It uses three things together: an <img> with a usemap attribute, a <map> element with a name, and one or more <area> elements inside it.
• Each area defines a shape such as rect, circle or poly, and a list of coords in pixels.
• Clicking inside an area follows that area link, exactly like clicking a normal <a> tag.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To make a map of India where each state opens a different page.
• To make a seat layout for a cinema or a train where each seat is clickable.
• To make a diagram where clicking a machine part opens its details.

3. Need of This Topic

• Sometimes the clickable regions are irregular shapes that cannot be made from rectangles and CSS.
• It appears in older enterprise applications, so you must be able to read and maintain it.
• Interviewers ask what usemap does and how coords are measured.
codeExamples: Click any state to see its college list.

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Irregular shapes. Polygons can follow a state border or a machine part outline.
• One image, many links. Only one file is downloaded for the whole map.
• No JavaScript needed. The browser handles all the clicking.
• Keyboard usable. Each area is focusable and works with the Tab key.

5. Disadvantages

• Not responsive. Coords are fixed pixel values, so they break when the image is resized on a phone.
• Hard to maintain. If the artwork changes even slightly, every coordinate must be measured again.
• Poor on touch screens. Small areas are difficult to tap accurately.
• Accessibility work. Every area needs its own alt text, and many developers forget it.
• Mostly replaced. Today the same result is usually built with inline svg, which scales properly.

6. Real Time Examples

• Government portals: a map of India where each state opens its own scheme page.
• Railway and bus booking: a coach layout where every berth is clickable.
• Cinema booking: a seat plan drawn as one image with clickable seats.
• College campus map: clicking a building opens the department page.
• Product diagrams: a machine drawing where clicking a part opens its spare part price.
• Old catalogue pages: a single banner image where each product region links to that product.
codeExamples:
Campus Map

Coach Layout

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• The map is bound by usemap pointing at the map name, not its id. The name is matched case sensitively and must be unique in the document.
• Coordinates are in intrinsic image pixels, so any CSS scaling, zoom or object-fit desynchronises the hit regions from what the user sees.
• Each <area> participates in the accessibility tree as a link, and its alt supplies the accessible name. Areas are keyboard focusable in document order.
• Overlapping areas resolve by document order, so the first matching area wins.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To maintain legacy enterprise screens such as plant diagrams and seat maps that still ship image maps.
• To migrate them safely to inline svg, which supports scaling, hover states and container queries.
• To keep hit regions correct on responsive layouts when a migration is not yet possible.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Responsive breakage is silent. The page looks fine but clicks land on the wrong link, which is a real production bug.
• Accessibility audits fail when areas lack alt or when the tab order does not match the visual order.
• Interview question: why do image maps break with responsive CSS, and what is the modern replacement.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Zero dependency. No library and no runtime cost when the image is displayed at its natural size.
• Native link semantics. Areas are real links, so middle click, open in new tab and keyboard focus all work.
• Server rendered friendly. Hit regions can be generated from a database at render time.
• Print correct. The picture prints as one image and the underlying links survive in PDF exports.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Fixed pixel coords are fundamentally incompatible with fluid layouts without a rescaling script.
• No hover or focus styling of the regions themselves, so users cannot see where they can click.
• Touch target size. Small areas violate the minimum touch target guidance for mobile.
• Maintenance cost. Any redesign of the artwork invalidates every coordinate.
• Inferior to svg. Inline svg gives scaling, styling, animation and per shape ARIA, which image maps cannot.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Government scheme portals: older India maps still ship as image maps, and teams add a resize handler to rescale coords until an svg rewrite lands.
• Railway and cinema booking: modern systems moved to svg or absolutely positioned buttons, because seat availability must also be coloured live from an API.
• Industrial dashboards: plant diagrams migrated to svg so each region can pulse red when a sensor crosses a threshold.
• Legacy intranet apps: banks and insurance firms still maintain image map screens, so reading coords remains a real job skill.
• Accessibility remediation projects: the standard fix is to add alt to every area, then replace the map with svg links in the next release.
• Email templates: image maps still appear in newsletters, since svg support in email clients is unreliable.
codeExamples: Cinema booking, Pune

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• <map> is the container that holds the clickable areas of an image map.
• It must have a name attribute, and that name is what the image points to using usemap.
• Inside the map we write one or more <area> elements.
• The map itself is invisible. It draws nothing on the page, it only defines the clickable regions.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To connect one picture with a group of link areas.
• To keep all the clickable regions of a diagram together in one place.
• To let the same map be reused by more than one image on the page.

3. Need of This Topic

• Without <map> the <area> tags have no meaning and the browser ignores them.
• A missing or misspelled name is the number one reason an image map does not work.
• Interviewers ask how usemap and the map name are matched.

4. Advantages

• Grouping. All the link regions of one picture stay in one block of code.
• Reusable. Two images can share the same map by using the same name.
• Invisible. It does not disturb the page layout in any way.
• Native. No JavaScript is needed for the linking to work.

5. Disadvantages

• Name must be unique in the whole page, and duplicates cause confusing bugs.
• Silent failure. A wrong name gives no error message, the image simply does not respond.
• No styling. You cannot highlight the map regions with CSS.
• Ties to fixed pixels. The areas inside it use fixed coordinates, so it does not scale.
• Old technique. Modern projects prefer inline svg links instead.

6. Real Time Examples

• Government portals: one map element holds every Indian state region for a scheme page.
• College site: a campus map with one map element listing all buildings.
• Cinema booking: a map element holding every seat area.
• Factory dashboards: a map element for a machine diagram, each part linking to its manual.
• Email newsletters: a map element on a banner image so each product region links separately.
• Old product catalogues: a map element on a scanned page linking each item to its price page.
codeExamples:
Scheme coverage by state

Newsletter banner

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <map> is a transparent content model element. Its children other than area render normally, which is how a progressive fallback list of links can live inside it.
• Binding is by name, matched case sensitively against the usemap fragment. In the DOM it is an HTMLMapElement exposing an areas collection.
• The name must be unique. Duplicate names produce undefined behaviour and are a validator error.
• The map contributes no box, so it cannot be styled, measured or animated.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To keep legacy diagram screens maintainable while a migration to svg is planned.
• To generate hit regions server side from a database, since the map block is trivially templated.
• To provide a text link fallback inside the map for clients that do not render image maps, such as some email readers.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Enterprise and government systems still ship these, so reading and fixing them is a genuine maintenance task.
• The DOM areas collection is what lets you write a rescaling or auditing script without touching the markup.
• Interview question: how does the browser bind usemap to a map, and what happens on a name clash.
codeExamples:
• Reception
  • Development floor
  • Canteen

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Trivially server generated. A template loop over database rows produces the whole map block.
• Progressive fallback. Normal links inside the map still work in restricted clients such as email readers.
• Scriptable. The areas collection makes rescaling and auditing straightforward without editing markup.
• No layout cost. The element itself creates no box and cannot cause layout shift.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Global name space. Names are page wide, which breaks badly when components are reused on one page.
• Not stylable. No hover or focus affordance for the regions, which is an accessibility weakness.
• Fragile with responsive CSS unless a resize script rewrites every coords value.
• Poor component fit. React or Angular components rendered twice will emit duplicate map names unless ids are generated.
• Superseded. Inline svg gives everything a map does plus scaling, styling and per shape ARIA.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Government scheme dashboards: the map block is generated by a server template from a states table, so adding a state needs no HTML edit.
• Email newsletters: map elements survive in mail clients where svg and CSS are stripped, so marketing teams still ship them for banners.
• Legacy insurance intranets: component libraries wrap the map in a widget that generates a unique name per instance to avoid clashes.
• Accessibility remediation: teams script over the areas collection to add missing alt text in bulk before a full svg rewrite.
• Factory HMI screens: a resize observer rescales every coords value so the legacy diagram keeps working on new widescreen panels.
• Print catalogues online: scanned pages use one map per page, generated from an OCR pass that produced the region boxes.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• <area> defines one clickable region inside an image map.
• It is an empty tag, written only inside a <map>.
• Main attributes are shape, coords, href and alt.
• Shapes are rect with four coords, circle with three coords, poly with many pairs, and default which covers the whole image.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To turn one part of a picture into a link, for example one state on a map of India.
• To create seat, berth or building links inside a single diagram.
• To give each region its own description with the alt attribute.

3. Need of This Topic

• Without area, the map element has nothing to do.
• Wrong coords is the usual reason clicks land on the wrong link.
• Interviewers ask how rect, circle and poly coordinates are counted.

4. Advantages

• Any shape. Polygons can follow the exact outline of a state or a building.
• Real link behaviour. Right click, open in new tab and keyboard focus all work.
• Own description. Every region carries its own alt text.
• Supports target and download just like a normal <a> tag.

5. Disadvantages

• Fixed pixel coords. Resizing the image breaks every region.
• Tedious to measure. A polygon may need twenty coordinate pairs typed by hand.
• No visual feedback. The user cannot see where the clickable parts are.
• Small touch targets are hard to tap on a phone.
• Overlaps are confusing. When two areas overlap, only the first one in the code responds.

6. Real Time Examples

• Government portals: one area per Indian state, each with a poly shape.
• Railway booking: one area per berth in the coach layout.
• Cinema booking: one area per seat with the price in the alt text.
• College campus map: one area per building linking to that department.
• Machine manuals: one area per spare part linking to its price page.
• Email banners: three areas on one banner, one per product category.
codeExamples:
Coach S5 berth selection

Festive mailer

Spare parts diagram

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <area> is a void element that behaves as a hyperlink. It accepts the full link attribute set: href, target, rel, download, ping, referrerpolicy and hreflang.
• Coordinates are always in intrinsic image pixel space, independent of CSS size, zoom or object-fit.
• Hit testing walks areas in document order, so the first area containing the point wins. shape default matches everything and must be written last.
• An area without href is a dead region that blocks areas behind it, which is a useful masking trick and a common accidental bug.
• In the DOM it is an HTMLAreaElement, exposing coords, shape and the usual URL parts such as pathname and search.

2. Purpose of This Topic (Advanced)

• To generate precise hit regions from geometry data, such as state boundary polygons from a GeoJSON file.
• To keep legacy diagrams functional under responsive CSS with a coordinate rescaling layer.
• To satisfy accessibility rules by giving every region a meaningful name and a large enough target.

3. Need of This Topic (Advanced)

• Overlap and ordering bugs silently route users to the wrong page, which is hard to spot in testing.
• Touch target minimums are a WCAG requirement, and hand written coords routinely violate them.
• Interview question: what happens when two areas overlap, and what does shape default do.

4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Full link semantics. rel, target, download and referrerpolicy all work, so security headers apply as usual.
• Data driven. Polygons can be produced from GeoJSON or from an OCR pass, removing hand measurement.
• Scriptable geometry. The coords property is writable, which makes a rescaling layer straightforward.
• Keyboard reachable. Areas join the tab order, so a map is operable without a mouse.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Ordering traps. A large area written before a small one permanently masks it.
• No focus visuals. The browser outline on an area is inconsistent, so keyboard users are often lost.
• Touch target violations. Hand authored coords routinely fall below the 44 by 44 pixel guidance.
• Rescaling is lossy. Rounding coordinates on every resize can drift over repeated events.
• Href less areas create silent dead zones that testers struggle to reproduce.

6. Real Time Examples (Advanced)

• Government GIS portals: state polygons are exported from GeoJSON and converted to area coords by a build script, so boundaries stay accurate.
• Railway and cinema booking: legacy screens use one area per seat with price in the alt, while new versions render svg so availability can be coloured live.
• Email marketing: banner areas are the only reliable multi link technique in mail clients, so the alt text carries the offer for image blocking users.
• Industrial HMI panels: a resize handler rescales coords from the stored originals so a legacy diagram works on new widescreen monitors.
• Accessibility remediation at banks: scripts iterate the areas collection to inject alt text and flag targets below 44 pixels before an svg rewrite.
• Digitised catalogues: OCR produces region boxes per product, and a generator writes one area per box linking to the product page.
codeExamples: Digitised catalogue page

beginner.content:
In HTML, a list is used to create organized and structured items.
There are two common types of lists:
• Unordered List (Bulleted list) using < ul > and < li > tags.
• Ordered List (Numbered list) using < ol > and < li > tags.

• < li > defines each list item.
codeExamples:
Unordered List Example

  • Apple
  • Banana
  • Mango

Ordered List Example

  1. Wake up
  2. Brush teeth
  3. Go to school

intermediate.content:
Types of HTML Lists

There are three types of lists in HTML:
1. Ordered List (< ol >)
2. Unordered List (< ul >)
3. Description List (< dl >)

Ordered List

• Used when sequence matters.
• Supports type attribute (1, A, a, I, i).
codeExamples:
Ordered List Types

  1. HTML
  2. CSS
  1. Java
  2. Python

intermediate.content:
Unordered List

• Used when order does not matter.
• Supports type: disc, circle, square.
codeExamples:
Unordered List Types

  • Red
  • Blue
  • Car
  • Bike

intermediate.content:
Description List

• Used for definitions.
• < dl > defines description list.
• < dt > defines term.
• < dd > defines description.
codeExamples:
Description List

HTML
HyperText Markup Language
CSS
Cascading Style Sheets

expert.content:
Nested Lists

• A list inside another list is called a nested list.
• Useful for menus and categories.
codeExamples:
Nested List

  • Fruits
    • Apple
    • Mango
  • Vegetables
    • Carrot
    • Potato

expert.content:
Styled Lists Using CSS

• Use list-style-type to change bullets.
• Use list-style-image for custom bullet image.
• Remove bullets using list-style: none.
codeExamples:
Styled List

  • Item One
  • Item Two

Custom Styled Menu

  • Home
  • About
  • Contact

expert.content:
Navigation Menu Using List

• Lists are commonly used to create navigation bars.
• Use display: inline for horizontal menu.
codeExamples:
• Home
  • Services
  • Contact

beginner.content:
The <ol> Tag

• Defines an ordered list: items where the sequence matters, such as steps or rankings.
• Each entry is an li element. Browsers number them 1, 2, 3 automatically.
• Reordering the items renumbers them, so you never type the numbers yourself.

When to Choose It

• Recipe or installation steps.
• A top 10 chart or a leaderboard.
• Anything you would refer to as "step 3" or "item 2".
codeExamples:
Install Java

  1. Download the JDK installer.
  2. Run the installer and accept the licence.
  3. Set the JAVA_HOME variable.
  4. Run java -version to check.

intermediate.content:
Attributes That Change the Numbering

• type picks the marker: 1, a, A, i or I.
• start begins counting from another number, useful when a list continues after a break.
• reversed counts downward, ideal for a countdown chart.
• On an li, the value attribute sets that item's number and the rest continue from it.

Common Mistakes

• Typing numbers inside the text as well, which gives "1. 1. Download".
• Using ol only to get indentation. If order is meaningless, use ul.

Try It Yourself

• Copy the example into the HTML Viewer, then change the list to start at 5 and make it count backwards. Watch how the numbers change without editing any text.
codeExamples:
Top 3 courses

  1. Spring Boot
  2. Core Java
  3. HTML and CSS

Appendix

  1. Glossary
  2. Index

expert.content:
Styling Numbers with CSS

• The ::marker pseudo-element styles the number itself: colour, size and weight.
• For custom formats, use list-style-type or CSS counters with counter-reset and counter-increment.
• Counters let you build "Step 1" labels or nested numbering such as 1.1 and 1.2.

Accessibility

• Screen readers announce "list, 4 items" and the position of each item, which only works when you use real ol and li elements.
• Resetting list-style: none on Safari used to remove list semantics. Add role="list" when you strip the markers on a list that must stay a list.
codeExamples:
1. Create the project
  2. Add the dependency
  3. Run the application

beginner.content:
The <ul> Tag

• Defines an unordered list: items with no meaningful sequence.
• Each item is an li, shown with a bullet marker.
• Swapping the items around does not change the meaning.

Typical Uses

• Feature lists and ingredient lists.
• Navigation menus, which are lists of links.
• Tags, categories and related articles.
codeExamples:
What you will learn

  • Variables and data types
  • Loops and conditions
  • Classes and objects

intermediate.content:
Changing the Bullet

• Use CSS list-style-type: disc, circle, square or none.
• list-style-image and list-style-position give more control.
• The old type attribute is obsolete. Style it in CSS.

Common Mistakes

• Putting anything but li (or script/template) as a direct child of ul. Text or a div there is invalid.
• Using ul for layout, such as columns. CSS grid or flex is the proper tool.

Try It Yourself

• Build a three item shopping list, then switch the bullets to squares with CSS. Next, remove the bullets completely and add your own tick mark using a pseudo-element.
codeExamples:
• Square bullets
  • Easy change
  • Checked item
  • Another item

expert.content:
Menus Are Lists

• A navigation bar is a list of links, so use nav > ul > li > a. Screen readers announce how many links the menu has.
• Style the list with flex, remove the bullets, and keep the semantic markup.

Accessibility

• When you remove markers with list-style: none, add role="list" so that Safari with VoiceOver still announces a list.
• Keep link text meaningful, since users can jump through the list of links.
codeExamples:
• Home
  • Courses
  • Contact

beginner.content:
The <li> Tag

• Defines one list item inside an ol or ul.
• It is a block-level item that the browser prefixes with a bullet or a number.
• An li can contain text, links, images and even other lists.

Rules

• li must be a direct child of ol, ul or menu.
• The closing tag may be omitted, but always write it.
codeExamples:
• Plain text
  • A link item
  • Bold and emphasised text

intermediate.content:
Rich Content in Items

• An item can hold several paragraphs, an image or a nested list.
• Wrap related text in a p inside the li when an item has more than one sentence block.

The value Attribute

• Inside an ol, the value attribute sets the number of that item, and later items continue from it.
• It has no effect inside a ul.

Try It Yourself

• Make a list where one item holds a link, one holds bold text and one holds a second paragraph. Then set the value of the third item to 10 inside an ordered list.
codeExamples:
1. Plan

    Write down the requirements first.

  2. This item is numbered 10
  3. This one is 11

expert.content:
Styling Items

• Use li + li to add spacing only between items.
• Use :nth-child(odd) for zebra striping and :first-child or :last-child for borders.
• Use display: flex on an li to align an icon and text.

Good Habits

• Keep one idea per item so the list scans quickly.
• Start every item the same way, for example with a verb, for consistency.
codeExamples:
• Read the lesson
  • Run the example
  • Take the quiz
  • Move to the next topic

beginner.content:
The <dl> Tag

• Defines a description list: a set of terms, each with a description.
• It uses dt for the term and dd for the details.
• Think of a glossary or a list of name and value pairs.

When to Choose It

• Glossaries and FAQs.
• Metadata such as Author, Date and Version.
• Product specifications.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Description list</title>
</head>
<body>
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The markup language for web pages.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The language that styles them.</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
Grouping Rules

• One term can have several descriptions, and several terms can share one description.
• You may wrap each dt and dd group in a div to style groups together. This is allowed as a direct child of dl.

Common Mistakes

• Using dl for layout with no term and description relationship.
• Putting dd before any dt.

Try It Yourself

• Write a glossary with three terms, and give one of them two descriptions. Then wrap each group in a div and lay the term and description side by side with flexbox.
codeExamples:
Name
JavaSchoolLab
Level
Beginner
Intermediate
Duration
12 weeks

expert.content:
Real-World Patterns

• Key and value tables on a settings or account page.
• Event details such as Date, Venue and Price.
• API reference pages that list a parameter and its meaning.

Accessibility

• Screen readers announce the list and the term and description relationship, so it is better than a table made of divs.
• Keep terms short and meaningful.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Event details</title>
<style>
  dl.event { display: grid; grid-template-columns: max-content 1fr; gap: 6px 16px; }
  dl.event dt { color: #6b7280; }
  dl.event dd { margin: 0; font-weight: 600; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<dl class="event">
  <dt>Date</dt><dd>25 October 2026</dd>
  <dt>Venue</dt><dd>Pune Tech Park</dd>
  <dt>Price</dt><dd>Free</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
The <dt> Tag

• Defines the term in a description list.
• It must be a child of dl (or of a div inside dl).
• It is normally followed by one or more dd elements holding its meaning.

What Goes Inside

• Short text such as a word, name or label.
• Avoid block-level headings or long paragraphs inside dt.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>dt term</title>
</head>
<body>
<dl>
  <dt>Compiler</dt>
  <dd>Translates source code into machine code.</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
Several Terms, One Meaning

• Place several dt elements in a row when they share a description, such as synonyms.
• Add the dfn element when this is the place where the term is defined in the text.

Styling

• dt is bold by default in some browsers only. Set font-weight yourself.
• Add a trailing colon with the ::after pseudo-element, not in the text.

Try It Yourself

• Create a description list where two terms share one description, and add a colon after each term using only CSS. Try linking to a term with a fragment link.
• Remember: a term is a label, so keep it short and consistent. If the label needs several sentences, it probably belongs in the description instead.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Synonyms</title>
<style>
  dt { font-weight: 700; }
  dt::after { content: ":"; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<dl>
  <dt>JVM</dt>
  <dt>Java Virtual Machine</dt>
  <dd>The engine that runs Java bytecode.</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Good Habits

• Keep terms parallel in form: all nouns or all questions in a FAQ.
• Do not put interactive content such as buttons inside dt unless you are building an accordion, where details and summary is a simpler choice.

Searchability

• Terms in a glossary give search engines clear definitions of concepts on the page.
• Give each term an id so other pages can link straight to it.
codeExamples:
See DOM for details.

DOM
The tree the browser builds from your HTML.

beginner.content:
The <dd> Tag

• Defines the description or value that goes with a dt term.
• Browsers indent it, usually about 40px from the left.
• It can hold text, links, lists and other flow content.

Rules

• It must follow a dt inside the dl.
• A term can have more than one dd.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>dd details</title>
</head>
<body>
<dl>
  <dt>Coffee</dt>
  <dd>A hot drink made from roasted beans.</dd>
  <dd>Often served with milk.</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
Rich Descriptions

• A dd may contain paragraphs, lists or images, so it is good for longer explanations.
• Remove the default indent with margin-left: 0 if you want the description aligned with the term.

Common Mistakes

• Using dd on its own for indentation.
• Leaving it empty. If there is no description, the term probably should not be there.

Try It Yourself

• Turn a short FAQ into a description list. Put a bulleted list inside one of the answers and remove the default indent from the dd elements.
• Remember: every description belongs to the term right before it. If you find a dd with no term above it, the structure is broken and a screen reader will confuse its meaning.
codeExamples:
Install Java

Follow these steps:

  • Download JDK
  • Run the installer

expert.content:
FAQ Pattern

• A frequently asked questions page is a natural dl: the question is a dt and the answer is a dd.
• For collapsible answers, use details and summary inside each group.

Accessibility

• Screen readers connect each description to its term, so keep them next to each other in the source.
• Avoid hiding dd with display none and then showing it with script only, because some users will not see it.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>FAQ list</title>
<style>
  dt { font-weight: 700; margin-top: 1rem; }
  dd { margin: 4px 0 0; color: #374151; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<dl>
  <dt>Is the course free?</dt>
  <dd>Yes, every lesson is free to read.</dd>
  <dt>Do I need to install anything?</dt>
  <dd>No. Examples run in your browser.</dd>
</dl>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What Is Nesting?

• A list placed inside an li of another list.
• It shows a hierarchy: a category with sub-items.
• Browsers indent the inner list and change the bullet style automatically.

The Golden Rule

• The inner list goes inside the li, before its closing tag, and not directly inside the outer ul.
codeExamples:
• Backend
    • Java
    • Spring Boot
  • Frontend
    • HTML
    • CSS

intermediate.content:
Mixing List Types

• Ordered lists can hold unordered lists and the reverse, such as steps with bullet details.
• Each level can use its own marker through CSS.

Common Mistakes

• Placing the nested ul as a direct child of the parent ul. That is invalid.
• Nesting too deeply. More than three levels is hard to read.

Try It Yourself

• Build a menu with two categories and three sub-items each. Mix an ordered outer list with unordered inner lists and give each level a different marker with CSS.
• Remember: a nested list is part of its parent item, so deleting the item removes the whole branch. Plan the hierarchy first, then write the markup from the outside in.
codeExamples:
1. Prepare
    • Install the JDK
    • Install an editor
  2. Build
    • Write the code
    • Run the tests

expert.content:
Menus and Trees

• Dropdown menus and file trees are nested lists with CSS on top.
• Keep the markup nested so that the structure works with CSS turned off and for screen readers.

Multi-level Numbering

• CSS counters can produce 1, 1.1, 1.2, 2 numbering across nested ol elements.
• This is useful for legal documents and outlines.
codeExamples:
1. Introduction
  2. Basics
    1. Tags
    2. Attributes
  3. Summary

beginner.content:
Attributes You Can Use

• type on ol selects the marker style: 1, a, A, i or I.
• start on ol sets the first number.
• reversed on ol counts down.
• value on li sets one item's number.

Quick Reminder

• These attributes change numbering only, so they belong to ol and li.
• A ul has no attributes of its own for this.
codeExamples:
1. First
  2. Second
  1. Item five
  2. Item six
  1. Third place
  2. Second place
  3. First place

intermediate.content:
HTML Attribute or CSS?

• start, reversed and value carry meaning (the actual numbers), so keep them in HTML.
• type is presentation. Prefer the CSS list-style-type property.

Marker Choices

• Roman numerals (i, ii, iii) suit outlines.
• Letters (a, b, c) suit sub-points.
• Counting starts at 1 for every marker type.

Try It Yourself

• Make three ordered lists: one with lowercase roman numerals, one starting at 7 and one reversed. Then redo the first one using CSS list-style-type instead of the type attribute.
• Remember: numbers set with start or value are real content, because they appear in print and are read by assistive tools, while a marker style is only decoration.
codeExamples:
1. Intro
  2. Body
  1. Option
  2. Option

expert.content:
Other Useful Properties

• list-style-position: inside puts the marker within the item box, so wrapped lines align under it.
• list-style-image or a ::marker rule can show a custom icon.
• The shorthand list-style sets all three at once.

Continuing a List

• To continue numbering after an interruption, use start with the next number, or CSS counters.
• Keep it as one list when possible, which is better for assistive technology.
codeExamples:
• Arrow marker
  • Another item
  1. Continues from four
  2. Then five

beginner.content:
A table is a collection of rows and columns used to display data in structured format.
• HTML tables are defined using the < table > tag.
• < tr > defines a table row.
• < th > defines a table header.
• < td > defines a table cell.
codeExamples:
HTML Table Example

Name Age City
Jiva 25 New York
Jane 30 London

intermediate.content:
Table Styling

• Use CSS to style tables.
• border-collapse is used to collapse borders.
• padding adds space inside cells.
• text-align aligns content.
codeExamples:
Styled Table

Name Age City
Jiva 25 New York
Jane 30 London

intermediate.content:
Colspan and Rowspan

• colspan is used to merge columns.
• rowspan is used to merge rows.
codeExamples:
Colspan and Rowspan Example

Name Phone
Bill Gates 123456 789012
Support 111111 222222
333333 444444

expert.content:
Advanced Table Styling

• Use nth-child() for alternate row colors.
• Use caption for table title.
• Apply styles to specific tables using id or class.
