• Storing numbers with formatting in the database.

Try It Yourself

• Create a mobile number field that expects ten digits starting with 6-9, shows its rule on hover and has a tel link next to it.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>pattern</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label for="p">Indian mobile</label>
  <input type="tel" id="p" pattern="[6-9][0-9]{9}" maxlength="10" title="10 digit mobile starting with 6-9" required>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Checkout and contact forms ask for phones with a clear format hint.
• OTP flows verify the number by sending an SMS.
• International sites store numbers in E.164 format such as +919876543210.
• Support pages link numbers with tel: so mobile users can call in one tap.

Best Practices

• Be forgiving about spaces and dashes.
• Validate on the server with a phone library.
• Verify ownership with a one-time code.
• Protect numbers like any personal data.

Interview Question

• Q: Why is tel better than number for phone numbers?
• A: It gives a dial pad but does not treat the value as a quantity, so plus signs, spaces and leading zeros are kept.
codeExamples: Call us: +91 20 1234 5678

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="url" is a field for a web address.
• The browser checks that the value starts with a valid scheme such as https://.
• Mobile keyboards show keys such as slash and dot.
• It helps users enter links correctly.

Key Points

• The scheme is required, so example.com alone fails but https://example.com passes.
• Use placeholder to show the expected format.
• Use pattern to restrict to https if needed.
• Combine with required to make it mandatory.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>url</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">Website</label>
<input type="url" id="w" name="site" placeholder="https://example.com">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use list with a datalist to suggest common addresses.
• Use autocomplete="url" for the saved address.
• Check validity.typeMismatch in scripts for custom messages.
• Add the https:// prefix automatically on blur if the user leaves it out.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting example.com to pass validation. The scheme is required.
• Accepting any URL without checking, which allows javascript: links when rendered.
• Showing a user-supplied URL as a link without rel noopener.
• Using type text and losing the keyboard help.

Try It Yourself

• Create a website field that requires https and automatically adds https:// when the user leaves it out.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>https only</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">Secure site</label>
<input type="url" id="w" pattern="https://.*" title="Must start with https://" placeholder="https://example.com">
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Profile pages store links to portfolios and social accounts.
• Link shorteners and bookmark tools take a URL as input.
• Servers validate the scheme and block dangerous ones.
• Preview cards fetch the URL title and image.

Best Practices

• Allow only http and https on the server.
• Add rel="noopener noreferrer" to user links.
• Offer to fix a missing scheme automatically.
• Do not follow links server side without checks.

Interview Question

• Q: Why must user-supplied URLs be validated on the server?
• A: Schemes such as javascript: can run code when rendered as a link, so the server should accept only http and https.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>auto prefix</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">Website</label>
<input type="url" id="w" placeholder="https://example.com">
<script>w.onblur = () => { if (w.value && !/^https?:\/\//.test(w.value)) w.value = 'https://' + w.value; };</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="search" is a field intended for search queries.
• It behaves like text but is styled by the platform as a search box.
• Many browsers add a clear (x) button when text is entered.
• Mobile keyboards often show a Search key.

Key Points

• Place it inside a form with role="search" or a search element.
• Use name="q" by convention.
• Add enterkeyhint="search" to label the keyboard return key.
• The incremental event is non-standard and should be avoided.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>search</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form role="search" action="/search">
  <label for="q">Search lessons</label>
  <input type="search" id="q" name="q" placeholder="e.g. flexbox">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use the search event or the input event to filter results as the user types.
• Debounce requests so you do not call the server on every key.
• Reset the native look with appearance: none if you want a custom style.
• Pair it with a datalist for suggestions.

Common Mistakes

• Triggering a request for each keystroke without debounce.
• Removing the visible label and leaving no accessible name.
• Styling away the clear button without offering another way to clear.
• Forgetting a submit option for users who press Enter.

Try It Yourself

• Build a filter box that hides non-matching list items as you type, with a label for screen readers and a 300 ms debounce.
codeExamples:
• HTML
  • CSS
  • Java
  • Spring

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Site-wide search boxes, documentation filters and command palettes use it.
• Search engines index results pages when they have clean URLs.
• Analytics track top queries to improve content.
• Accessible search needs a landmark and a label.

Best Practices

• Wrap the form in role="search" or the search element.
• Debounce live search by 200 to 300 ms.
• Show a clear no-results message.
• Keep the query in the URL so results can be shared.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the benefit of type search over type text?
• A: It gives the browser and assistive technology a hint that this is a search field, adds a native clear button and tunes the mobile keyboard.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="date" shows a date picker for choosing a day, month and year.
• The value is always in the format YYYY-MM-DD, whatever the display language is.
• The browser shows the format of the user locale.
• Mobile devices show a native wheel or calendar.

Key Points

• Use min and max to limit the dates.
• Use step in days to skip dates, such as 7 for weekly.
• The value is an empty string when nothing is chosen.
• Use valueAsDate or valueAsNumber to work with the value in script.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>date</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="d">Date of birth</label>
<input type="date" id="d" name="dob" min="1950-01-01" max="2026-12-31">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Set today as the minimum with a short script, for bookings.
• Use autocomplete="bday" for birthdates.
• Convert the value to a Date with new Date(value) but beware of time zones.
• Provide a text fallback for browsers with no picker.

Common Mistakes

• Sending the displayed locale format to the server instead of the value format.
• Parsing the value with Date in a way that shifts the day because of time zones.
• Using a date input to collect only a month or year.
• Not setting min for bookings, which allows the past.

Try It Yourself

• Make a booking form with check-in and check-out dates where the earliest check-in is today and check-out cannot be before check-in.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>min today</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="d">Check-in</label>
<input type="date" id="d">
<script>d.min = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Booking forms, birthdays and deadlines use date inputs.
• Server code receives the ISO date format directly.
• Calendar libraries are used when a custom look or range selection is needed.
• Accessibility is good in native pickers across platforms.

Best Practices

• Store dates as ISO strings in the database.
• Handle time zones deliberately.
• Show examples of the expected format for text fallbacks.
• Test the picker in several browsers.

Interview Question

• Q: In which format does a date input send its value?
• A: Always as YYYY-MM-DD, regardless of how the browser displays the date for the user locale.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>range</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="a">From</label><input type="date" id="a">
<label for="b">To</label><input type="date" id="b">
<script>a.onchange = () => b.min = a.value;</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="time" shows a time picker for hours and minutes.
• The value uses a 24-hour format HH:MM, such as 14:30.
• The browser may display it as AM or PM based on locale.
• It does not include a date or time zone.

Key Points

• min and max set the allowed times.
• step is in seconds. 900 allows only quarter-hour values.
• A step below 60 adds a seconds field.
• The value is an empty string when blank.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>time</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="t">Meeting time</label>
<input type="time" id="t" name="time" min="09:00" max="18:00" step="900" value="10:00">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use time together with a date input for a full appointment.
• Use datetime-local when you need both in one control.
• Convert to minutes with a small script to compare times.
• Use step to prevent odd minute values.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting the picker to enforce min and max while scrolling. It validates on submit.
• Forgetting that no time zone is stored.
• Parsing the value as a number.
• Ignoring that 12-hour display can confuse test writers.

Try It Yourself

• Create start and end time fields in 15 minute steps between 9:00 and 18:00 and show the length of the meeting in minutes.
codeExamples: Minutes: 90

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Opening hours editors, alarms and schedules use time inputs.
• Backends store time as text such as 14:30 or as minutes since midnight.
• Global apps combine it with a separate time zone selector.
• A native picker is accessible and quick on mobile.

Best Practices

• Send the value as given and add the time zone yourself.
• Offer reasonable steps such as 15 minutes.
• Validate ranges on the server.
• Label fields with AM or PM expectations when needed.

Interview Question

• Q: Does a time input store a time zone?
• A: No. It holds only hours and minutes as local clock time, so your application must add a time zone if one matters.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>range</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="t">Pick a slot (9-5, every 30 min)</label>
<input type="time" id="t" min="09:00" max="17:00" step="1800">
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="datetime-local" lets the user pick a date and a time together.
• The value is formatted as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM.
• It has no time zone, so it means local time.
• It replaces the old datetime type, which was removed.

Key Points

• min and max accept the same format.
• step is in seconds.
• Use valueAsNumber for a timestamp in milliseconds treated as UTC.
• The picker adapts to the platform.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>datetime-local</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">Appointment</label>
<input type="datetime-local" id="w" name="when" value="2026-11-01T10:30">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Convert to a Date with new Date(value), which treats it as local time.
• Send the user time zone separately when the server needs a global instant.
• Format display values with toLocaleString.
• Use min to block past slots.

Common Mistakes

• Saving the raw value as UTC. It is local time without an offset.
• Forgetting the T separator when setting values from script.
• Assuming every browser shows seconds.
• Using separate date and time fields when one control would do.

Try It Yourself

• Make an appointment picker that blocks past times and prints the chosen moment in a full readable format below the field.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>min now</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">When</label>
<input type="datetime-local" id="w">
<script>
  const n = new Date(); n.setMinutes(n.getMinutes() - n.getTimezoneOffset());
  w.min = n.toISOString().slice(0, 16);
</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Scheduling tools, reminders and event forms use it.
• APIs combine the value with the user time zone to create a UTC timestamp.
• Calendars show events in the viewer local time.
• Testing across time zones prevents off-by-hours bugs.

Best Practices

• Be explicit about time zones in the user interface.
• Store UTC on the server.
• Show the chosen time back in a readable format.
• Guard against daylight saving gaps.

Interview Question

• Q: Why is a datetime-local value not safe to store directly?
• A: It carries no time zone offset, so the same string means different instants for different users. Convert it to UTC with the correct zone first.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="month" lets the user pick a month and a year.
• The value is formatted as YYYY-MM.
• Support is good in Chrome, Edge and Safari on mobile, but desktop Firefox shows a text box.
• It is useful for credit card expiry and reporting periods.

Key Points

• min and max use the same format.
• Use step in months to skip values.
• The value is blank when nothing is chosen.
• valueAsNumber returns months since 1970.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>month</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="m">Card expiry</label>
<input type="month" id="m" name="expiry" min="2026-11" max="2036-12">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Provide a pattern and placeholder as a fallback for browsers without a picker.
• Split into two selects for maximum compatibility if needed.
• Use autocomplete="cc-exp" for card expiry.
• Parse the value with split("-") rather than Date to avoid time zone shifts.

Common Mistakes

• Relying on the picker in browsers that show plain text.
• Parsing with Date and getting the previous month in some time zones.
• Allowing past expiry dates.
• Using it for full dates, where date is better.

Try It Yourself

• Create a card-expiry field that cannot be earlier than the current month and shows the chosen year and month separately.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>fallback</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="m">Month</label>
<input type="month" id="m" pattern="[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}" placeholder="2026-11">
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Billing reports, subscription starts and payslip pages use months.
• Credit card forms may prefer two selects for compatibility.
• APIs often take the year and month as separate numbers.
• Charts group data by month using the same format.

Best Practices

• Always include a text fallback hint.
• Validate the format on the server.
• Keep month names localised in the display only.
• Avoid time zone conversions for month values.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the value format of a month input?
• A: YYYY-MM, for example 2026-11, no matter how the control is displayed.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="week" lets the user pick a week of a year.
• The value is formatted as YYYY-Www, such as 2026-W44.
• Weeks follow the ISO 8601 rule, where week 1 contains the first Thursday.
• Support is limited to some desktop browsers.

Key Points

• min and max use the same format.
• The picker shows a calendar with week numbers.
• Safari on desktop and Firefox may show a plain text box.
• The value is blank when nothing is chosen.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>week</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="w">Choose a week</label>
<input type="week" id="w" name="week" value="2026-W44">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Convert a week to dates by finding the Monday of that ISO week.
• Offer a text fallback with a pattern such as [0-9]{4}-W[0-9]{2}.
• Use it for timesheets and weekly planners.
• Store the value as text and compute dates on the server.

Common Mistakes

• Assuming every browser supports a picker.
• Using calendar weeks that start on Sunday while ISO weeks start on Monday.
• Mixing the week year and the calendar year around New Year.
• Parsing it with new Date, which fails.

Try It Yourself

• Create a week picker that prints the Monday date of the selected week and includes a pattern fallback.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Timesheets, school timetables and sprint planners work in weeks.
• ISO week numbers are common in European business systems.
• Libraries handle week calculations reliably.
• Reporting APIs often accept the week as text.

Best Practices

• Use a library for week arithmetic.
• Show the date range of the week next to the value.
• Include a fallback for browsers without support.
• Be careful around the turn of the year.

Interview Question

• Q: What does the value 2026-W44 mean?
• A: The 44th ISO week of 2026, where weeks start on Monday and week 1 is the one containing the first Thursday of the year.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>fallback</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input type="week" pattern="[0-9]{4}-W[0-9]{2}" placeholder="2026-W44" aria-label="Week">
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="color" shows a colour picker.
• The value is a seven character hex string such as #ea580c.
• The default colour is black (#000000).
• It has no alpha channel, so transparency is not possible.

Key Points

• Use the value attribute to set a starting colour.
• Listen to the input event for live changes and change for the final choice.
• The value is always lowercase hex.
• It works well on desktop and mobile browsers.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>color</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="c">Pick a colour</label>
<input type="color" id="c" name="theme" value="#ea580c">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Apply the colour to the page with style.setProperty("--accent", value).
• Save the choice in localStorage to remember it.
• Show the hex value next to the control for copy and paste.
• Provide a datalist of preset colours.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting rgba or alpha values. Use a separate range input for opacity.
• Using text inputs for colours, which accept invalid values.
• Forgetting to give users a label for the control.
• Choosing colours without contrast checking.

Try It Yourself

• Build a theme picker that changes a heading colour live and saves the chosen colour in localStorage so it is restored on reload.
codeExamples: Theme preview

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Theme builders and drawing tools use colour inputs.
• Dashboards let users choose chart colours.
• Design tools convert the hex value to HSL for adjustment.
• Accessibility checks compare text and background contrast.

Best Practices

• Check contrast after the user picks a colour.
• Store and send hex values consistently.
• Offer preset swatches for quick choices.
• Do not rely on colour alone to convey meaning.

Interview Question

• Q: Does a colour input support transparency?
• A: No. It returns an opaque hex value, so use an extra range input and combine it into rgba yourself if you need alpha.
codeExamples: Sample text

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="file" lets users choose files from their device.
• The browser shows a button and the selected file name.
• For the form to upload the file, it needs method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data".
• The value shown in script is a fake path for privacy.

Key Points

• accept limits file types, such as image/* or .pdf.
• multiple allows choosing several files.
• capture opens the camera on mobile devices.
• Files are available through input.files as a FileList.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>file</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <label for="f">Upload a photo</label>
  <input type="file" id="f" name="photo" accept="image/*">
  <button>Upload</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Read file name, size and type from files[0].
• Check the size in script before uploading.
• Preview images with URL.createObjectURL.
• Drag and drop zones can wrap a file input for a better experience.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting enctype multipart/form-data, so only the file name is sent.
• Trusting the accept attribute. Always check type and size on the server.
• Uploading huge files with no limit.
• Trying to set the value from script, which is not allowed.

Try It Yourself

• Create an image uploader that shows the file name, size and a thumbnail, and refuses files larger than 2 MB with a message.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Profile pictures, documents and CSV imports use file inputs.
• Large uploads use chunking or direct-to-storage signed URLs.
• Servers scan files and reject unsafe types.
• Accessible dropzones keep the real input for keyboard users.

Best Practices

• Validate type, size and content on the server.
• Show progress and clear errors.
• Limit the size in the client for quick feedback.
• Never serve uploaded files from the same origin without care.

Interview Question

• Q: Why is accept not enough to secure uploads?
• A: It is only a hint for the file chooser. A user can bypass it, so the server must verify the real type, size and content of every file.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="hidden" stores a value in the form that the user does not see.
• The value is submitted with the form like any other field.
• It takes no space on the page and cannot be focused.
• It is commonly used for ids and tokens.

Key Points

• It needs a name and a value.
• The value is visible in the page source, so it is not secret.
• Script can read and change it.
• It is ignored by validation.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>hidden</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form method="post" action="/update">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="42">
  <label for="t">Title</label>
  <input id="t" name="title" value="Intro">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use it for the record id in an edit form, or an anti-CSRF token.
• Update it with script when state changes, for example the current step.
• Do not store prices or permissions in hidden fields, because users can edit them.
• The server must re-check every hidden value.

Common Mistakes

• Trusting hidden values such as price or role. Users can change them in the browser tools.
• Putting secrets in hidden fields.
• Hiding something that should be visible, such as an important choice.
• Forgetting that autofill ignores hidden fields.

Try It Yourself

• Make a two-step form where a hidden field carries the step number and print the submitted data on the page using FormData.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Multi-step wizards carry earlier answers in hidden fields.
• Frameworks add CSRF tokens as hidden inputs automatically.
• Return URLs after login are passed through a hidden field.
• Security testers try editing hidden values to find flaws.

Best Practices

• Treat hidden values as user input.
• Generate tokens on the server and verify them.
• Keep sensitive state on the server in the session.
• Name fields clearly for debugging.

Interview Question

• Q: Is a hidden input safe for storing a price?
• A: No. Anyone can edit it in the browser tools, so the server must recompute the price from its own data.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>csrf</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="a1b2c3-token-from-server">
  <button>Delete</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="range" shows a slider for picking a number in a range.
• It is best when the exact value is not important, such as volume or brightness.
• The default range is 0 to 100 with a step of 1.
• The value is a string like other inputs.

Key Points

• Set min, max, step and value.
• There is no built-in label for the current value, so add an output element.
• Keyboard arrows move the handle one step.
• Tick marks can be added with a datalist.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>range</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="v">Volume</label>
<input type="range" id="v" min="0" max="100" value="40">
<output id="o">40</output>
<script>v.oninput = () => o.textContent = v.value;</script>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use the output element with the for attribute to show the value.
• Style the track and thumb with vendor pseudo-elements.
• Add a datalist with list for labelled steps.
• Provide a number input beside the slider for precision.

Common Mistakes

• Using a slider where exact entry is needed, such as a price.
• Not showing the current value.
• Making the thumb too small for touch.
• Forgetting accessible names and units.

Try It Yourself

• Build an opacity control with a range input, a live output and a number input that stays in sync with the slider.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>ticks</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="r">Rating</label>
<input type="range" id="r" min="1" max="5" step="1" list="t" value="3">
<datalist id="t"><option value="1" label="1"><option value="3" label="3"><option value="5" label="5"></datalist>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Audio and video players use sliders for volume and seek.
• Filters in shops use two range inputs for a price span.
• Image editors adjust brightness and contrast.
• Accessible sliders need clear labels and value text.

Best Practices

• Show the value and unit next to the slider.
• Keep a keyboard friendly step size.
• Use aria-valuetext for friendly values such as 3 stars.
• Combine with a number field for precise input.

Interview Question

• Q: Why add an output element next to a range input?
• A: A slider shows only the handle position, not the number. An output element displays the current value so users know exactly what they chose.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>with number</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input type="range" id="r" min="0" max="100" value="25" aria-label="Opacity">
<input type="number" id="n" min="0" max="100" value="25" aria-label="Opacity value">
<script>r.oninput = () => n.value = r.value; n.oninput = () => r.value = n.value;</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="checkbox" is a box that can be ticked or cleared.
• Several checkboxes with the same name form a group where many can be chosen.
• A checked box submits its value. An unchecked box submits nothing.
• The default value sent is the text on.

Key Points

• Add checked to start ticked.
• Use a value for each box to say what it stands for.
• Always connect a label so the text is clickable.
• The indeterminate state is set by script for mixed groups.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>checkbox</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="topic" value="html" checked> HTML</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="topic" value="css"> CSS</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="topic" value="js"> JavaScript</label>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Read the state with input.checked in script.
• Use required for a single box such as "I accept the terms".
• Use :checked in CSS to style the label or reveal content.
• Group boxes in a fieldset with a legend.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting an unchecked box to send false. It sends nothing.
• Using small clickable areas without labels.
• Using a checkbox when only one choice is allowed, which needs radio buttons.
• Using a checkbox for an immediate action, where a switch with role is clearer.

Try It Yourself

• Build a topic selector with three checkboxes and a select-all box that shows an indeterminate state when only some are ticked.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Terms and consent boxes, filters and to-do lists use checkboxes.
• Bulk actions in tables use a header checkbox for select all.
• Server code receives repeated names as a list.
• Custom checkboxes must keep keyboard and screen reader behaviour.

Best Practices

• Use a fieldset and legend for groups.
• Make the label text clear and short.
• Do not pre-tick consent boxes.
• Keep a large click target.

Interview Question

• Q: What does the server receive for an unchecked checkbox?
• A: Nothing at all. Only checked boxes are submitted, so the server should treat a missing name as false.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>indeterminate</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label><input type="checkbox" id="p"> Parent</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" class="k"> One</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" class="k"> Two</label>
<script>
  const ks = [...document.querySelectorAll('.k')];
  ks.forEach(k => k.onchange = () => {
    const n = ks.filter(x => x.checked).length;
    p.checked = n === ks.length; p.indeterminate = n > 0 && n < ks.length;
  });
</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="radio" is a round button for choosing exactly one option from a group.
• Radio buttons share the same name to form the group.
• Selecting one clears the others.
• The selected button submits its value.

Key Points

• Give every button in a group the same name and different values.
• Add checked to one to set a default.
• Use required to force a choice.
• Arrow keys move between the options in a group.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>radio</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Level</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="basic" checked> Basic</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="level" value="pro"> Pro</label>
  </fieldset>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Wrap the group in a fieldset with a legend, which screen readers announce.
• Read the choice with form.level.value or querySelector(":checked").
• Use the :checked + label selector for card style options.
• Keep options to about seven or fewer. Use a select for longer lists.

Common Mistakes

• Using different names, so several options can be selected.
• Having no default when a choice is required, which leaves the user stuck.
• Using radio buttons for a single yes or no choice. A checkbox is simpler.
• Hiding the real input without keeping it accessible.

Try It Yourself

• Create a plan chooser using radio buttons styled as cards that stay keyboard accessible, and display the chosen value below.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>card options</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  input { position: absolute; opacity: 0; }
  label.card { display: inline-block; padding: 10px 16px; border: 2px solid #cbd5e1; border-radius: 8px; margin-right: 8px; }
  input:checked + label.card { border-color: #ea580c; background: #fff7ed; }
  input:focus-visible + label.card { outline: 2px solid #2563eb; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input type="radio" name="p" id="a" value="free" checked><label class="card" for="a">Free</label>
<input type="radio" name="p" id="b" value="pro"><label class="card" for="b">Pro</label>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Payment method, shipping option and survey questions use radio groups.
• Frameworks bind the selected value to a single variable.
• Wizards store the choice in state and show different steps.
• Visual cards improve touch targets but must stay keyboard accessible.

Best Practices

• Always provide a legend for the group.
• Preselect the most common safe option.
• Make the whole label clickable.
• Test arrow key navigation.

Interview Question

• Q: How do radio buttons know they belong to the same group?
• A: They share the same name attribute within the same form. The browser then allows only one of them to be selected.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="submit" is a button that sends the form to the server.
• It can be written as an input element or as a button element.
• It is the default type for a button inside a form.
• Pressing Enter in most text fields triggers it too.

Key Points

• For input, the value is the label. For button, the content is the label.
• formaction, formmethod and formtarget override the form settings for that button.
• formnovalidate skips validation, for example for a Save draft button.
• The name and value of the clicked button are sent too.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>submit</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="e">Email</label>
  <input id="e" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Listen to the submit event on the form, not click on the button.
• Call preventDefault() to handle the form with fetch.
• Disable the button during sending to prevent double submissions.
• Use form.requestSubmit() to submit with validation from script.

Common Mistakes

• Handling click instead of submit, so Enter does not work.
• Putting a button without type inside a form and submitting by accident.
• Using a generic label like Submit instead of Subscribe or Save.
• Not showing feedback after sending.

Try It Yourself

• Create a form that validates on submit, sends data with fetch, disables the button while waiting and shows a success message afterwards.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Every form ends with a submit button that names the action.
• Single page apps intercept the event and call an API.
• Several submit buttons can save a draft or publish.
• Double click prevention is a common bug fix.

Best Practices

• Use clear verbs on the button.
• Give feedback and handle errors.
• Validate on the server as well.
• Keep the primary action visually obvious.

Interview Question

• Q: Why listen to the submit event instead of the click on the button?
• A: The form can also be submitted by pressing Enter in a field, which fires submit but not a click on the button.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>two buttons</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/save" method="post">
  <input name="title" required>
  <button name="act" value="publish">Publish</button>
  <button name="act" value="draft" formnovalidate>Save draft</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="reset" is a button that restores all fields to their initial values.
• It does not send anything to the server.
• The defaults are the values written in the HTML, not empty fields.
• It fires a reset event on the form.

Key Points

• It is written as <button type="reset"> or an input with type reset.
• It clears typed text and restores checked and selected states.
• It affects only the form that contains it.
• There is no confirmation dialog.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>reset</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <input name="n" value="Asha">
  <input name="c" value="Pune">
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
  <button type="reset">Reset</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Listen to the reset event to clear custom state such as error messages or previews.
• Use form.reset() in script.
• Place the button away from the submit button to avoid accidents.
• Confirm before resetting long forms.

Common Mistakes

• Placing reset next to submit, so users clear the form by mistake.
• Expecting it to empty all fields. It restores the defaults.
• Forgetting to clear dynamically added content.
• Using it in short forms where it adds clutter.

Try It Yourself

• Create a filter form with a reset button that restores defaults and shows a message in a reset event handler.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Search filters often have a Clear filters link that resets the form.
• Long data entry forms rarely include reset because it is risky.
• Custom widgets listen to reset to restore their state.
• Single page apps reset state after a successful submit.

Best Practices

• Use reset only when it helps users.
• Do not style it like the primary button.
• Give feedback or undo for destructive resets.
• Keep default values meaningful.

Interview Question

• Q: Does a reset button empty the fields?
• A: Not necessarily. It restores each field to the value written in the HTML, so a field with a default value goes back to that value rather than becoming empty.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>confirm</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form id="f"><input name="n" value="Draft text"><button type="reset">Reset</button></form>
<script>f.addEventListener('reset', e => { if (!confirm('Discard changes?')) e.preventDefault(); });</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The button element creates a clickable button.
• Unlike input type button, it can contain text, icons and other elements.
• Inside a form its default type is submit.
• Its type can be submit, reset or button.

Key Points

• Use type="button" for buttons that do not submit.
• Use disabled to turn it off.
• Use name and value to tell the server which button was used.
• It can be styled freely with CSS.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>button</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button type="button" onclick="alert('Clicked!')">Click me</button>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Add text or an icon with an aria-label when the button has only an icon.
• Use aria-pressed for toggle buttons and aria-expanded for disclosure buttons.
• Use :hover, :active and :focus-visible for feedback.
• Use a link, not a button, for navigation.

Common Mistakes

• Using a div as a button, which loses keyboard and screen reader support.
• Leaving off type inside a form and submitting it by accident.
• Removing the focus outline without a replacement.
• Using a button for a link to another page.

Try It Yourself

• Create a toggle button that switches aria-pressed and updates its text, then add an icon-only close button with an accessible name.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>toggle</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  button[aria-pressed="true"] { background: #ea580c; color: #fff; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button type="button" aria-pressed="false" id="b">Dark mode: off</button>
<script>
  b.onclick = () => {
    const on = b.getAttribute('aria-pressed') !== 'true';
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', on);
    b.textContent = 'Dark mode: ' + (on ? 'on' : 'off');
  };
</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Menus, tabs, accordions and dialogs are all opened with buttons.
• Design systems wrap button with variants such as primary and danger.
• Icon buttons need accessible names.
• Loading buttons show a spinner and block repeat clicks.

Best Practices

• Use the right element: button for actions, a for navigation.
• Give every button a clear accessible name.
• Make the touch target at least 44 by 44 pixels.
• Keep focus styles visible.

Interview Question

• Q: Why use a button instead of a clickable div?
• A: A button is focusable, works with Enter and Space, has the right role for screen readers and needs no extra code. A div needs all of that added manually.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>icon button</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button type="button" aria-label="Close" style="width:44px;height:44px">×</button>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The label element gives a form control a visible, clickable name.
• Clicking the label focuses or toggles its control.
• Screen readers announce the label when the control gets focus.
• It is the most important accessibility feature of forms.

Key Points

• Connect them with for on the label and a matching id on the control.
• Or wrap the control inside the label, with no id needed.
• One control can have several labels.
• A label increases the click area, which helps touch users.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>label</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="e">Email address</label>
<input id="e" type="email">

<label><input type="checkbox"> I agree to the terms</label>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Place labels above fields on small screens for readability.
• Use aria-label only when a visible label is truly not possible.
• Combine with hint text through aria-describedby.
• Mark required fields in the label text, not only with a star.

Common Mistakes

• Using placeholders instead of labels.
• Using a for value that does not match any id.
• Duplicate ids, which break the link.
• Hiding labels with display none, which hides them from screen readers.

Try It Yourself

• Make a small form where each field has a label connected by for and id, a hint linked with aria-describedby and a checkbox wrapped inside its label.
codeExamples: At least 8 characters.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Accessibility audits first check that every control has a label.
• Floating label designs must still keep a real label element.
• Inline label and checkbox groups make tap targets larger.
• Forms in design systems wrap label, input and error into one component.

Best Practices

• Always use a visible label.
• Keep label text short and descriptive.
• Place the error message near the field and reference it with aria-describedby.
• Use visually hidden labels only when the context is clear.

Interview Question

• Q: What are the two ways to connect a label to a control?
• A: Use the for attribute matching the control id, or place the control inside the label element. Both let clicks and screen readers link them.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>hidden label</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  .sr { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="s" class="sr">Search</label>
<input id="s" type="search" placeholder="Search...">
<button>Go</button>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The textarea element is a multi-line text field.
• It is used for comments, messages and descriptions.
• Its initial content goes between the tags, not in a value attribute.
• Line breaks typed by the user are kept.

Key Points

• Use rows and cols for a starting size, or set size with CSS.
• Use maxlength and minlength to control the length.
• Use placeholder, required and readonly like other fields.
• Users can resize it unless you set resize: none.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>textarea</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="m">Message</label>
<textarea id="m" name="message" rows="4" cols="40" placeholder="Write here..."></textarea>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Add a live counter showing remaining characters.
• Use wrap="hard" with cols to submit hard line breaks.
• Auto-grow the field by setting its height from scrollHeight.
• Use spellcheck and autocapitalize to control hints.

Common Mistakes

• Using a value attribute. The text must go between the tags.
• Leaving extra whitespace between the tags, which becomes content.
• Removing resizing without a replacement.
• Not limiting size on the server.

Try It Yourself

• Create a message box with a 200 character limit, a live counter and automatic height growth as the user types.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>auto grow</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  textarea { width: 300px; overflow: hidden; resize: none; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<textarea id="m" rows="2" aria-label="Notes"></textarea>
<script>m.oninput = () => { m.style.height = 'auto'; m.style.height = m.scrollHeight + 'px'; };</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Comment boxes, reviews and support forms use textareas.
• Markdown editors build previews next to the textarea.
• Mentions and hashtags are added through scripts.
• Server code must escape the text before showing it in HTML.

Best Practices

• Escape user text when displaying it.
• Offer a character counter near limits.
• Set a sensible minimum height.
• Preserve line breaks with white-space: pre-wrap when showing the text.

Interview Question

• Q: How do you set initial text in a textarea?
• A: Put the text between the opening and closing tags. A textarea has no value attribute in HTML, though its value property works in script.
codeExamples: 120 characters left

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The select element creates a drop-down list of options.
• Each choice is an option element inside it.
• The user picks one option, or several with the multiple attribute.
• Its value is the value of the chosen option.

Key Points

• Use name so the choice is submitted.
• Use required with an empty first option to force a choice.
• multiple turns it into a list box, and size sets the visible rows.
• Group options with optgroup.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>select</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="c">Country</label>
<select id="c" name="country">
  <option value="in">India</option>
  <option value="us">United States</option>
  <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
</select>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Read the choice with select.value and the label with select.selectedOptions[0].text.
• Use the change event to react when the user picks another option.
• A disabled placeholder option such as "Choose..." guides the user.
• Fill options from data with a short script.

Common Mistakes

• Using a select for two options, where radio buttons are easier.
• Forgetting values, so the visible text is sent instead.
• Making long lists with no search, such as a thousand cities.
• Styling selects heavily, which can break keyboard use on some platforms.

Try It Yourself

• Build two linked drop-downs, category and item, where the second list is refilled from an object when the first one changes.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Country, state and category pickers use selects.
• Linked dropdowns update the second list when the first changes.
• For long lists, searchable comboboxes replace the native select.
• Mobile browsers show native pickers that are quick to use.

Best Practices

• Provide a label and an empty first option when a choice is required.
• Sort options in a way that makes sense.
• Keep native behaviour unless you must change it.
• Use datalist or a combobox pattern for very long lists.

Interview Question

• Q: How is the value of a select determined?
• A: It is the value attribute of the selected option, or the option text when no value attribute exists.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>dependent</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select id="a"><option>Fruits</option><option>Vegetables</option></select>
<select id="b"></select>
<script>
  const data = { Fruits: ['Apple', 'Banana'], Vegetables: ['Carrot', 'Peas'] };
  const fill = () => b.innerHTML = data[a.value].map(x => '<option>' + x + '</option>').join('');
  a.onchange = fill; fill();
</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The option element defines one choice inside a select, optgroup or datalist.
• The text between the tags is shown to the user.
• The value attribute is what gets submitted.
• If value is missing, the text is used.

Key Points

• selected marks the default choice.
• disabled makes a choice visible but not selectable.
• label can shorten what is displayed in some browsers.
• It cannot contain other elements, only text.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>option</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select name="size">
  <option value="s">Small</option>
  <option value="m" selected>Medium</option>
  <option value="l">Large</option>
  <option value="xl" disabled>Extra large (sold out)</option>
</select>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Create options in script with new Option(text, value).
• Add them with select.add() or append.
• Read option.selected and option.index in loops.
• Use hidden to remove an option from the list without deleting it.

Common Mistakes

• Writing markup inside an option. Browsers show only text.
• Using values with spaces and expecting the server to trim them.
• Having two options selected in a single select.
• Leaving out values, so display text becomes data.

Try It Yourself

• Fill a select from an array using new Option, mark one choice as default and disable one that is unavailable.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>create options</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select id="s"></select>
<script>
  ['Java', 'Spring', 'HTML'].forEach((t, i) => s.add(new Option(t, 'v' + i)));
  s.onchange = () => document.title = s.value;
</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Dynamic option lists are filled from APIs after the page loads.
• Disabled options show out-of-stock sizes without hiding them.
• Labels can show a short code while the dropdown shows the full name.
• Frameworks map arrays to options with keys.

Best Practices

• Always set explicit values.
• Use a clear default and mark it with selected.
• Avoid very long option text.
• Keep values stable even if labels change.

Interview Question

• Q: What does an option send if it has no value attribute?
• A: Its text content, trimmed. That is why explicit values are safer, because translating or renaming the label would change the data.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>disabled option</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select><option>Pick a plan</option><option>Basic</option><option disabled>Premium (coming soon)</option></select>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The optgroup element groups related options inside a select.
• The label attribute gives the group a heading.
• The heading is shown but cannot be chosen.
• It makes long lists easier to scan.

Key Points

• optgroup is a child of select and the parent of option.
• Adding disabled to the group disables all options in it.
• Nesting groups inside groups is not allowed.
• Groups can have different numbers of options.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>optgroup</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select name="lang">
  <optgroup label="Backend">
    <option>Java</option>
    <option>Python</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Frontend">
    <option>HTML</option>
    <option>CSS</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Style the group heading limited by browser support, mostly font weight and colour.
• Use groups for categories such as continents and countries.
• Combine with the multiple attribute for a grouped list box.
• Order groups alphabetically or by usage.

Common Mistakes

• Using optgroup with no label, which shows an empty heading.
• Nesting optgroup elements.
• Putting options outside groups when some are grouped, which looks confusing.
• Using it where a simple list would do.

Try It Yourself

• Create a timezone picker grouped by continent, with one group disabled to mark regions that are not yet supported.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>multiple grouped</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select multiple size="6">
  <optgroup label="Fruits"><option>Apple</option><option>Mango</option></optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Vegetables"><option>Carrot</option><option>Peas</option></optgroup>
</select>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Country selectors group by region.
• Timezone pickers group by area, such as Asia and Europe.
• Product pickers group by category.
• Disabling a group greys out a whole unavailable section.

Best Practices

• Keep group names short and clear.
• Do not create groups with only one option.
• Test the look on mobile, where groups appear in a native picker.
• Maintain consistent ordering.

Interview Question

• Q: Can you select an optgroup label?
• A: No. The label is only a heading. Only the option elements inside the group can be chosen.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>disabled group</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select>
  <optgroup label="Available"><option>Java</option></optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Coming soon" disabled><option>Rust</option><option>Go</option></optgroup>
</select>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The datalist element offers suggestions for a text input.
• The input connects to it through the list attribute.
• Unlike select, the user can still type any value.
• It behaves like a simple combobox.

Key Points

• The datalist needs an id and the input uses list="that-id".
• Each suggestion is an option with a value.
• Browsers filter suggestions as you type.
• It works with text, url, email, number, date and colour inputs.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>datalist</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="b">Browser</label>
<input id="b" list="browsers" name="browser">
<datalist id="browsers">
  <option value="Chrome">
  <option value="Firefox">
  <option value="Safari">
</datalist>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Show a label with the option text while the value is submitted.
• Fill the list from an API as the user types.
• Pair with autocomplete="off" if the browser history interferes.
• Validate the final value on the server, since any text is allowed.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting it to restrict input to the list. It does not.
• Using the same id twice.
• Forgetting that styling the suggestion popup is limited.
• Large lists that make the popup slow.

Try It Yourself

• Create a city input that suggests five cities from a datalist and uses a pattern to accept only those cities.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>dynamic</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="c" list="cities" placeholder="City">
<datalist id="cities"></datalist>
<script>
  ['Pune', 'Mumbai', 'Delhi', 'Chennai'].forEach(x => cities.append(new Option(x)));
</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Search boxes with common queries, city fields and tag inputs use datalist.
• It needs no JavaScript for simple cases.
• For rich results with images, a custom combobox is needed.
• Screen reader support varies between browsers.

Best Practices

• Use it for convenience suggestions only.
• Validate against allowed values on the server if required.
• Keep the list under a few hundred items.
• Provide a visible label.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between datalist and select?
• A: A select forces a choice from the list, while a datalist only suggests values and still allows free text.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>restrict</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="c" list="l" pattern="Pune|Mumbai|Delhi" title="Choose a listed city" required>
<datalist id="l"><option>Pune</option><option>Mumbai</option><option>Delhi</option></datalist>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The fieldset element groups related form controls.
• Browsers draw a border around the group.
• Its first child can be a legend, which names the group.
• It helps both visual and screen reader users understand the structure.

Key Points

• Use it for radio button groups and sets of checkboxes.
• Add disabled to disable every control inside it at once.
• The name and form attributes exist but are rarely used.
• It can be styled like any block.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>fieldset</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Delivery</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="d" value="home" checked> Home</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="d" value="store"> Pickup</label>
  </fieldset>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Reset the default border and padding with CSS for a flat look.
• Group address fields in a fieldset with the legend Billing address.
• Disable a whole section while it is not applicable.
• Use nested fieldsets sparingly.

Common Mistakes

• Using it purely for visual boxes. Use a div for that.
• Forgetting the legend, which loses the accessible name.
• Nesting too deeply.
• Expecting display flex to work easily on older browsers.

Try It Yourself

• Build a checkout form with a billing fieldset and a shipping fieldset that becomes enabled only when a checkbox is ticked.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>disabled group</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label><input type="checkbox" id="g"> Ship to a different address</label>
  <fieldset id="a" disabled>
    <legend>Shipping address</legend>
    <input placeholder="Street"> <input placeholder="City">
  </fieldset>
</form>
<script>g.onchange = () => a.disabled = !g.checked;</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Checkout pages group billing and shipping data.
• Surveys group questions that belong together.
• Settings pages group switches by topic.
• Disabled fieldsets save a lot of script code.

Best Practices

• Always pair fieldset with a legend.
• Use it for radio and checkbox groups.
• Keep groups small and logical.
• Restyle it for consistency.

Interview Question

• Q: What happens to inputs inside a disabled fieldset?
• A: They are all disabled, cannot be focused or edited, and are not submitted with the form.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>flat style</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  fieldset { border: 0; padding: 0; margin: 16px 0; }
  legend { font-weight: 700; padding: 0; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<fieldset><legend>Preferences</legend><label><input type="checkbox"> Email me</label></fieldset>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The legend element is the caption of a fieldset.
• It must be the first child of the fieldset.
• Browsers draw it on the top border line.
• Screen readers read it before each control in the group.

Key Points

• It names the group, such as Payment method.
• It can contain text and phrasing elements.
• Only one legend is allowed per fieldset.
• It is essential for radio button groups.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>legend</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<fieldset>
  <legend>Choose a payment method</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="p" value="card"> Card</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="p" value="upi"> UPI</label>
</fieldset>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Style it with font, colour and padding.
• Move it away from the border by setting float: left and width: 100% if you need full control.
• Use a visually hidden legend if the design shows another heading.
• Combine with required marks in the text.

Common Mistakes

• Placing the legend anywhere but first.
• Replacing it with a heading, which loses the group link.
• Hiding it with display none.
• Writing very long legends.

Try It Yourself

• Create a survey question as a fieldset with a legend and three radio options, then visually hide the legend while keeping it available to screen readers.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>custom legend</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  fieldset { border: 1px solid #cbd5e1; }
  legend { background: #ea580c; color: #fff; padding: 2px 10px; border-radius: 4px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<fieldset><legend>Level</legend><label><input type="radio" name="l"> Beginner</label><label><input type="radio" name="l"> Advanced</label></fieldset>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Accessibility checks report radio groups without legends.
• Questionnaires use the question as the legend.
• Design systems provide a RadioGroup component wrapping fieldset and legend.
• Consistent legends improve screen reader navigation.

Best Practices

• Write the legend as the question or group title.
• Do not repeat the legend in each option.
• Keep it short.
• Hide visually, never remove, when the design requires.

Interview Question

• Q: Why does a radio group need a legend?
• A: Screen readers announce the legend before each option, so users know what the question is. Without it, the options alone are ambiguous.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>visually hidden</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  .sr { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<fieldset style="border:0"><legend class="sr">Rating</legend>
<label><input type="radio" name="r"> Good</label> <label><input type="radio" name="r"> Bad</label></fieldset>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The output element shows the result of a calculation or user action.
• It is announced politely by screen readers when its content changes.
• It can be linked to the inputs it depends on with the for attribute.
• Its name and value can take part in the form.

Key Points

• Write the result with output.value or textContent.
• The for attribute lists the ids of the related inputs.
• It has an implicit role of status.
• The oninput handler on the form can update it.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>output</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form oninput="r.value = Number(a.value) + Number(b.value)">
  <input type="number" id="a" value="2"> +
  <input type="number" id="b" value="3"> =
  <output name="r" for="a b">5</output>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use it for totals, slider values and live previews.
• Reset restores its default content.
• Style it like inline text.
• Pair with a range input to show the current value.

Common Mistakes

• Using a span, which loses the live announcement.
• Forgetting the for attribute.
• Updating too often, which makes screen readers talk constantly.
• Using it for important errors, where role alert is better.

Try It Yourself

• Build a price estimator with quantity and unit price fields that updates an output element as the user types.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>slider value</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input type="range" id="v" min="0" max="100" value="30">
<output for="v" id="o">30</output>%
<script>v.oninput = () => o.value = v.value;</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Calculators, price estimators and unit converters rely on output.
• It marks results clearly for assistive technology.
• The value can be submitted with the form when named.
• Frameworks render derived values into output elements.

Best Practices

• Keep announcements short.
• Debounce frequent updates.
• Include units in the result.
• Use alerts for errors and output for neutral results.

Interview Question

• Q: What does output give you compared with a span?
• A: It is linked to its inputs, announced as a live status to screen readers and can be part of the form data.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>estimator</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form id="f" oninput="t.value = (q.value * p.value).toFixed(2)">
  Qty <input type="number" id="q" value="2" min="1"> x Price <input type="number" id="p" value="49.5" step="0.01">
  = <output id="t" name="t" for="q p">99.00</output>
</form>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The meter element shows a value within a known range, like a gauge.
• Examples are disk usage, battery level and a score out of ten.
• It is not for progress of a task. Use progress for that.
• Browsers draw a coloured bar.

Key Points

• value, min and max define the position.
• low and high define the ranges that change colour.
• optimum tells which end is good.
• The text between the tags is a fallback.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>meter</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="d">Disk usage</label>
<meter id="d" min="0" max="100" value="60">60%</meter>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Browsers colour the bar green, yellow or red based on low, high and optimum.
• Style it with vendor pseudo-elements.
• Add an aria-label or a visible label.
• Update value from script for live gauges.

Common Mistakes

• Using meter for progress such as a download. Use progress.
• Forgetting max when the scale is not 0 to 1.
• Providing no label.
• Using colours as the only signal.

Try It Yourself

• Create a storage meter with warning zones and a button that increases its value in steps.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>zones</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<meter min="0" max="100" low="30" high="70" optimum="100" value="85">85</meter>
<meter min="0" max="100" low="30" high="70" optimum="100" value="20">20</meter>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Dashboards show usage and quota with meters.
• Quiz results show scores.
• Password strength indicators use them.
• Printing shows the same bar without scripts.

Best Practices

• Add a text value next to the bar.
• Choose low, high and optimum thoughtfully.
• Use an accessible name.
• Do not rely on default colours alone.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between meter and progress?
• A: meter shows a measurement within a range, while progress shows how far a task has advanced toward completion.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>live</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<meter id="m" min="0" max="100" value="10" aria-label="Battery"></meter>
<button onclick="m.value = Math.min(100, m.value + 15)">Charge</button>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The progress element shows how much of a task is complete.
• It displays a bar that fills from left to right.
• Without a value it shows an indeterminate animation.
• Use it for downloads, uploads and multi-step forms.

Key Points

• value is the amount done and max is the total.
• The default max is 1.
• Omit value for an unknown duration.
• The inner text is shown by very old browsers.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>progress</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="p">Upload</label>
<progress id="p" max="100" value="45">45%</progress>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Update value from script as the task moves ahead.
• Style with pseudo-elements such as ::-webkit-progress-value.
• Add aria-label or associate a label.
• Show a text percentage beside the bar.

Common Mistakes

• Using progress for static values, where meter is better.
• Forgetting a label.
• Never reaching 100% on completion.
• Leaving the indeterminate bar on forever.

Try It Yourself

• Make a progress bar that fills to 100% in ten steps and shows the percentage in text beside it.
codeExamples: 0%

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• File uploaders, installers and quizzes show progress.
• Fetch with streams or XHR upload events drive value.
• Wizards show the number of finished steps.
• Skeleton screens replace it for page loading.

Best Practices

• Prefer determinate progress when you know the total.
• Announce completion to screen readers.
• Do not fake progress.
• Keep contrast high.
