Interview Question

• Q: How does progress behave without a value attribute?
• A: It becomes indeterminate and shows an animated bar, which means the task is running but the amount done is unknown.
codeExamples: Loading...

beginner.content:
What It Is

• Form validation checks the data before it is sent.
• HTML offers built-in rules through attributes such as required, pattern, min and max.
• The browser blocks submission and shows a message when a rule fails.
• It improves the experience but does not replace server checks.

Key Points

• Rules: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, pattern and the input type.
• The pseudo-classes :valid and :invalid style the state.
• novalidate on the form turns it off.
• The Constraint Validation API gives script access.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>validation</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  input:invalid { border-color: crimson; }
  input:valid { border-color: seagreen; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label for="e">Email</label>
  <input id="e" type="email" required>
  <label for="a">Age (18-60)</label>
  <input id="a" type="number" min="18" max="60" required>
  <button>Send</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use setCustomValidity for custom messages and reset it with an empty string.
• Check form.checkValidity() or reportValidity() in script.
• Show your own error text near each field with aria-describedby.
• Validate again on the server.

Common Mistakes

• Relying only on client validation.
• Showing errors before the user touches the field.
• Vague messages such as Invalid input.
• Forgetting to clear custom validity, which keeps the field invalid.

Try It Yourself

• Create a sign-up form with required fields, a custom error message area linked with aria-describedby and server-style checks inside a submit handler.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Sign-up forms combine HTML rules with live messages.
• Servers return field errors that scripts show in the same places.
• Accessible error patterns link messages with aria-describedby and use aria-invalid.
• Automated tests submit invalid data to check both layers.

Best Practices

• Validate on both sides.
• Explain how to fix the problem.
• Mark invalid fields with aria-invalid.
• Move focus to the first error.

Interview Question

• Q: Why must forms be validated on the server too?
• A: Client rules can be bypassed by editing the page or sending requests directly, so only server validation protects your data.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The required attribute says a field must be filled before the form is sent.
• It is a boolean attribute: its presence is enough.
• It works on input, select and textarea.
• The browser blocks submission and shows a message.

Key Points

• For a checkbox it must be ticked.
• For radio buttons, one in the group must be chosen.
• For a select, the first option should have an empty value.
• Whitespace-only text counts as filled.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>required</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label for="n">Name *</label>
  <input id="n" name="name" required>
  <label><input type="checkbox" required> I accept the terms</label>
  <button>Send</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Mark required fields visually and in text, not just with colour.
• Use :required in CSS to style them.
• Use aria-required only on custom controls, since native required is announced already.
• Trim values in script when whitespace should not count.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting that a select with a non-empty first option always counts as filled.
• Marking every field required.
• Using only a red star with no explanation.
• Not validating again on the server.

Try It Yourself

• Make a form with required text, checkbox and select fields, style required inputs with CSS and explain the red star in a note.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>style</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  label.req::after { content: " *"; color: crimson; }
  input:required { border-left: 3px solid #ea580c; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label class="req" for="e">Email</label>
<input id="e" type="email" required>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Contact and checkout forms mark required fields clearly.
• Optional fields are labelled optional instead, when most are required.
• Servers reject empty values with field errors.
• Screen readers announce required automatically.

Best Practices

• Only require what you truly need.
• Tell users what the star means.
• Do not remove native required semantics.
• Show errors next to fields.

Interview Question

• Q: How does required work for a radio group?
• A: Setting required on any radio button of the group means one of the group must be chosen before submit.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>trim</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form id="f"><input id="n" required><button>Go</button></form>
<script>f.onsubmit = e => { n.value = n.value.trim(); if (!n.value) { n.setCustomValidity('Please type something'); } else n.setCustomValidity(''); };</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The pattern attribute checks input against a regular expression.
• It works on text, search, url, tel, email and password inputs.
• The whole value must match the pattern.
• Use title to explain the rule in the error message.

Key Points

• Write the pattern without slashes, such as [A-Za-z]{3,}.
• The pattern is matched as if wrapped in ^(?: and )$.
• Empty values pass unless required is set.
• Invalid patterns are ignored by the browser.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>pattern</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form>
  <label for="c">Course code (ABC-123)</label>
  <input id="c" pattern="[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{3}" title="Three capital letters, a dash and three digits" required>
  <button>Check</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Style the field with :invalid and show the title text near it.
• Test your expression in a regex tester before using it.
• Use patterns for formats like postal codes and IDs.
• Do not use patterns for passwords strength rules that need nuance.

Common Mistakes

• Writing slashes or flags in the attribute.
• Making patterns so strict that valid input fails, such as names.
• Forgetting that server validation is still needed.
• Using unescaped special characters like a dash inside a class.

Try It Yourself

• Create a course-code field with a pattern, a helpful title and a visible hint, then test valid and invalid values.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>postal code</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="z">PIN code</label>
<input id="z" pattern="[1-9][0-9]{5}" inputmode="numeric" maxlength="6" title="Six digits, not starting with 0">
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Vehicle numbers, SKUs and ticket codes use patterns.
• Libraries add friendlier messages on top of pattern.
• International formats may need a script rather than a single pattern.
• Accessible hints explain the pattern before an error appears.

Best Practices

• Show the format in the label or hint.
• Keep patterns readable and tested.
• Accept common variants, such as spaces.
• Repeat the same rule on the server.

Interview Question

• Q: Does pattern require the whole value to match?
• A: Yes. The browser treats the pattern as anchored at both ends, so partial matches do not pass.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>hint</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  small { color: #64748b; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="v">Vehicle number</label>
<input id="v" pattern="[A-Z]{2}[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{1,2}[0-9]{4}" aria-describedby="h" placeholder="MH12AB1234">
<small id="h">Format: MH12AB1234</small>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The min attribute sets the smallest allowed value of an input.
• It works with number, range, date, month, week, time and datetime-local.
• The browser shows an error when the value is lower.
• It also limits how far the picker or spinner can go down.

Key Points

• The value uses the same format as the input type.
• For dates it is YYYY-MM-DD.
• For numbers it is a plain number.
• It does not stop typing a lower number, only submission.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>min</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="a">Age (at least 18)</label>
<input id="a" type="number" min="18" required>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Set min from script, such as today for booking dates.
• Combine with max to form a range.
• Use validity.rangeUnderflow to detect the error.
• Update min dynamically when another field changes.

Common Mistakes

• Using min with text inputs, where it has no effect.
• Wrong formats such as 1/1/2026 for dates.
• Expecting it to block typing.
• Forgetting the server check.

Try It Yourself

• Create a booking form where the check-in minimum is today and the check-out minimum follows the check-in date.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>today</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="d">Delivery date</label>
<input type="date" id="d">
<script>d.min = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Age limits, quantity floors and booking dates use min.
• Dependent fields adjust min in change handlers.
• APIs validate with the same limits.
• Tests cover boundary values such as exactly min.

Best Practices

• Keep client and server limits in one shared constant.
• Explain the limit in text.
• Test the boundaries.
• Handle time zones for dates.

Interview Question

• Q: Does min stop the user from typing a smaller number?
• A: No. It only makes the value invalid at validation time and limits the stepper, so the form cannot be submitted until it is fixed.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>dependent</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input type="date" id="a"> to <input type="date" id="b">
<script>a.onchange = () => b.min = a.value;</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The max attribute sets the largest allowed value of an input.
• It works on the same types as min.
• The browser rejects higher values at submit time.
• It also caps the stepper arrows.

Key Points

• For numbers it is a plain number, and for dates an ISO date.
• On a range input, it sets the right end of the slider.
• The default max of a range is 100.
• Use it together with min.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>max</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="q">Quantity (max 5)</label>
<input id="q" type="number" min="1" max="5" value="1">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use validity.rangeOverflow to show a custom message.
• Set max from script when stock changes.
• Prevent future dates for birthdays by setting max to today.
• Combine with step to control allowed values.

Common Mistakes

• Using max on text fields.
• Confusing max with maxlength.
• Forgetting that typing a larger number is still possible.
• Hard-coding limits that the server does not share.

Try It Yourself

• Create a quantity field with a maximum of 5 that shows a friendly message when the value is too high.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>birthday</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="b">Date of birth</label>
<input type="date" id="b">
<script>b.max = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Stock limits, purchase caps and age ranges use max.
• Inventory pages update max after each change.
• Tests include values just above the limit.
• APIs return a clear message when the limit is exceeded.

Best Practices

• Show the limit near the field.
• Handle overflow messages kindly.
• Keep max in sync with real stock.
• Validate on the server.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between max and maxlength?
• A: max limits the numeric or date value, while maxlength limits the number of characters typed in a text field.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The minlength attribute sets the minimum number of characters in a text field.
• It works on text, search, url, tel, email, password and textarea.
• The browser shows an error if the value is shorter.
• An empty field is allowed unless it is required.

Key Points

• The count is in UTF-16 code units, so some emoji count as two.
• The error appears when the user has typed something shorter than the limit.
• Use validity.tooShort to detect it.
• It does not stop the user from deleting characters.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>minlength</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="p">Password (min 8 characters)</label>
<input id="p" type="password" minlength="8" required>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Pair with maxlength to bound the size.
• Show the rule in a hint next to the field.
• Update the message live as the user types.
• Use it for usernames and comments that need substance.

Common Mistakes

• Setting minlength too high, which blocks real names.
• Expecting the check to run while typing. It runs on submit.
• Using it on number fields, where it has no effect.
• Relying on it alone for security.

Try It Yourself

• Create a password field with a minimum of 8 characters and a live hint showing how many characters have been typed.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>live count</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="p" minlength="8" aria-describedby="h">
<small id="h"></small>
<script>p.oninput = () => h.textContent = p.value.length + ' / 8 characters minimum';</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Password rules and review forms use minlength.
• Servers enforce the same minimum.
• Strength meters complement it.
• Accessible hints say the requirement up front.

Best Practices

• Tell users the requirement before they fail.
• Keep minimums reasonable.
• Validate on the server.
• Count characters consistently.

Interview Question

• Q: When does the browser check minlength?
• A: When the form is submitted, and only if the field has some text, because an empty optional field passes unless required is also set.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>review</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="r">Review (at least 20 characters)</label>
<textarea id="r" minlength="20" required rows="3"></textarea>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The maxlength attribute sets the maximum number of characters a user can type.
• The browser stops typing when the limit is reached.
• It works on text-like inputs and textarea.
• Pasted text is cut at the limit.

Key Points

• Unlike max, it really blocks extra characters.
• It counts UTF-16 code units.
• Existing values longer than the limit are not changed.
• Use validity.tooLong only when script sets the value.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>maxlength</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="t">Title (max 30)</label>
<input id="t" maxlength="30">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Show a counter so users see how many characters are left.
• Match the limit to database column sizes.
• Allow a little slack for editing, such as showing a warning near the limit.
• Use it for tweets, SMS-like fields and codes.

Common Mistakes

• Setting limits too low for names.
• Confusing it with max.
• Cutting pasted text silently with no message.
• Not enforcing on the server.

Try It Yourself

• Create a bio field limited to 100 characters with a live counter and a warning when fewer than 10 characters remain.
codeExamples: 100 left

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Profile bios and titles use character limits.
• SMS and push notification editors show counts.
• Databases define matching limits.
• APIs return errors for oversize data.

Best Practices

• Show remaining characters.
• Choose limits from real needs.
• Handle line breaks carefully in counts.
• Repeat the limit on the server.

Interview Question

• Q: Does maxlength stop pasted text from exceeding the limit?
• A: Yes. Browsers truncate pasted text to the maximum length, so the user should be told when text is cut.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>warning</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="t" maxlength="20">
<small id="w"></small>
<script>t.oninput = () => w.textContent = t.value.length >= 18 ? 'Almost at the limit' : '';</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The step attribute sets the increment of a number or date style input.
• It also defines which values are valid.
• The default step is 1 for numbers.
• The special value any allows every number.

Key Points

• For a number input, step="0.5" accepts 0, 0.5, 1 and so on.
• The valid values are counted from min.
• For time, the unit is seconds and for date it is days.
• Arrow keys and spinners move by one step.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>step</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="p">Price</label>
<input id="p" type="number" step="0.01" min="0" value="9.99">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use step="any" for free decimals such as measurements.
• Use stepUp() and stepDown() in script.
• Set min so steps start from the right base value.
• For range sliders, step controls how the handle snaps.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting step for decimals, so 2.5 is invalid.
• Setting min to a value that shifts valid steps.
• Using step with text inputs.
• Relying on floating point comparisons in script.

Try It Yourself

• Create a price field with step 0.01, a time field in 30 minute steps and a counter with buttons that call stepUp and stepDown.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>quarter hours</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="t">Appointment</label>
<input id="t" type="time" step="900" min="09:00" max="17:00">
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Currency fields use step 0.01.
• Time slots use steps in seconds, like 1800 for half-hours.
• Sliders with ten positions use step 10.
• Validation messages mention the nearest valid values.

Best Practices

• Choose step to match the data.
• Display units near the field.
• Test with decimals and negative numbers.
• Validate on the server.

Interview Question

• Q: What does step="any" mean?
• A: It disables step validation, so any number with any number of decimals is accepted, while the spinner arrows move by one.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>stepUp</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="n" type="number" step="5" value="0">
<button onclick="n.stepUp()">+5</button> <button onclick="n.stepDown()">-5</button>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The placeholder attribute shows a short hint inside an empty field.
• The text disappears when the user starts typing.
• It works on text-like inputs and textarea.
• It is a hint about the expected format, not a label.

Key Points

• Use examples such as name@example.com.
• Style it with the ::placeholder pseudo-element.
• Default colour is grey with low contrast.
• It is not submitted with the form.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>placeholder</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="e">Email</label>
<input id="e" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Keep placeholders short, such as a sample value.
• Improve contrast with ::placeholder and a darker colour.
• Use hint text outside the field for important rules.
• Do not repeat the label word for word.

Common Mistakes

• Using the placeholder instead of a label.
• Putting long instructions inside it.
• Light grey text that is hard to read.
• Making users guess the format once the text disappears.

Try It Yourself

• Create a form with visible labels and sample-value placeholders, and style the placeholders with higher contrast.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>style</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  input::placeholder { color: #64748b; font-style: italic; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="p">Phone</label>
<input id="p" type="tel" placeholder="+91 98765 43210">
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Search boxes show example queries as placeholders.
• Forms show date formats like DD/MM/YYYY.
• Floating label designs keep a real label too.
• Accessibility audits flag placeholder-only fields.

Best Practices

• Always provide a visible label.
• Use sample values, not instructions.
• Meet contrast ratios.
• Put rules in a hint text with aria-describedby.

Interview Question

• Q: Why is a placeholder a poor replacement for a label?
• A: It vanishes when typing starts, often has low contrast, and may not be announced by assistive technology as the field name.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The readonly attribute makes a field visible but not editable.
• The value is still submitted with the form.
• The field can be focused and its text can be selected.
• It works on text-like inputs and textarea.

Key Points

• It is a boolean attribute.
• It does not apply to checkboxes, radio buttons, selects or buttons.
• Readonly fields take part in validation only if they have constraints.
• Style it with the :read-only pseudo-class.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>readonly</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label for="i">Order ID</label>
<input id="i" name="id" value="ORD-1024" readonly>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use it for generated values such as an id or total price that users copy.
• Toggle it in script to allow editing after pressing Edit.
• Do not rely on it for security because users can remove the attribute.
• Style it differently so it does not look editable.

Common Mistakes

• Confusing it with disabled, which blocks submission.
• Trusting readonly values on the server.
• Making it look identical to editable fields.
• Using it on checkboxes and expecting a block.

Try It Yourself

• Create a profile field that is readonly until an Edit button toggles it, and style the readonly state with :read-only.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>toggle edit</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
  input:read-only { background: #f1f5f9; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="n" value="Asha" readonly>
<button onclick="n.readOnly = !n.readOnly; this.textContent = n.readOnly ? 'Edit' : 'Lock'">Edit</button>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Profile pages show non-editable fields until the user clicks edit.
• Receipts and invoices show locked totals.
• Copy-to-clipboard fields use readonly inputs.
• Servers recompute readonly values.

Best Practices

• Choose readonly when the value should be submitted.
• Use disabled when it should not.
• Never trust the submitted value.
• Make the state visible.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between readonly and disabled?
• A: A readonly field can be focused and is submitted. A disabled field cannot be focused or edited and is not submitted.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>copy</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<input id="k" value="sk_live_demo_123" readonly>
<button onclick="navigator.clipboard.writeText(k.value)">Copy</button>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The disabled attribute turns a control off.
• The user cannot click, focus or edit it.
• Its value is not submitted with the form.
• Browsers show it greyed out.

Key Points

• It works on buttons, inputs, selects, textareas and fieldsets.
• On a fieldset it disables everything inside.
• It is a boolean attribute.
• Style it with the :disabled pseudo-class.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>disabled</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button disabled>Pay now</button>
<input value="Locked" disabled>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Disable the submit button while a request is running.
• Enable it only when the form is valid.
• Explain why a control is disabled near it.
• Use aria-disabled when the control must stay focusable for a hint.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting disabled values to be submitted.
• Disabling a button with no explanation.
• Using it for security.
• Low contrast, so users cannot read the field.

Try It Yourself

• Create a form whose submit button stays disabled until all required fields are valid, and disable it again while a fake request runs.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>enable when valid</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form id="f">
  <input id="e" type="email" required placeholder="Email">
  <button id="b" disabled>Subscribe</button>
</form>
<script>f.oninput = () => b.disabled = !f.checkValidity();</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Loading buttons are disabled during requests.
• Wizards disable the Next button until a step is complete.
• Fieldsets switch off sections that do not apply.
• Accessible patterns keep focusable disabled looking buttons with an explanation.

Best Practices

• Give a reason for a disabled state.
• Keep text readable.
• Avoid disabling submit forever.
• Use readonly when the value should still be sent.

Interview Question

• Q: Is the value of a disabled input submitted?
• A: No. Disabled controls are excluded from the form data, so use readonly or a hidden input when the value must be sent.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>loading</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button id="b">Save</button>
<script>b.onclick = () => { b.disabled = true; b.textContent = 'Saving...'; setTimeout(() => { b.disabled = false; b.textContent = 'Save'; }, 1200); };</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The checked attribute sets a checkbox or radio button to be selected by default.
• It is a boolean attribute.
• The default state is also what reset restores.
• The current state is available as the checked property.

Key Points

• In a radio group only one button should have it.
• A checked checkbox submits its value.
• Use :checked in CSS to style it.
• The attribute and the property can differ after the user clicks.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>checked</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="n" checked> Email me updates</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p" value="a" checked> Plan A</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p" value="b"> Plan B</label>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Set input.checked = true in script to change the state.
• Use defaultChecked to read the attribute value.
• Use :checked with a sibling combinator to reveal content.
• Pre-tick only options that are safe and expected.

Common Mistakes

• Pre-ticking marketing consent boxes, which breaks privacy rules.
• Expecting setAttribute to change the live state after interaction.
• Giving several radio buttons the checked attribute.
• Forgetting a default for required radio groups.

Try It Yourself

• Create a settings form where saved options are rendered as checked, a checkbox reveals a text area, and a reset button restores the defaults.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>reveal</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<label><input type="checkbox" id="c"> Add a note</label>
<textarea id="t" hidden placeholder="Your note"></textarea>
<script>c.onchange = () => t.hidden = !c.checked;</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Preferences pages restore saved choices with checked.
• Server templates render checked from stored data.
• Frameworks bind checked to state.
• Tests assert the checked state after clicks.

Best Practices

• Use sensible defaults.
• Never pre-tick consent.
• Reflect saved data on load.
• Test reset behaviour.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between the checked attribute and the checked property?
• A: The attribute sets the default state, while the property reflects the current state after the user interacts with the control.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The selected attribute marks an option as the default choice in a select.
• It is a boolean attribute.
• Without it the first option is selected.
• In a multiple select, several options can have it.

Key Points

• Only one option should have it in a normal select.
• The state is available through option.selected in script.
• Use select.value to read the current choice.
• Reset restores the options marked selected.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>selected</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select name="lang">
  <option value="en">English</option>
  <option value="hi" selected>Hindi</option>
  <option value="mr">Marathi</option>
</select>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Set the selected option from saved data on the server or with script.
• Set select.value = "mr" to choose by value.
• Use selectedIndex to select by position.
• Combine disabled and selected for a placeholder option.

Common Mistakes

• Putting selected on several options of a single select.
• Expecting the attribute to update after user changes.
• Using selected to preselect a risky choice.
• Forgetting a placeholder when a choice is required.

Try It Yourself

• Create an edit form where a select is preselected from a variable, and a second multiple select starts with two options chosen.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>from data</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select id="s"><option value="en">English</option><option value="hi">Hindi</option><option value="mr">Marathi</option></select>
<script>s.value = 'mr';</script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Edit forms preselect stored values.
• Language pickers preselect the browser language.
• Placeholder options use selected and disabled.
• Frameworks bind value rather than selected.

Best Practices

• Preselect safe defaults.
• Keep values stable.
• Use a placeholder for required choices.
• Test the reset behaviour.

Interview Question

• Q: Which option is selected when none has the selected attribute?
• A: The first non-disabled option in a single select. A multiple select starts with nothing selected.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>multiple</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<select multiple size="4"><option selected>HTML</option><option>CSS</option><option selected>JS</option><option>Java</option></select>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• Form submission sends the form data to a server.
• It happens when a submit button is clicked or Enter is pressed in a field.
• The action attribute says where to send it.
• The method attribute says how, GET or POST.

Key Points

• Each field is sent as name=value pairs.
• Fields without a name, and disabled fields, are not sent.
• enctype controls the encoding, and multipart is needed for files.
• The browser navigates to the response unless script intercepts it.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>submission</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="e">Email</label>
  <input id="e" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button>Subscribe</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use fetch and FormData to submit without a page reload.
• Use target to open the response in another tab.
• Handle errors from the server and show them near the fields.
• Prevent double submission by disabling the button.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting name attributes.
• Using GET for sensitive data.
• Not handling server validation errors.
• Breaking Enter-key submission with click handlers.

Try It Yourself

• Create a form that submits with fetch and FormData, prints the data as JSON on the page and disables the button while it works.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Classic sites rely on full page form posts.
• Modern apps send JSON through fetch.
• File uploads use multipart.
• Servers redirect after a successful post to avoid duplicates.

Best Practices

• Validate on the server.
• Use HTTPS.
• Redirect after POST.
• Show clear success and error states.

Interview Question

• Q: What decides which fields are sent in a form submission?
• A: Only successful controls: those with a name that are not disabled, and checked or selected for checkboxes, radios and options.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>fetch json</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form id="f"><input name="name" value="Asha"><button>Save</button></form>
<script>
  f.onsubmit = async e => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const body = JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(new FormData(f)));
    console.log('would POST', body);
  };
</script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• A GET form sends its data in the URL query string.
• It is the default method when none is set.
• The URL looks like /search?q=java&level=basic.
• Reloading or sharing the URL repeats the same request.

Key Points

• Use it for searches and filters that are safe to repeat.
• Data is visible in the address bar and browser history.
• URLs have length limits, roughly a couple of thousand characters.
• It should not change data on the server.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>get</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input name="q" placeholder="Search">
  <select name="level"><option>basic</option><option>advanced</option></select>
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Links to filtered results can be bookmarked and shared.
• Search engines can crawl GET URLs.
• Use URLSearchParams to read the values.
• Encode special characters, which the browser does automatically.

Common Mistakes

• Sending passwords or personal data through GET.
• Using GET for actions that change data.
• Very long forms that exceed URL limits.
• Forgetting names, so fields are missing from the URL.

Try It Yourself

• Create a search form using GET with a text field and checkboxes and show the resulting query string on the page after submitting.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Search pages and product filters use GET.
• Pagination keeps filters in query parameters.
• Analytics track search terms from URLs.
• Caches can store GET responses.

Best Practices

• Use GET only for read-only requests.
• Keep URLs clean and short.
• Do not put secrets in query strings.
• Support the back button.

Interview Question

• Q: Why should login forms not use GET?
• A: GET puts the data in the URL, where it is stored in browser history, server logs and referrer headers, exposing the password.
codeExamples: Query string:

beginner.content:
What It Is

• A POST form sends its data in the request body.
• It does not show the data in the URL.
• It is used when the request creates or changes something.
• Set it with method="post".

Key Points

• The size is not limited by URL length.
• Files need enctype="multipart/form-data".
• Reloading the result asks the browser to resend, with a warning.
• The server should redirect after a successful post.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>post</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="u">User</label><input id="u" name="user">
  <label for="p">Password</label><input id="p" name="pass" type="password">
  <button>Sign in</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use HTTPS so the body is encrypted in transit.
• Add a CSRF token as a hidden field to protect actions.
• Return a redirect (the Post/Redirect/Get pattern) so refresh does not resend.
• Send JSON through fetch for API style requests.

Common Mistakes

• Assuming POST is secure by itself. It needs HTTPS.
• Missing CSRF protection.
• Leaving the response page to be refreshed and resent.
• Not validating the data on the server.

Try It Yourself

• Create a POST form with a hidden CSRF field, a file input with multipart encoding and a fetch version that prints the request method.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>multipart</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: sans-serif; }
  label { display: block; margin: 10px 0 4px; font-weight: 600; }
  input, select, textarea, button { font: inherit; padding: 6px 8px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/upload" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="doc">
  <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="token123">
  <button>Upload</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Logins, orders and comments are posted.
• APIs receive form-encoded or JSON bodies.
• Rate limits and captchas protect public forms.
• Servers store the data and redirect to a confirmation page.

Best Practices

• Use POST for anything that changes data.
• Protect with HTTPS and CSRF tokens.
• Redirect after success.
• Limit body size on the server.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern?
• A: After a successful POST the server answers with a redirect to a GET page, so refreshing does not resend the form and create duplicates.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• Semantic HTML means using tags that describe the meaning of the content, not its appearance.
• <header> says this is a header. <div class="header"> says nothing at all.
• The tag itself carries the information.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To make a web page understandable by machines, not only by human eyes.
• Browsers, screen readers and search engines all read the tags to work out the structure.
• To replace the old habit of building everything from <div> elements.

3. Need of This Topic

• A page built only from divs looks fine but is meaningless to software.
• A blind user cannot jump to the navigation if nothing is marked as navigation.
• Google cannot tell your article from your sidebar advertisement.
• This directly affects accessibility compliance and SEO ranking.
codeExamples:

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Accessibility - screen reader users can jump between landmarks instead of listening to the whole page.
• SEO - search engines identify the real content and rank it better.
• Readable code - <nav> is instantly clear; <div class="nv"> is not.
• Easier maintenance - a new developer understands the structure immediately.
• Default behaviour for free - <button> is keyboard operable with no code.
• Future proof - reader modes and AI assistants extract semantic pages correctly.

5. Disadvantages

• Learning curve - you must know which tag means what.
• Easy to misuse - using <section> everywhere instead of <div> is a very common mistake and is worse than using a div.
• No visual difference - beginners see no reward, so they skip it.
• Overthinking - developers waste time debating section versus article.
• Not a magic fix - semantic tags alone do not make a page accessible; you still need correct headings, labels and contrast.

• Government portals - Indian government sites must meet GIGW accessibility rules, which require semantic landmarks.
• E-commerce - Flipkart marks product details in <section> and recommendations in <aside>.
• Blogs - WordPress themes generate header, nav, main, article, aside and footer automatically.
• JavaSchoolLab - the sidebar is <nav>, the topic body is <main>, the notes panel is <aside>.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• Semantic elements map to ARIA landmark roles in the browser's accessibility tree.
• <nav> exposes role="navigation", <main> exposes role="main", <aside> exposes role="complementary".
• This mapping is what assistive technology actually consumes - the visual page is irrelevant to it.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To build a correct accessibility tree without writing a single ARIA attribute.
• The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA if a native element already does the job.

3. Need (Advanced)

• Accessibility is a legal requirement in many markets - the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act in India, ADA in the USA, EN 301 549 in Europe.
• Automated audits such as Lighthouse and axe check landmark structure directly.
• Retrofitting semantics into a div-only codebase is far more expensive than doing it correctly first.
codeExamples:

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Zero ARIA needed - native semantics cannot go out of sync with behaviour the way hand-written ARIA can.
• Landmark navigation - NVDA and JAWS users press a single key to cycle landmarks.
• Reader mode and AI extraction - Safari Reader and content scrapers rely on article and main.
• Structured data synergy - semantic markup plus JSON-LD gives rich search results.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Role loss through nesting - header, footer and aside silently stop being landmarks inside article or section. Most developers do not know this.
• section without a name is not a region - a bare <section> contributes nothing to the accessibility tree, so overusing it is pure noise.
• Multiple main elements - only one may be visible; more is an accessibility error.
• Unlabelled duplicate landmarks - three <nav> elements with no aria-label are announced as "navigation, navigation, navigation".
• Semantics do not fix a broken heading order.

• The Hindu and NDTV - use article plus JSON-LD NewsArticle so stories appear in Google News carousels.
• Screen reader users - roughly 70 percent navigate by headings and landmarks rather than reading top to bottom, according to WebAIM survey data.
• Safari Reader mode - activates only when it detects a clear article structure.
• Enterprise procurement - large clients demand a VPAT accessibility report, which fails without landmarks.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• The <header> element holds introductory content for a page or a section.
• Typically a logo, the site title, a search box and the navigation.
• It is a block element.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To mark the top area of a page or of a section as its introduction.
• To replace the old <div id="header"> pattern with a tag that has real meaning.

3. Need of This Topic

• A screen reader user needs to know where the page banner is so they can skip it.
• Search engines use it to identify the site identity area.
• Without it, the top of your page is just an anonymous box.
codeExamples:

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Clear meaning - anyone reading the code knows this is the introduction.
• Landmark for screen readers - the page header becomes the banner landmark.
• Reusable - the same tag works for a page header and an article header.
• No extra classes needed - you can style header directly in CSS.
• SEO - helps search engines identify your site branding area.

5. Disadvantages

• Role depends on position - it is only the banner landmark when it is a direct child of body. Inside article or section it is just a header.
• Cannot be nested - a header inside another header is invalid.
• Cannot contain footer or main.
• Confusion with <head> - beginners mix up <head> (metadata, invisible) and <header> (visible content).
• Not required - a page is still valid without one, so it is easy to forget.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <header> maps to the ARIA banner role, but only when it is not inside article, aside, main, nav or section.
• Nested inside any of those, it has no landmark role at all - it is a plain grouping element.
• There may be only one banner landmark per page.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To expose the site identity region to assistive technology so it can be skipped or jumped to.

3. Need (Advanced)

• Screen reader users press a key to move between landmarks; without a banner they must tab through the entire menu on every page load.
• Sticky headers introduce a second, subtler problem: they cover the target of in-page anchor links.
• Both issues are routinely flagged in accessibility audits.
codeExamples:
Page header
Section intro
Article title area

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Free landmark - no ARIA attribute needed for the common case.
• Styling hook - position: sticky on header gives a fixed bar with no JavaScript.
• Container queries - a header can adapt to its own width rather than the viewport.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Sticky headers break anchor links - clicking a table-of-contents link scrolls the target under the fixed bar, hiding it. The fix is scroll-margin-top on the targets.
• Sticky headers also break focus visibility - keyboard users tab to an element that is hidden behind the header.
• Multiple banners - adding role="banner" to several headers is an accessibility violation.
• Height changes cause layout shift - a header that grows when a promo bar loads damages your Cumulative Layout Shift score.
• z-index wars - a sticky header must sit above content but below modals, which is a frequent source of bugs.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• The <nav> element contains navigation links.
• It marks a block of links used to move around the site.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To identify the main navigation areas of a page.
• To let users of assistive technology jump straight to the menu, or skip past it.

3. Need of This Topic

• A menu built from plain links inside a div is invisible to software.
• Screen reader users would have to tab through every menu item on every page.
• <nav> makes the menu a landmark they can reach or skip in one keystroke.
codeExamples:

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Landmark navigation - one keystroke reaches the menu.
• Skip link support - users can jump past the whole navigation block.
• Clear code - the purpose of the block is obvious.
• SEO - helps search engines map your site structure.
• Styling hook - style nav a directly with no extra class.

5. Disadvantages

• Overuse - not every group of links is navigation. A list of links inside a paragraph is not.
• Unlabelled duplicates - several nav elements with no aria-label are all announced simply as "navigation".
• No automatic styling - it looks exactly like a div until you add CSS.
• Does not make a menu accessible by itself - a dropdown still needs keyboard support and ARIA state.
• Beginners wrap the footer link list in nav, which adds noise rather than value.

expert.content:
1. Definition (Advanced)

• <nav> maps to the ARIA navigation role.
• Unlike header and footer it keeps that role wherever it is nested.
• The specification says it is for major navigation blocks only, not every group of links.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To create a small, meaningful set of navigation landmarks the user can cycle through.

3. Need (Advanced)

• The value of landmarks falls as their number rises. Ten navigation landmarks are no more useful than none.
• Naming each one with aria-label is what makes multiple landmarks usable.
• aria-current is needed as well, because visual highlighting alone is invisible to a screen reader.
codeExamples:

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Keeps its role anywhere, unlike header, footer and aside.
• Attribute selectors such as nav[aria-label="Breadcrumb"] let you style by meaning rather than by class.
• aria-current gives a free, semantic "you are here" state that CSS can also target.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Landmark dilution - wrapping every link group in nav destroys the usefulness of landmark navigation.
• Redundant labels - aria-label="Main navigation" is announced as "Main navigation navigation".
• Dropdown menus need real work - nav gives you nothing for keyboard operation, focus trapping, Escape to close or aria-expanded state.
• Mobile hamburger menus are frequently inaccessible: the button has no aria-expanded, and focus is not moved into the opened panel.
• role="menu" is usually wrong - that role is for application menus, not site navigation, and it changes how a screen reader lets the user interact.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• The <main> element holds the main content of the page.
• It is the part that is unique to this page, not repeated on every page.
• There must be only one visible main element per page.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To clearly separate the page's real content from the header, navigation, sidebar and footer.
• To give screen reader users a single place to jump to.

3. Need of This Topic

• Every page repeats the same menu, logo and footer.
• Without <main>, a blind user must listen through all of it on every single page.
• With it, one keystroke skips straight to what is new.
codeExamples:

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Skip link target - the single biggest accessibility win for very little effort.
• One keystroke - screen reader users jump to main directly.
• Reader mode - Safari and Firefox use it to find the article text.
• Clear code - anyone can see where the real content begins.
• SEO - helps search engines separate content from boilerplate.
• Simple styling - style main directly with no class needed.

5. Disadvantages

• Only one allowed - a second visible main is an accessibility error.
• Cannot be nested inside article, aside, footer, header or nav.
• Easy to forget - a page is still valid without it, so nothing warns you.
• People include the wrong things - putting the sidebar inside main defeats the purpose.
• No default styling - it behaves exactly like a div until you add CSS.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>main rules</title></head>
<body>

  <!-- DISADVANTAGE 1: only ONE main is allowed -->
  <!-- WRONG
  <main>First</main>
  <main>Second</main>
  -->

  <!-- The ONE exception: extra mains must be hidden.
       Single page apps use this when caching screens. -->
  <main>Visible page content</main>
  <main hidden>Cached previous screen</main>

  <!-- DISADVANTAGE 2: main cannot be nested in these -->
  <!-- WRONG
  <article><main>Not allowed</main></article>
  <nav><main>Not allowed</main></nav>
  -->

  <!-- DISADVANTAGE 3: putting repeated content INSIDE main -->
  <!-- WRONG - the sidebar is on every page, so it is not main content
  <main>
    <article>Real content</article>
    <aside>Repeated sidebar</aside>
  </main>
  -->

  <!-- RIGHT - aside sits outside main -->
  <!--
  <main><article>Real content</article></main>
  <aside>Repeated sidebar</aside>
  -->

</body>
</html>

1. Definition (Advanced)

• <main> maps to the ARIA main landmark role.
• The specification allows several main elements only if all but one are hidden.
• It must not be a descendant of article, aside, footer, header or nav.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To mark the single content region an assistive technology user actually came for.

3. Need (Advanced)

• WCAG success criterion 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks requires a way to skip repeated content.
• A skip link plus a main landmark is the standard, accepted way to satisfy it.
• In a single page application, focus must also be moved to main after a route change, or the screen reader stays where it was and the user has no idea the page changed.
codeExamples:

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Satisfies WCAG 2.4.1 with two lines of markup.
• Focus target for SPA routing - tabindex="-1" on main is the standard React and Angular pattern.
• Print stylesheets - printing only main is a one-line CSS rule.
• Content extraction - reader modes and scrapers key off it.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Focus outline - focusing main draws a visible outline around the whole page unless you suppress it, which then risks hiding focus for keyboard users elsewhere.
• Duplicate mains in SPAs - route transition animations often render two screens at once, briefly creating two main landmarks. They must be hidden, not merely positioned off screen.
• Skip link often broken - hidden with display:none it is unreachable, so it must be moved off screen and revealed on focus instead.
• aria-hidden misuse - hiding main from screen readers while it is still visible is a serious violation.
• Nesting violations are not reported by browsers, only by validators.

THE COMPLETE SPA ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST

1. Exactly one visible <main>
2. main has tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus

4. After every route change:
     a. update document.title
     b. move focus to main

5. Never aria-hidden a visible main

Why each step matters:
  Without (a) the browser tab and history show the wrong page.
  Without (b) the screen reader cursor stays on the old page.
  Without (c) nothing is spoken at all after navigation.

1. Definition

• The <article> element holds content that is complete and independent on its own.
• The test: if you cut it out and paste it elsewhere, does it still make sense?
• If yes, it is an article.

2. Purpose of This Topic

• To mark self-contained pieces such as a blog post, a news story, a product card or a user comment.
• To let software extract that one piece cleanly.

3. Need of This Topic

• RSS readers, Google News and social previews all need to know where one item begins and ends.
• Without <article>, a list of ten blog posts is just one undifferentiated blob of divs.

1. Definition (Advanced)

• <article> maps to the ARIA article role.
• It is a sectioning content element, so it creates its own outline scope for header and footer.
• A header or footer inside it is scoped to the article and loses its banner or contentinfo landmark role.

2. Purpose (Advanced)

• To define a syndication boundary: the unit that can be independently distributed, cached or rendered.

3. Need (Advanced)

• Feed readers, AMP, Google Discover and social crawlers all need a reliable item boundary.
• In component frameworks, the article boundary usually maps exactly to one component, which makes it a useful architectural marker too.

expert.content:
4. Advantages (Advanced)

• Safe header and footer reuse - scoping prevents landmark duplication automatically.
• Component boundary - maps cleanly onto a React or Angular component.
• Caching unit - an article is a natural fragment for edge caching or partial hydration.
• aria-labelledby on an article gives every feed item a distinct accessible name.

5. Disadvantages (Advanced)

• Headings still do not auto-nest - the outline algorithm was never implemented, so an h1 inside an article is still an h1. Heading levels must be managed by hand.
• Unlabelled articles - a feed of fifty articles with no accessible names is announced as "article, article, article".
• Over-nesting - articles inside articles inside articles become impossible to navigate.
• Not a landmark - article is not in the landmark rotation, so users cannot jump between articles the way they jump between nav and main.
• Confused with section even by experienced developers, and the wrong choice silently degrades the outline.
