What It Is

• Metadata is information about the page rather than content shown in the page.
• It lives inside the head element and is read by browsers, search engines and social sites.
• Typical metadata: the title, character encoding, viewport, description and icons.

Key Points

• The head holds title, meta, link, style, script and base elements.
• Nothing in head is rendered directly, except the title in the tab.
• Put the charset meta first so the browser reads the text correctly.
codeExamples: Metadata lives in the head

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Search results and link previews are built from your metadata, so a good head directly affects traffic.
• Keep the title under about 60 characters and the description under about 160.
• Add lang to the html tag so tools know the language of the page.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting the viewport meta, which breaks mobile layouts.
• Duplicate titles across pages, which makes pages hard to tell apart in search.
• Placing meta tags in the body, where they are ignored.

Try It Yourself

• Open any website, view the page source and list five tags you find in the head. Then add a description and a theme-color to your own page.
codeExamples: Core Java

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Frameworks such as Next.js and Angular generate head tags per route for SEO and sharing.
• Teams keep a checklist: title, description, canonical, viewport, icons and social tags.

Best Practices

• Keep metadata unique per page and accurate to the content.
• Test link previews with the social platform debuggers before launch.

Interview Question

• Q: Where does metadata go and why does it matter?
• A: It goes in the head. Browsers use it for encoding and layout, and search engines and social sites use it to build result snippets and link previews.
codeExamples: Spring Boot Guide

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The meta element gives the browser a piece of metadata as a name and value pair.
• It is a void element, so it has no closing tag.
• It only appears inside head.

Key Points

• charset sets the text encoding, almost always UTF-8.
• name and content pair up: for example name="description".
• http-equiv mimics an HTTP header, such as a refresh.
codeExamples: meta tags

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Common names: description, viewport, robots, author and theme-color.
• The property attribute is used by Open Graph tags for social sharing.
• Use name="robots" content="noindex" to keep a page out of search results.

Common Mistakes

• Putting charset after other tags. It must appear within the first 1024 bytes.
• Writing keywords meta tags for SEO. Search engines ignore them.
• Using http-equiv refresh for redirects, which hurts accessibility. Use a server redirect.

Try It Yourself

• Add a description, an author and a robots tag to a page. Change the robots value to noindex and think about which pages of your site should use it.
• Remember: most meta tags work silently, so verify them with the browser tools or an online checker instead of assuming they are right.
codeExamples: Not for search engines

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• The theme-color meta tints the browser toolbar on mobile.
• A noindex robots meta is common on staging and thank-you pages.

Best Practices

• Keep the number of meta tags small and meaningful.
• Use a single viewport tag, never two.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between the name and property attributes on meta?
• A: name is used by standard metadata such as description and viewport. property is used by Open Graph tags such as og:title.
codeExamples: CSP and color-scheme meta

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers how wide the page should be and how to scale it.
• Without it, phones pretend to be about 980px wide and shrink the page.
• It is the first step of every responsive layout.

Key Points

• Standard value: width=device-width, initial-scale=1.
• width=device-width matches the layout width to the screen.
• initial-scale=1 sets the zoom level on load.
codeExamples:
Hello phone

This text is a readable size on small screens.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Media queries only work properly on phones when this tag is present.
• Test with the browser device toolbar and on a real phone.
• viewport-fit=cover helps with notched screens when you use safe-area insets.

Common Mistakes

• Adding user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1, which blocks pinch zoom and harms accessibility.
• Setting a fixed width such as 600, which breaks other screen sizes.
• Forgetting the tag on one template and having only that page look tiny.

Try It Yourself

• Remove the viewport meta tag from the example, open it in the phone view of your browser tools and compare. Put it back and watch the layout change.
codeExamples: Resize the window: yellow on small, green on wide.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Every modern site includes it in its base layout.
• Combine it with CSS units such as rem, %, and clamp for fluid design.

Best Practices

• Allow zoom so low-vision users can enlarge text.
• Keep one shared layout template so the tag is never forgotten.

Interview Question

• Q: Why does a site look tiny on a phone without the viewport meta tag?
• A: Mobile browsers assume a desktop width of about 980 pixels and scale the page down. The viewport tag makes the layout width match the device.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">
  <title>Safe areas</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; padding: env(safe-area-inset-top) env(safe-area-inset-right) env(safe-area-inset-bottom) env(safe-area-inset-left); }
    header { background: #ea580c; color: #fff; padding: 1rem; }
  </style>
</head>
<body><header>Respects notches</header></body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• SEO meta tags help search engines understand and display your page.
• The key ones are the title, the description, the canonical link and the robots tag.
• They do not guarantee ranking, but they control how the page looks in results.

Key Points

• The title is the clickable headline in search results.
• The description is the snippet below it. Search engines may rewrite it.
• canonical points to the preferred URL when the same content has many addresses.
codeExamples: HTML Tables

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Write a unique title and description for each page and include the main topic naturally.
• Use robots with noindex for thin pages such as search results or thank-you pages.
• Use canonical to merge pages that differ only by tracking parameters.

Common Mistakes

• Stuffing keywords into the title or description.
• Using the same description on every page.
• A canonical that points to a different page by mistake, which removes the page from search.

Try It Yourself

• Write a title under 60 characters and a description under 160 for a page of your own. Add a canonical link that points to the clean version of its URL.
• Remember: titles and descriptions are written for people first. A clear, honest sentence that matches the page content earns more clicks than a list of keywords.
codeExamples: Search

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Product and article pages add structured data on top of the basic tags.
• Multi-language sites add alternate links with hreflang.

Best Practices

• Check results in a search console after releases.
• Keep titles descriptive and descriptions written for humans.

Interview Question

• Q: What does rel="canonical" do?
• A: It tells search engines which URL is the preferred version when the same content is reachable at several addresses, which avoids duplicate content issues.
codeExamples: Java

beginner.content:
What It Is

• Open Graph is a set of meta tags that control how your page looks when it is shared on social platforms and chat apps.
• It was created by Facebook and is now read by LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Slack and others.
• Tags use the property attribute and start with "og:".

Key Points

• The core four: og:title, og:description, og:image and og:url.
• og:type describes the content, such as website or article.
• Without them, platforms guess and often choose the wrong image.
codeExamples: Spring Boot Tutorial

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use an image of about 1200 by 630 pixels for a sharp large preview.
• Use an absolute image URL, not a relative path.
• Twitter or X has its own twitter:card tag, and falls back to Open Graph.

Common Mistakes

• Using a tiny image that is cropped or ignored.
• Not updating the tags after a title change, since platforms cache previews.
• Relative URLs in og:image.

Try It Yourself

• Add the four core Open Graph tags to a page and test the link in a social preview debugger. Change the image and see how the preview updates.
• Remember: platforms cache previews for days, so test before you share widely, and add a version query string to the image when you replace it.
codeExamples: CSS Grid

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Every article and course page should generate its own tags from the content data.
• Shared links get more clicks with a clear title and a branded image.

Best Practices

• Test with the platform preview debuggers after publishing.
• Keep titles under about 60 characters so they are not cut off.

Interview Question

• Q: Which Open Graph tags are essential for a good share preview?
• A: og:title, og:description, og:image and og:url. The image should be an absolute URL, about 1200 by 630 pixels.
codeExamples: Article

beginner.content:
What It Is

• A favicon is the small icon shown in the browser tab, bookmarks and history.
• You add it with a link element in the head.
• Sites without one show a blank or default icon, which looks unfinished.

Key Points

• The classic form is rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico".
• Modern browsers also accept PNG and SVG files.
• Sizes of 32 by 32 and 16 by 16 pixels are the most common.
codeExamples: Look at the tab icon

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• An SVG icon scales perfectly and can even adapt to dark mode with a media query inside it.
• Add an apple-touch-icon of 180 by 180 for iPhone home screens.
• A web app manifest lists larger icons for Android installs.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting that browsers cache favicons for a long time, so changes seem not to apply.
• Using a detailed logo that is unreadable at 16 pixels.
• Wrong paths that cause a 404 on every page.

Try It Yourself

• Create a simple 32 by 32 icon, link it in the head and reload the tab. Add an SVG version and an apple-touch-icon as well.
• Remember: icons are tiny, so test the design at 16 pixels, and check it on both light and dark browser themes before you publish it.
codeExamples: Several icon formats

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Real sites ship several icon files and a manifest for installable apps.
• Maskable icons give clean shapes on Android.

Best Practices

• Keep the design simple with high contrast.
• Use a versioned file name when you update the icon.

Interview Question

• Q: How do you provide icons for different devices?
• A: Use several link tags: an ICO or SVG for browsers, an apple-touch-icon for iOS, and icons listed in a web app manifest for Android.
codeExamples: Manifest links the larger icons

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The link element connects the current page to an external resource.
• It is a void element placed in the head.
• It is most often used for stylesheets, icons and preloading files.

Key Points

• rel says what the relationship is, such as stylesheet or icon.
• href gives the URL of the resource.
• Do not confuse it with the a element, which creates clickable links in the body.
codeExamples: Linked resources

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• rel="preload" asks the browser to fetch a key file early, with the as attribute naming its type.
• rel="preconnect" opens a connection to another domain ahead of time.
• media loads a stylesheet only when a condition matches, such as print.

Common Mistakes

• Preloading too many files, which slows the page instead of speeding it up.
• Forgetting the crossorigin attribute on font preloads, so the file downloads twice.
• Using a link element for navigation.

Try It Yourself

• Add a stylesheet with link, then add a preconnect for a font host. Open the Network panel and compare when the font request starts.
• Remember: every extra preload competes for bandwidth with the rest of the page. Add one at a time and measure whether first paint really improved.
codeExamples: Faster first paint

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Performance tuning of fonts and hero images usually relies on preload and preconnect.
• Print stylesheets use media="print".

Best Practices

• Preload only the few resources that affect first paint.
• Measure with the browser performance tools before and after.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between preload and preconnect?
• A: preload fetches a specific file early. preconnect only opens the network connection to another origin so later requests start faster.
codeExamples: Different CSS per medium

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The base element sets the default URL and target for all relative links in the page.
• There can be only one, and it must be inside head.
• It is a void element.

Key Points

• href becomes the starting point for every relative URL.
• target sets the default window for links, such as _blank.
• It must appear before any element that uses a relative URL.
codeExamples: Resolves to /course/java

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• It is handy when a page is served from a different path than its assets.
• Every link, image and script with a relative path is affected, so test carefully.
• Fragment links like #top also resolve against the base URL.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting that anchors such as #section may now jump to the base page.
• Adding a second base element. Only the first is used.
• Setting target="_blank" globally without adding rel="noopener".

Try It Yourself

• Add a base element to a page with relative links and see where they point. Remove it again and compare, paying attention to fragment links.
• Remember: when something odd happens to links or images, check for a base element first. It silently changes the meaning of every relative URL on the page.
codeExamples: Intro Fragment resolves to /docs/#top

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Single-page apps with client-side routing often need a base href so deep links load assets correctly.
• Email templates use it rarely, since many clients strip it.

Best Practices

• Prefer root-relative paths such as /css/app.css and avoid base when possible.
• If you use base, document it for your team.

Interview Question

• Q: What risks come with the base element?
• A: It changes how every relative URL and fragment link resolves, so links and assets can break unexpectedly. Only one base is allowed and it should come first.
codeExamples: Help (opens in a new tab)

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The script element adds JavaScript to a page, either inline or from a file.
• The browser downloads and runs it, and by default stops parsing HTML while it does.
• It can sit in head or at the end of body.

Key Points

• src loads an external file.
• Inline code goes between the tags.
• Scripts run in the order they appear unless you use async, defer or type="module".
codeExamples: Loading...

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Place classic scripts at the end of body, or use defer in head, so the page appears first.
• type="application/json" or ld+json embeds data that the browser does not run.
• The integrity attribute checks a CDN file against a hash.

Common Mistakes

• Blocking scripts in head with no defer, which delays the first paint.
• Loading libraries from untrusted hosts without integrity checks.
• Putting the closing script tag in a string without escaping it.

Try It Yourself

• Write one inline script that changes a heading. Move it from the head to the end of the body and observe why it only works after the element exists.
codeExamples: Structured data is in the head

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Analytics, chat widgets and ad code are all script tags, and they heavily influence page speed.
• Structured data for SEO is added as ld+json.

Best Practices

• Audit third-party scripts regularly and remove those you do not need.
• Use a content security policy to limit what scripts can run.

Interview Question

• Q: Why is a blocking script in the head a performance problem?
• A: The browser stops parsing HTML until the script is downloaded and run, so the page appears later. defer or async avoids that.
codeExamples: Library with a hash check

beginner.content:
What It Is

• noscript holds content shown only when JavaScript is disabled or unavailable.
• It can be used in head or body.
• It is a fallback message, not a replacement for a working page.

Key Points

• In the body it displays normal markup when scripts are off.
• In the head it may contain link, style and meta only.
• Browsers with scripting on ignore it completely.
codeExamples: My App

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Show a short, polite message with how to enable scripting.
• Provide plain links so key content stays reachable.
• Tracking pixels are often wrapped in noscript as a fallback.

Common Mistakes

• Hiding the whole app behind a vague "Please enable JavaScript" line.
• Expecting it to run when scripting fails because of a script error. It only reacts to scripting being off.
• Putting scripts inside noscript.

Try It Yourself

• Turn JavaScript off in the browser settings, open your page and check what noscript shows. Improve the message so it explains what to do.
• Remember: noscript is a safety net, not a design strategy. The best fallback is a page whose main content is already in the HTML when it arrives.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Progressive enhancement means the core content works without scripts, and noscript covers the gaps.
• Server-rendered pages need noscript far less than client-only apps.

Best Practices

• Test your site with scripts off to see what really breaks.
• Keep important content in the HTML itself.

Interview Question

• Q: When does the browser show noscript content?
• A: Only when scripting is disabled or unsupported. It does not run when a script fails with an error.
codeExamples: Without scripts the button is hidden.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• async tells the browser to download a script in parallel and run it as soon as it arrives.
• Parsing of the HTML pauses only for the moment the script runs.
• It only applies to scripts with a src attribute.

Key Points

• Execution order is not guaranteed between async scripts.
• Good for independent scripts such as analytics.
• Syntax: <script async src="a.js"></script>.
codeExamples: The page does not wait for analytics

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use async for code that does not depend on the DOM or on other scripts.
• Combine with defer on other scripts to keep your app code ordered.
• Check the Network panel waterfall to see the parallel downloads.

Common Mistakes

• Using async for scripts that depend on each other, which causes random errors.
• Expecting the DOM to be ready. It may not be when an async script runs.
• Adding async to an inline script. It has no effect.

Try It Yourself

• Add two async scripts that log a message when they run. Reload several times and notice that the order can change.
• Remember: async trades order for speed. If one script needs another, or needs the page to be ready, switch to defer so the order is guaranteed.
codeExamples: Independent scripts use async, app code uses defer

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Tag managers, analytics and ad scripts are loaded with async so they do not delay the page.
• Module scripts are deferred by default and can also take async.

Best Practices

• Do not depend on load order between async files.
• Measure the effect on Largest Contentful Paint.

Interview Question

• Q: How do async scripts differ in order of execution?
• A: They run as soon as they are downloaded, so the order is unpredictable. That is why dependent scripts should not use async.
codeExamples: Module scripts can be async too

beginner.content:
What It Is

• defer downloads a script in parallel and runs it after the HTML is parsed.
• Deferred scripts run in the order they appear.
• It is the best default for scripts that need the DOM.

Key Points

• Runs just before the DOMContentLoaded event.
• Only works on external scripts with a src.
• Syntax: <script defer src="app.js"></script>.
codeExamples: Title

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Put deferred scripts in the head so the download starts early without blocking the page.
• Use defer for libraries and then your app code, since order is kept.
• The DOM is fully parsed, so getElementById works without waiting for an event.

Common Mistakes

• Using defer on inline scripts, where it does nothing.
• Assuming deferred scripts run after images load. They run after parsing, not after load.
• Mixing async and defer on the same tag. async wins.

Try It Yourself

• Place a deferred script in the head that reads an element near the bottom of the body. It works, because the DOM is already parsed.
• Remember: defer scripts run after parsing but before the DOMContentLoaded event, so you rarely need to wrap their code in a load listener at all. Compare the Network panel with and without defer to see the download start earlier while the page keeps rendering.
codeExamples: library.js always runs before app.js

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Most modern sites use defer for the main bundle.
• Frameworks add defer or type="module" automatically in their HTML output.

Best Practices

• Default to defer unless a script must run immediately.
• Keep render-critical code small and inline.

Interview Question

• Q: async or defer for your main application bundle?
• A: defer. It keeps the order of scripts and runs them after the HTML is parsed, so the DOM is ready.
codeExamples: Waiting

beginner.content:
What It Is

• type="module" turns a script into an ES module, which can use import and export.
• Modules are deferred by default and run in strict mode.
• Each module has its own scope, so variables do not leak into the global scope.

Key Points

• Syntax: <script type="module" src="main.js"></script>.
• Inside the file you can write import { x } from "./x.js".
• The browser downloads each imported file once.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Inline modules are allowed and are also deferred.
• Use a nomodule script as a fallback for very old browsers.
• Modules need to be served over http, so file:// may block them because of CORS.

Common Mistakes

• Opening the page from the file system and getting a CORS error.
• Forgetting the file extension in an import path.
• Expecting top-level variables to appear on window.

Try It Yourself

• Create a module that declares a variable, then check typeof window.variable. Compare with a classic script that declares the same variable.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Build tools such as Vite output module scripts for modern browsers.
• Import maps let you use bare names such as "lodash" in the browser.

Best Practices

• Prefer modules for new code.
• Split code into small files and let the browser cache them.

Interview Question

• Q: What are two behaviours that differ between a module and a classic script?
• A: Modules are deferred by default and have their own scope with strict mode, so top-level variables do not become globals.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• Web Components let you create your own reusable HTML elements with built-in browser features.
• They are made from three standards: custom elements, shadow DOM and HTML templates.
• No framework is needed, and they work in any page.

Key Points

• A custom element has a name with a hyphen, such as user-card.
• Shadow DOM hides its internal markup and styles.
• Templates hold markup that is cloned when needed.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>First web component</title></head>
<body>
  <hello-tag name="JavaSchoolLab"></hello-tag>
  <script>
    class HelloTag extends HTMLElement {
      connectedCallback() {
        this.textContent = 'Hello, ' + this.getAttribute('name') + '!';
      }
    }
    customElements.define('hello-tag', HelloTag);
  </script>
</body>
</html>

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• You can use a web component inside React, Angular or plain HTML.
• Attributes and properties let you pass data in, and events send data out.
• Slots let users put their own content inside your component.

Common Mistakes

• Using a name without a hyphen. The browser rejects it.
• Forgetting to register the element before using it.
• Expecting global CSS to style the inside of a shadow root.

Try It Yourself

• Define a custom tag that shows a greeting from an attribute. Wrap its content in a shadow root and style it so the page CSS cannot affect it.
codeExamples: Tip: Slots show your own content.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Design systems share buttons and dialogs across teams as web components.
• Libraries such as Lit make writing them shorter.

Best Practices

• Keep each component small with a clear public API.
• Document the attributes, events and CSS custom properties.

Interview Question

• Q: Which three standards make up web components?
• A: Custom elements, shadow DOM and HTML templates (with slots). Together they allow reusable, encapsulated elements without a framework.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• A custom element is an HTML tag you define yourself with a JavaScript class.
• The name must contain a hyphen, such as my-counter.
• You register it with customElements.define.

Key Points

• The class extends HTMLElement.
• connectedCallback runs when the element is added to the page.
• disconnectedCallback runs when it is removed.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Declare observedAttributes and implement attributeChangedCallback to react to attribute changes.
• Use properties for complex data and attributes for simple strings.
• Customised built-in elements use the is attribute but are not supported in Safari.

Common Mistakes

• Doing heavy work in the constructor. Use connectedCallback.
• Forgetting to clean up timers or listeners in disconnectedCallback.
• Reading children in the constructor, where they may not exist yet.

Try It Yourself

• Build a star-rating element driven by a value attribute. Update the attribute from a button and confirm that the display refreshes.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Observed attributes</title></head>
<body>
  <star-rating value="3"></star-rating>
  <button onclick="document.querySelector('star-rating').setAttribute('value', 5)">Set 5</button>
  <script>
    class StarRating extends HTMLElement {
      static get observedAttributes() { return ['value']; }
      attributeChangedCallback() { this.render(); }
      connectedCallback() { this.render(); }
      render() { this.textContent = '★'.repeat(this.getAttribute('value') || 0); }
    }
    customElements.define('star-rating', StarRating);
  </script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Components such as date pickers, tabs and rating stars are common custom elements.
• Server-rendered pages can upgrade plain markup into interactive components.

Best Practices

• Make them accessible: keyboard support, roles and labels.
• Choose clear, prefixed names such as jsl-card to avoid conflicts.

Interview Question

• Q: What rule applies to custom element names?
• A: The name must contain a hyphen and be lowercase, such as user-card, so it never clashes with a built-in element.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>Lifecycle</title></head>
<body>
  <tick-clock></tick-clock>
  <script>
    class TickClock extends HTMLElement {
      connectedCallback() {
        this.timer = setInterval(() => this.textContent = new Date().toLocaleTimeString(), 1000);
      }
      disconnectedCallback() { clearInterval(this.timer); }
    }
    customElements.define('tick-clock', TickClock);
  </script>
</body>
</html>

beginner.content:
What It Is

• Shadow DOM gives an element its own hidden DOM tree with scoped styles.
• Styles inside do not leak out, and page styles do not leak in.
• You create it with element.attachShadow({ mode: "open" }).

Key Points

• The hidden tree is called the shadow root.
• mode: "open" allows outside code to reach it through element.shadowRoot.
• Built-in elements such as video use shadow DOM for their controls.
codeExamples: Outside: red

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Outside styling is allowed through CSS custom properties, which pass through the boundary.
• The ::part() selector lets you style elements the component exposes.
• The :host selector styles the host element itself from inside.

Common Mistakes

• Expecting document.querySelector to find elements inside a shadow root.
• Using global class names and wondering why they have no effect.
• Not using slots, so the component ignores the content placed between its tags.

Try It Yourself

• Attach a shadow root to a div and give its paragraph a different colour from the page. Then expose a CSS variable to change that colour from outside.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="UTF-8"><title>:host</title></head>
<body>
  <fancy-card></fancy-card>
  <script>
    class FancyCard extends HTMLElement {
      constructor() {
        super();
        this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML =
          '<style>:host{display:block;padding:12px;border:2px solid #ea580c;border-radius:8px}</style>A scoped card';
      }
    }
    customElements.define('fancy-card', FancyCard);
  </script>
</body>
</html>

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Third-party widgets use shadow DOM so their styles never clash with the host site.
• Design systems expose theming through custom properties and parts.

Best Practices

• Expose a small, documented styling API.
• Keep accessibility in mind, since focus and labels cross the boundary.

Interview Question

• Q: How can you theme a component that uses shadow DOM?
• A: Through CSS custom properties, which cross the boundary, and through ::part() for elements the component exposes.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• An HTML template is markup that the browser parses but does not render or run until you use it.
• You define it with the template element.
• JavaScript clones it whenever you need a new copy.

Key Points

• Content inside a template is inert: images do not load and scripts do not run.
• You read it through the content property, a document fragment.
• Use cloneNode(true) to make a copy.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Templates keep markup in HTML instead of long strings in JavaScript.
• Fill in the clone with data before adding it to the page.
• Combine templates with shadow DOM to build components.

Common Mistakes

• Inserting the template content itself rather than a clone, which empties it.
• Expecting it to be visible. It is never displayed.
• Using innerHTML with untrusted data when filling templates.

Try It Yourself

• Create a template for a course card and render three cards from an array of names. Use textContent to fill them in.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Lists of cards, rows and comments are often rendered from one template.
• Lightweight alternative to a framework for small pages.

Best Practices

• Set text with textContent to avoid injection bugs.
• Keep one template per repeated pattern.

Interview Question

• Q: Why use a template instead of a string in JavaScript?
• A: The markup stays in HTML, is parsed once and is inert until cloned. It is easier to read and avoids repeated string concatenation.
codeExamples: Slotted content

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The template element is a container for markup that stays hidden and inactive until JavaScript copies it.
• It can be placed anywhere in head, body or even inside a table.
• Its children belong to a separate document fragment.

Key Points

• Read the contents through template.content.
• The element itself has the display value none by default.
• There is also a declarative shadow DOM form using shadowrootmode.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Because it can sit inside a table or select, it avoids the parsing problems of a div in those places.
• Use importNode when cloning across documents such as an iframe.
• Declarative shadow DOM lets server HTML create a shadow root with no JavaScript.

Common Mistakes

• Querying the page for elements inside a template. They are not part of the live DOM.
• Reusing the same fragment object. Clone it each time.
• Forgetting that scripts inside run only after being inserted into the page.

Try It Yourself

• Place a template inside a table body and add rows to it with a button. Notice that the template itself never appears on the page.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Server-rendered web components use declarative shadow DOM for faster first paint.
• Client-side widgets use templates for rows and modals.

Best Practices

• Keep templates close to the code that uses them.
• Give each template a clear id.

Interview Question

• Q: What is declarative shadow DOM?
• A: A template with the shadowrootmode attribute that creates a shadow root directly from HTML, so server-rendered components need no JavaScript to attach it.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The slot element is a placeholder inside a web component where the user can insert their own markup.
• It works only inside a shadow tree.
• Content passed in from outside is called slotted content.

Key Points

• A default slot has no name and receives all unnamed content.
• A named slot uses name="title" and receives elements with slot="title".
• Text inside a slot is the fallback content when nothing is passed in.
codeExamples: This text goes into the slot.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Slotted nodes stay in the light DOM, so outside CSS can still style them.
• Use ::slotted(selector) inside the component to style slotted elements.
• The slotchange event fires when the assigned content changes.

Common Mistakes

• Using slot outside a shadow root, where it does nothing.
• Targeting nested slotted children with ::slotted, which only reaches direct children.
• Forgetting the fallback content.

Try It Yourself

• Build a card component with a named title slot, a default slot and an action slot. Pass a heading, a paragraph and a button into it.
codeExamples:
Course tip

Practice a little every day.

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Cards, dialogs and tab panels expose slots for title, body and actions.
• It gives the flexibility of children in React with plain browser features.

Best Practices

• Name slots clearly and document them.
• Provide fallback text for empty slots.

Interview Question

• Q: What is the difference between a default slot and a named slot?
• A: A default slot receives all content with no slot attribute. A named slot receives only elements whose slot attribute matches its name.
codeExamples:
• One
  • Two
    •

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The dialog element is a built-in popup window for messages, forms and confirmations.
• It is hidden until opened, and the browser handles focus and layering.
• It replaces many custom modal scripts.

Key Points

• dialog.showModal() opens it as a modal with a backdrop and traps focus.
• dialog.show() opens a non-modal version.
• dialog.close() or a form with method="dialog" closes it.
codeExamples: Hello from a dialog!

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Style the dimmed area behind a modal with the ::backdrop pseudo-element.
• A form with method="dialog" closes the dialog and gives the clicked button value as returnValue.
• The Escape key closes a modal dialog by default.

Common Mistakes

• Using the open attribute to show a modal, which skips focus trapping. Use showModal.
• Forgetting a visible close button.
• Not restoring focus to the button that opened it.

Try It Yourself

• Make a confirm-delete dialog with Cancel and Delete buttons inside a form with method dialog. Show the chosen button value on the page after it closes.
codeExamples: Delete this item?

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Confirm delete boxes, login forms and image viewers are good fits.
• Most browsers now support it fully, so custom modal libraries are often unnecessary.

Best Practices

• Give the dialog a heading and use aria-labelledby.
• Keep content short and the main action obvious.

Interview Question

• Q: Why prefer showModal() over setting the open attribute?
• A: showModal() adds a backdrop, traps focus, makes the rest of the page inert and lets Escape close it. The open attribute only makes it visible.
codeExamples: Styled backdrop

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The Popover API shows floating content such as menus, tips and toasts with HTML alone.
• You mark an element with the popover attribute.
• A button with popovertarget toggles it.

Key Points

• Popovers appear in the top layer, above all other content.
• They close when you click outside or press Escape (in auto mode).
• popover="manual" disables light dismiss.
codeExamples: Practice every day to improve faster.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use popovertargetaction with show, hide or toggle for exact control.
• Style the open state with the :popover-open pseudo-class.
• Anchor positioning in CSS can place a popover next to its button.

Common Mistakes

• Using it for modal behaviour that needs focus trapping. Use dialog for that.
• Forgetting that hidden popovers use display none by default.
• Nesting popovers incorrectly so the parent closes the child.

Try It Yourself

• Create a help popover opened by a button. Add a second manual popover that acts as a toast and hides itself after two seconds.
codeExamples: Menu content

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Dropdown menus, tooltips, and notification toasts replace JavaScript show and hide code.
• Combine with CSS transitions using allow-discrete behaviour for smooth appearance.

Best Practices

• Provide an accessible name and keep keyboard use in mind.
• Pick manual mode for toasts that auto-dismiss.

Interview Question

• Q: When would you choose dialog instead of popover?
• A: Choose dialog when you need modal behaviour such as focus trapping and blocking the page. Popover suits lightweight, dismissable content like menus and tips.
codeExamples: Saved!

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The contenteditable attribute makes any element editable by the user in the browser.
• Clicking inside the element places a text cursor.
• It turns plain HTML into a basic rich text area.

Key Points

• contenteditable="true" (or just the attribute) enables editing.
• "false" disables it again inside an editable parent.
• Edits live only in the DOM until you save them yourself.
codeExamples:
Click here and edit this heading

You can edit this paragraph too.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Read the edited HTML with innerHTML or the plain text with innerText.
• Listen for the input event to react to changes.
• Use spellcheck and autocapitalize attributes to control hints.

Common Mistakes

• Saving innerHTML from users without sanitising it, which allows script injection.
• Expecting form submission to include the content. It does not, unlike a textarea.
• Copy and paste bringing in unwanted styles.

Try It Yourself

• Make a note box that is editable and show a live character count. Then try pasting formatted text and try the plaintext-only value.
• Remember: contenteditable only changes what the user sees. Nothing is saved or sent to the server until your own code reads the content and stores it.
codeExamples:
Type here

Characters: 0

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Inline editing of titles, notes and table cells uses it.
• Rich text editors are built on top of it with lots of extra handling.

Best Practices

• Prefer contenteditable="plaintext-only" where supported for plain text.
• Always sanitise before storing or displaying other people content.

Interview Question

• Q: How do you read user edits safely from a contenteditable element?
• A: Use innerText for plain text, or sanitise innerHTML before storing or showing it, because it can contain injected markup.
codeExamples: Paste formatted text here. Only plain text is kept.

beginner.content:
What It Is

• The HTML Drag and Drop API lets users pick up an element and drop it somewhere else.
• Add draggable="true" to the item and listen for events.
• It powers file upload zones, sortable lists and boards.

Key Points

• Key events: dragstart, dragover, drop and dragend.
• You must call preventDefault() in dragover to allow dropping.
• Data travels in the dataTransfer object.
codeExamples:
Drag me
Drop here

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• Use dataTransfer.setData in dragstart and getData in drop to pass an id.
• Highlight the drop zone during dragenter and dragleave for feedback.
• File drops expose dataTransfer.files.

Common Mistakes

• Forgetting preventDefault on dragover, so nothing can be dropped.
• Not supporting touch screens, where native drag and drop is limited.
• Providing no keyboard alternative.

Try It Yourself

• Build two boxes and drag an item between them. Add a highlight while the item is over the target and a button as a keyboard alternative.
codeExamples:
Drag this text

Drop zone

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Kanban boards, image uploaders and playlist editors use it.
• For touch support, many projects use pointer events or a small library.

Best Practices

• Always offer buttons or keyboard shortcuts as an alternative.
• Show clear visual feedback for valid drop targets.

Interview Question

• Q: Why does a drop event not fire on your target?
• A: You must call preventDefault() in the dragover handler to mark the element as a valid drop target.
codeExamples: Drop files here

beginner.content:
What It Is

• data-* attributes let you store custom data on any HTML element.
• The name starts with "data-" followed by your own lowercase name, such as data-user-id.
• They are ignored by the browser display but available to CSS and JavaScript.

Key Points

• Read them in JavaScript with element.dataset.userId (camelCase).
• Write them with element.dataset.userId = "7".
• Values are always strings.

intermediate.content:
In Practice

• CSS can select them with [data-state="open"] and show them with attr(data-label).
• They link markup to behaviour, such as which modal a button opens.
• Event delegation reads event.target.dataset to know which item was clicked.

Common Mistakes

• Putting sensitive data in them. Anyone can read the page source.
• Using them for styling that normal classes can do.
• Storing large JSON in attributes, which bloats the HTML.

Try It Yourself

• Add data-id to every item of a list, then use one click listener on the list to show which id was clicked. Style items by their data-status value.
codeExamples: Build Tests

expert.content:
Real-World Use

• Analytics tags, test selectors such as data-testid and UI libraries rely on them.
• Server-rendered pages pass initial values to scripts through them.

Best Practices

• Use clear names and keep values short.
• Do not rely on data attributes for content that should be visible to search engines.

Interview Question

• Q: How do data attributes map to the dataset property?
• A: data-user-id becomes dataset.userId. Names switch from kebab-case to camelCase, and all values are strings.
codeExamples:
• Java
  • Spring
  • HTML

Click an item

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
• CSS is used to style HTML elements.
• It controls colors, fonts, spacing, layout, and design.
• CSS saves time by controlling multiple pages at once.
• CSS files are saved with .css extension.

Why Use CSS?

• Makes website attractive.
• Separates content (HTML) from design (CSS).
• Easy to maintain website design.

intermediate.content:
Ways to Add CSS

CSS can be added in 3 ways:

1. Inline CSS
• Uses style attribute inside HTML tag.
• Applies style to single element.

2. Internal CSS
• Written inside <style> tag.
• Placed inside <head> section.
• Applies to single page.

3. External CSS
• Written in separate .css file.
• Linked using <link> tag.
• Can style multiple pages.

Basic CSS Syntax

selector { property: value; }

Selector → selects HTML element.
Property → what you want to change.

expert.content:
CSS Cascade & Specificity

• CSS follows cascading rule (priority system).
• The cascade resolves in the order importance → specificity → source order. Inline styles win on specificity, but between an internal <style> block and an external sheet of equal specificity, whichever comes LATER in the document wins.
• Specificity decides which rule applies.
• ID selector (#id) has higher priority than class (.class).

Example of Specificity Order:
Inline > ID > Class > Element

• Class Selector → .classname
• ID Selector → #idname
• Group Selector → h1, p
• Universal Selector → *
• Descendant Selector → div p

CSS Box Model

Every element consists of:
• Content
• Padding
• Border
• Margin

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• CSS History is the story of how Cascading Style Sheets came into the web and slowly replaced presentation tags like <font> and <center>.
• CSS was proposed by Hakon Wium Lie in October 1994 while he was working with Tim Berners-Lee at CERN.
• The W3C published CSS Level 1 as a Recommendation in December 1996.
• The word Cascading means many style rules can apply to one element and the browser decides a winner using a fixed order.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To show why styling was pulled out of HTML and placed in a separate language.
• To help you understand why some old college portal pages still use <font color="red"> and why that is now wrong.
• To give you the timeline so that words like CSS1, CSS2.1 and CSS3 make sense when you read documentation.

3. Need of this topic

• Before CSS, colour and font were repeated inside every tag, so a 200 page Flipkart style catalogue needed 200 edits for one colour change.
• Old presentation markup made pages heavy, hard to read and impossible for screen readers to understand.
• Knowing the history explains why modern rules exist, for example why the cascade and specificity were designed the way they are.

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Separation of concerns. HTML holds the content, CSS holds the look. A college portal team can change the theme without touching the marks table markup.
• One change, many pages. A single external stylesheet updates a whole website.
• Smaller pages. Removing repeated <font> tags cuts file size, which matters on slow mobile data in India.
• Accessibility. Clean HTML is easier for screen readers and for search engines.

5. Disadvantages

• Slow browser support in the early years. Netscape and Internet Explorer implemented CSS1 differently, so developers wrote hacks for years.
• Legacy code still exists. Many old government and college sites still mix presentation tags with CSS, which is confusing to maintain.
• The language grew fast. CSS now has hundreds of properties, so beginners feel lost.
• No version switch. You cannot tell the browser to use CSS1 only, so you must test features yourself.

expert.content:
1. Definition

• CSS is a declarative, cascading, level based styling language standardised by the W3C CSS Working Group.
• Since CSS2.1 the specification was split into independent modules, each with its own level number, instead of one monolithic version.
• The cascade algorithm defined in CSS1 and refined in the Cascading and Inheritance module still decides every declared value in a modern browser.

2. Purpose of this topic

• For an architect, history explains today's compatibility matrix. Knowing that CSS2.1 froze in 2011 and modules ship independently tells you why caniuse.com checks are per feature, not per version.
• It explains the design intent of the cascade so that you can debug specificity wars in a large codebase instead of adding !important.

3. Need of this topic

• Enterprise codebases carry a decade of layers: table layouts, float grids, flexbox and now grid and container queries. You must recognise each era to refactor safely.
• Interview panels ask why CSS has a cascade at all. The answer comes from the original 1994 proposal where author, user and user agent stylesheets were meant to negotiate.
codeExamples: Order confirmed for Rs. 2499

expert.content:
4. Advantages

• Module independence lets browsers ship :has() or container queries without waiting for a whole CSS4 release.
• Backwards compatibility is a hard rule. Code written for CSS1 still renders, which protects long lived enterprise portals.
• Forward compatible parsing. Browsers drop declarations they do not understand, so progressive enhancement is safe by design.

5. Disadvantages

• No single version number means you cannot say the app targets CSS3. You must maintain a feature support policy.
• Historical baggage. Quirks such as margin collapsing and the default content box model survive only for compatibility.
• Vendor prefix debt. Old codebases carry -webkit- and -moz- rules that are dead weight but risky to delete blindly.
• Specificity was designed before component architecture, which is why teams needed BEM, CSS Modules and now @layer.

• Migration projects. Indian banking portals moving from 2008 table layouts to flexbox keep a compatibility stylesheet for old branch machines running Internet Explorer mode.
• Design system versioning. Bootstrap 3 used floats, Bootstrap 4 moved to flexbox, Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery and prefixes. Each jump mirrors a CSS era.
• Feature gates in production. Teams wrap new colour spaces in @supports so that an old Android WebView on a low cost phone still gets a usable page.
• Interview question. Explain why !important exists. Answer, it came from the original user versus author negotiation model, not as a developer convenience.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• CSS Versions are the numbered levels of the CSS specification: CSS1 (1996), CSS2 (1998), CSS2.1 (2011) and then CSS3 onwards.
• From CSS3 the specification is not one document. It is split into modules such as Selectors Level 4, Colour Level 4 and Flexbox Level 1.
• A level number belongs to a module, so there is no single official CSS4 release.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To let you read documentation correctly when it says CSS Colour Module Level 4.
• To help you judge whether a property is safe to use for your users.
• To avoid the common beginner mistake of asking which CSS version a browser supports.

3. Need of this topic

• A college project that uses a brand new property may break on the lab computers which run older browsers.
• Knowing versions helps you pick a fallback so nothing looks broken.
• Job interviews often ask the difference between CSS2 and CSS3.
codeExamples:
CSS1 style text

CSS2 positioned text

CSS3 module button for Rs. 499

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Faster delivery. Because modules are independent, a useful feature can ship without waiting for the whole language.
• Clear reading path. You can study just the Flexbox module instead of a giant book.
• Stability. Older levels remain valid, so your CSS1 rules never stop working.

5. Disadvantages

• Confusing naming. People say CSS3 for anything modern even though CSS3 is not a real single release.
• Support varies per feature. One browser may support a Level 4 selector but not a Level 4 colour function.
• You must check support manually using @supports or a site like caniuse.
• Tutorials go stale because a module changes after the tutorial is written.

6. Real Time Examples

• Flipkart mobile site. Uses flexbox from a CSS3 module for the product row and a simple float fallback for very old Android browsers.
• Bootstrap 5. Its documentation lists which CSS modules it depends on, such as custom properties and flexbox.
• College exam portals. Often stuck on CSS2 style table layouts because lab machines run outdated browsers.
• GitHub. Uses Selectors Level 4 features like :focus-visible for keyboard users with a plain :focus fallback.
• Tailwind CSS. Ships utilities that map straight onto modern module features such as gap and aspect-ratio.

expert.content:
1. Definition

• A CSS level is a superset of the previous level of the same module. Level 4 of Selectors contains everything in Level 3 plus new items.
• Each module moves through W3C maturity stages: Working Draft, Candidate Recommendation, Proposed Recommendation, Recommendation.
• CSS Snapshot documents are published yearly to describe the state of the whole language at that moment. That is the closest thing to a version number today.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To define a browser support policy for a product. You decide which modules are allowed based on your analytics.
• To communicate risk to a team. Saying the feature is a Working Draft is a concrete statement about stability.

3. Need of this topic

• Enterprise apps must guarantee rendering on a fixed browser matrix, for example Chrome on Windows kiosks in bank branches.
• Build tools such as PostCSS and Autoprefixer are configured with a browserslist that maps directly to module support.

4. Advantages

• Independent shipping means a bug fix in one module does not block another.
• Precise conversations. Saying Colour Level 4 relative colour syntax is unambiguous in a code review.
• Tooling alignment. Browserslist, Autoprefixer and Lightning CSS can downlevel newer syntax to older syntax automatically.

5. Disadvantages

• Fragmented mental model. New joiners must learn where each feature lives.
• Partial implementations. A browser may ship half of a module, so @supports must test the exact value, not the property alone.
• Spec churn. Syntax in a Working Draft can change, which breaks early adopters.
• Snapshot documents are advisory, not enforceable, so there is no compliance badge to test against.

6. Real Time Examples

• Browserslist in CI. A team sets targets like last 2 versions and greater than 0.5 percent in India, and the build fails if a disallowed feature appears.
• Design token pipelines. Tokens are authored in OKLCH from Colour Level 4 and compiled down to hex for older targets.
• Payment gateway pages. Razorpay and similar checkout pages avoid brand new modules because they must work inside embedded WebViews of many apps.
• Interview question. Is there a CSS4. Correct answer, no. Modules have levels, and Snapshots describe the language yearly.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<title>Expert Point 6 - Token Pipeline Output</title>

  :root {
    --brand: #2874f0;        /* compiled fallback for old WebViews */
    --brand-2: #f57224;
  }

  @supports (color: oklch(0.5 0.1 200)) {
    :root {

      --brand-2: oklch(0.70 0.17 55);
    }
  }

  .pay-btn {
    background: var(--brand);
    color: #fff;
    border: none;
    padding: 12px 20px;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    border-radius: 6px;
  }
  .pay-btn.alt { background: var(--brand-2); }
</style>

<button class="pay-btn alt">Pay Later</button>

</body>

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• CSS3 is the common name for the generation of CSS that arrived after CSS2.1, delivered as separate modules instead of one big document.
• It introduced rounded corners, shadows, gradients, transitions, animations, media queries, flexbox, grid and web fonts.
• Strictly speaking there is no file called CSS3. The name is a habit that developers use for modern CSS.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To give you the modern toolkit that removes the need for images and JavaScript for simple visual effects.
• To make responsive design possible using media queries.
• To make layout simple with flexbox and grid instead of floats and tables.

3. Need of this topic

• Before CSS3 a rounded button needed three sliced images. That was slow on Indian mobile data.
• Websites must work on a 5 inch phone and a 24 inch monitor, and only media queries make that practical.
• Every modern framework like Bootstrap and Tailwind is built on CSS3 features, so you cannot use them without knowing this.

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• No images needed for corners, shadows and gradients, so pages load faster.
• Responsive by default using media queries, one site for phone, tablet and desktop.
• Animation without JavaScript using transition and @keyframes, which runs smoothly on the browser compositor.
• Simple layout with flexbox and grid, no more clearfix hacks.

5. Disadvantages

• Too many options. Beginners overuse shadows and gradients and the page looks noisy.
• Performance traps. Animating width or left causes layout work every frame and drops frames on low cost phones.
• Support gaps in very old browsers, so a fallback is still needed for some users.
• Complexity. Grid has a large vocabulary and takes real practice to learn.

expert.content:
1. Definition

• In engineering terms CSS3 is a marketing label for the modular era. What matters technically is which module and which level a feature belongs to.
• The high value modules are Selectors, Colour, Flexbox, Grid, Media Queries, Transitions, Animations, Custom Properties, Cascade and Containment.
• Several CSS3 features moved rendering work to the compositor thread, which is why transform and opacity animate at 60 frames per second.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To design systems that scale: tokens with custom properties, layout with grid, theming with colour functions.
• To reduce JavaScript. Many interactions that once needed a library are now declarative CSS.

3. Need of this topic

• Performance budgets on Indian mobile networks make CSS driven UI far cheaper than JavaScript driven UI.
• Accessibility rules such as prefers-reduced-motion are only expressible in CSS media queries.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Expert Point 1, 2, 3 - Compositor Friendly and Accessible</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 16px; }

  /* POINT 1: custom properties as design tokens */
  :root { --brand: #2874f0; --radius: 10px; --speed: 240ms; }

  .cta {
    background: var(--brand);
    color: #fff; border: none; padding: 12px 18px;
    border-radius: var(--radius);
    /* RIGHT: only compositor friendly properties are animated */
    transition: transform var(--speed) ease, opacity var(--speed) ease;
    will-change: transform;
  }
  .cta:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
  .cta:active { transform: translateY(0); opacity: 0.9; }

  /* POINT 3: accessibility, respect the user setting */
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .cta { transition: none; }
  }
</style>
</head>
<body>

<button class="cta">Place Order Rs. 2199</button>

</body>
</html>

expert.content:
4. Advantages

• Declarative theming. Custom properties cascade and can be changed at runtime, which powers dark mode without a page reload.
• Layout correctness. Grid handles two dimensional layout that floats could never express reliably.
• Reduced bundle size. Replacing a carousel or accordion script with CSS scroll snap or details styling cuts JavaScript.

5. Disadvantages

• Custom property inheritance cost. Changing a variable on a high level element invalidates the subtree, which can be expensive in huge DOM trees.
• Overuse of will-change creates unnecessary compositor layers and increases memory on low RAM phones.
• Grid and flexbox interaction bugs around min-width auto surprise even senior developers.
• Animation of layout properties is still possible, so the language does not stop you from writing slow code.

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• CSS Syntax is the set of writing rules for CSS code.
• A rule has a selector and a declaration block written inside curly braces.
• Each declaration is a property, then a colon, then a value, then a semicolon.
• Example: h1 { color: blue; font-size: 24px; }

2. Purpose of this topic

• To make sure the browser can read your CSS. Wrong syntax means the rule is silently ignored.
• To teach the exact punctuation: colon between property and value, semicolon after each declaration.
• To build the habit of clean formatting that a team can read.

3. Need of this topic

• CSS never shows an error message. If you type colour instead of color, nothing happens and you waste an hour.
• A missing semicolon can break the next declaration too, so one typo can hide several bugs.
• Every later topic, from selectors to grid, is written using this same syntax.
codeExamples:
JavaSchoolLab

Course Fees

Rs. 6000

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Very simple grammar. Only selectors, braces, colons and semicolons, so it is easy to learn in one day.
• Forgiving. An unknown property is skipped and the rest of the file still works.
• Readable. Anyone on the team can open a stylesheet and understand the structure.
• Groupable. Comma separated selectors avoid repeating the same block.

5. Disadvantages

• Silent failures. No error message when you make a spelling mistake.
• A missing closing brace can break every rule that follows it in the file.
• Whitespace is not enforced, so untidy files become unreadable without a formatter.
• Values are not type checked. Writing font-size: 20 without a unit simply does nothing.

6. Real Time Examples

• College assignment. A student writes background-color : #fff with a space before the colon. That is legal. But writing background_color is not.
• Flipkart stylesheet. Grouped selectors like .btn-primary, .btn-secondary share font and padding, then differ only in colour.
• Bootstrap source. Every rule follows the same syntax, which is why tools can minify it safely.
• Prettier and Stylelint. Team tools that format and check CSS syntax automatically before a commit.
• Browser DevTools. Chrome shows a small warning triangle next to an invalid declaration, which is the fastest way to spot a syntax error.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Point 6 - Grouped Selectors Like a Real Stylesheet</title>
<style>
  /* POINT 6: exactly how a production button set is written */
  .btn-primary,
  .btn-secondary,
  .btn-danger {
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    font-size: 15px;
    padding: 10px 18px;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 4px;
    color: #ffffff;
    cursor: pointer;
  }

  .btn-primary   { background: #2874f0; }   /* Flipkart blue */
  .btn-secondary { background: #6c757d; }   /* Bootstrap grey */
  .btn-danger    { background: #dc3545; }
</style>
</head>
<body>

<button class="btn-primary">Buy Now</button>
<button class="btn-secondary">Save For Later</button>
<button class="btn-danger">Cancel Order</button>

</body>

expert.content:
1. Definition

• Formally CSS syntax is defined by the CSS Syntax Module Level 3, which describes tokenization and parsing rules.
• The parser produces qualified rules (selector plus block) and at-rules such as @media, @supports, @layer and @font-face.
• Parsing is forward compatible: an unknown declaration is dropped, an unknown at-rule block is skipped, and an invalid selector in a list invalidates the whole list.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To write CSS that degrades safely and to understand exactly what a browser throws away.
• To reason about tooling: minifiers, PostCSS plugins and CSS-in-JS all depend on this grammar.

3. Need of this topic

• A single invalid selector in a comma list silently kills valid rules, a real production bug.
• Custom properties have a different parsing rule than normal properties, which trips up many senior developers.
codeExamples:
Card
Panel

expert.content:
4. Advantages

• Deterministic error recovery. The spec tells you exactly what happens on bad input, so behaviour is identical across browsers.
• Safe progressive enhancement. You can stack a fallback declaration and a modern one in the same block.
• Tool friendly. The grammar is simple enough that source maps, minification and autoprefixing are reliable.

5. Disadvantages

• Silent invalidation means bugs surface only in visual review, not in a build error, unless you run Stylelint.
• Invalid at computed value time. A bad var() substitution does not fall back to the previous declaration, it falls back to inherited or initial, which surprises people.
• Selector list fragility forces defensive use of :is() or duplicated rules.
• Custom properties are untyped by default, so typos travel far before failing.
codeExamples:
Order failed to turn blue

Order stays brand blue

Typed custom property

expert.content:
6. Real Time Examples

• Stylelint in CI. Indian product teams block a merge if a declaration is invalid or a shorthand overrides a longhand.
• PostCSS pipelines. Nesting and modern colour syntax are parsed and rewritten to plain CSS at build time.
• Design system audits. Grepping for var( with no fallback finds the exact bug shown above.
• Interview question. What happens when one selector in a comma separated list is invalid. Answer, the entire rule is dropped unless you wrap it in :is() or :where().

beginner.content:
1. Definition

• A CSS rule (also called a rule set) is one complete styling instruction: a selector followed by a block of declarations.
• Example rule: .price { color: red; font-weight: bold; }
• A stylesheet is simply a list of rules read from top to bottom.
• There are also at-rules that start with @, such as @media, @import and @font-face.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To teach you the unit of work in CSS. You do not style one element, you write a rule that matches many elements.
• To show the difference between a normal rule and an at-rule.
• To explain the order in which rules are applied.

3. Need of this topic

• Without rules you would need an inline style on every element, which is impossible for a site with thousands of pages.
• Understanding rule order explains why the last rule usually wins.
• At-rules are how responsive design and custom fonts are added.
codeExamples:
Redmi Note Rs. 13999
Boat Earbuds Rs. 1299

beginner.content:
4. Advantages

• Reusable. One rule styles every matching element on every page.
• Maintainable. Change one rule and the whole site updates.
• Organised. Related declarations sit together in one block.
• Conditional styling becomes possible with at-rules like @media and @supports.

5. Disadvantages

• Rule order matters, so moving a block in the file can change the design unexpectedly.
• Too many rules make a large stylesheet slow to load and hard to search.
• Duplicate rules for the same selector spread across a file cause confusion.
• Unused rules pile up over years and nobody dares delete them.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Point 4 and 5 - Rule Order and Duplicates</title>
<style>
  body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 16px; }

  /* POINT 5 DISADVANTAGE: WRONG - the same selector defined twice far apart */
  .btn { background: #2874f0; color: #fff; padding: 10px 16px; border: none; }

  .some-other-rule { margin: 0; }
  .another-rule { padding: 0; }

  /* a developer added this months later without seeing the rule above */
  .btn { background: grey; }   /* this wins, the blue is lost */

  /* POINT 4 ADVANTAGE: RIGHT - one rule, then a clear modifier class */

expert.content:
1. Definition

• The CSS Object Model classifies rules as CSSStyleRule (qualified rules) and various at-rule types such as CSSMediaRule, CSSSupportsRule, CSSLayerBlockRule and CSSFontFaceRule.
• Rules are evaluated by the cascade using origin, importance, cascade layer, specificity and finally document order.
• Nested at-rules do not add specificity. @media never changes how strong a selector is.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To structure a large stylesheet so that override behaviour is predictable rather than accidental.
• To use @layer to make architectural intent explicit instead of relying on file order.

3. Need of this topic

• In a monorepo with several teams, file concatenation order decides winners. That is fragile and must be replaced by layers.
• Runtime rule manipulation through the CSSOM is used by theming engines and must be understood for performance.

4. Advantages

• Predictable overrides. Layers remove the specificity arms race and the need for !important.
• Third party isolation. Import a vendor stylesheet into its own layer so it can never beat your components.
• Conditional grouping. @supports and @media let one file describe several environments without duplication.

5. Disadvantages

• !important reverses layer order. An important declaration in the lowest layer beats an important one in the highest, which confuses teams.
• Unlayered rules beat all layered rules, so a single stray rule outside a layer can break the architecture.
• Runtime CSSOM edits such as insertRule force style recalculation and can be costly in a loop.
• Deeply nested at-rules are hard to read and hard to lint.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To target exactly the elements you want, not more and not less.
• To avoid adding a class to every single tag in the HTML.
• To react to user state such as hover, focus and checked without JavaScript.

3. Need of this topic

expert.content:
1. Definition

• Selectors are specified by the Selectors Level 4 module. A complex selector is a chain of compound selectors joined by combinators.
• Browsers match selectors right to left starting from the key selector (the rightmost compound), which is why the rightmost part should be the most specific.
• Level 4 adds :is(), :where(), :has(), :not() with a list, and case insensitive attribute matching with the i flag.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To control specificity deliberately: :is() takes the highest specificity inside it, :where() always contributes zero.
• To express parent and sibling conditions with :has() and remove JavaScript class toggling.

3. Need of this topic

• Design systems need zero specificity defaults so consumer code can override without !important.
• Large tables and lists benefit from cheap key selectors to keep style recalculation fast on low end devices.
codeExamples: Checkout

expert.content:
4. Advantages

• Specificity control. :where() gives a zero weight baseline, which is the cleanest way to build a component library.
• Parent selection. :has() removes whole categories of JavaScript that only existed to add a class to a parent.
• Compact rules. :is() collapses long comma lists and stays readable.
• Forgiving lists. :is() and :where() ignore invalid items instead of dropping the whole rule.

5. Disadvantages

• :has() can be expensive on very large or frequently mutated DOM trees because it may invalidate ancestors.
• :is() specificity surprises. Putting an id inside :is() silently makes the rule as strong as an id selector.
• Universal and very generic key selectors increase style recalculation cost.
• Attribute selectors on frequently changing attributes trigger repeated restyling.

2. Purpose of this topic

1. Definition

• The Values and Units Module defines value stages: specified value, computed value, used value and actual value.
• A specified value is what you wrote. A computed value is after inheritance and relative unit resolution. A used value is after layout, for example a percentage width turned into pixels.
• Math functions include calc(), min(), max(), clamp() and the newer round(), mod() and rem().

2. Purpose of this topic

• To predict exactly what inherits. Children inherit computed values, not the text you typed.
• To build fluid design systems with clamp() instead of stacking many media queries.

3. Need of this topic

• A fluid typography scale is expected in modern responsive work and is impossible to reason about without the value stages.

1. Definition

• A CSS comment is a note in the stylesheet that the browser ignores.
• It starts with a slash star and ends with a star slash.
• CSS has only this one comment style. The double slash used in Java and JavaScript does not work in plain CSS.
• Comments can span many lines.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To explain why a rule exists, not what it does. The code already says what.
• To divide a long stylesheet into readable sections.
• To temporarily switch off a rule while testing.

3. Need of this topic

• Six months later you will not remember why a magic number like margin-top: 37px was needed.

• Comments are visible to everyone. Anyone can view the stylesheet, so never write passwords or private notes.
• They increase file size if not removed during the build.
• Stale comments lie. A comment that was not updated is worse than no comment.
• Cannot be nested. The first star slash ends the comment, which can accidentally re enable code.

1. Definition

• A <style> element creates a render blocking stylesheet that is parsed as part of the HTML document and belongs to the author origin.
• Its position in the document matters for the cascade when specificity and layer are equal, because document order breaks the tie.
• It participates in the CSSOM as a CSSStyleSheet, so it can be manipulated at runtime through document.styleSheets.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To implement critical CSS and improve Largest Contentful Paint on slow networks.
• To ship page scoped overrides in server rendered applications without polluting the global bundle.

3. Need of this topic

• Core Web Vitals directly affect search ranking, and eliminating a render blocking request for above the fold styles is one of the highest impact fixes.
• Content Security Policy environments need a nonce or hash for inline style blocks, which is an operational concern.

• Works under offline first strategies because the styles live in the cached HTML shell.

5. Disadvantages

• Not cacheable separately. Every navigation re downloads the same bytes, which is worse for repeat visitors.
• CSP friction. style-src without unsafe-inline requires a nonce or hash on every page render.
• Duplication across pages inflates total transfer for multi page sites.
• Harder to lint and test because the CSS is embedded in templates rather than in .css files.

1. Definition

• External CSS means the CSS lives in its own file with a .css extension, for example style.css.
• The HTML page links to it using a <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> tag inside the <head>.
• One CSS file can be shared by hundreds of HTML pages.
• The .css file contains only CSS rules, no HTML tags and no <style> tag.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To write the styles once and use them everywhere.
• To keep HTML clean so it only describes content.
• To let the browser cache the stylesheet so repeat visits are faster.

3. Need of this topic

• A real website has many pages. Copying CSS into each one is impossible to maintain.
• A brand colour change should be one edit, not fifty.
• Teams split work: one person on HTML, another on CSS, without file conflicts.

4. Advantages

• Reusable across every page. One file styles the whole site.
• Browser caching. The file is downloaded once and reused, which saves mobile data on repeat visits.
• Clean HTML. Content and presentation are fully separated.
• Team friendly. Designers work in CSS files while developers work in HTML.

5. Disadvantages

• Extra network request. The page cannot paint until the stylesheet arrives, because a stylesheet is render blocking.
• Broken path breaks everything. A wrong href shows an unstyled page.
• Flash of unstyled content can appear on very slow connections.
• Global scope. A careless rule in the shared file can break an unrelated page.

expert.content:
1. Definition

• A linked stylesheet is a separate resource fetched by the browser. By default it is render blocking for the media it applies to.
• A link with a non matching media attribute, for example media="print", is fetched at low priority and does not block rendering.
• External sheets can be layered at import time with @import url(x.css) layer(vendor), which is the cleanest way to control third party CSS.

2. Purpose of this topic

• To design a loading strategy: what blocks, what is deferred, what is preloaded.
• To control cascade architecture across many independently deployed files.

3. Need of this topic

• Core Web Vitals penalise a long critical request chain, and @import inside a CSS file creates exactly that.
• Micro frontends ship separate CSS bundles, so origin, order and layers must be planned rather than accidental.
codeExamples:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
<title>Expert Point 1, 2, 3 - Loading Strategy</title>

<!--
  POINT 2: production loading strategy

  RIGHT: preload the critical sheet so it starts early
  <link rel="preload" as="style" href="/css/app.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/app.css">

  RIGHT: deferred non critical sheet, does not block first paint
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/below-fold.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">

  RIGHT: vendor CSS placed in its own cascade layer at import time
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/layers.css">
     where layers.css starts with
     @layer reset, vendor, components, utilities;
     @import url("bootstrap.min.css") layer(vendor);

  WRONG: @import chains inside CSS create a serial request waterfall
  (app.css imports theme.css which imports tokens.css)
-->

<style>
/* Simulated layers.css */
@layer reset, vendor, components, utilities;

@layer vendor {
  .btn.btn-primary { background: #0d6efd; color: #fff; padding: 8px 14px; border: none; }
}
@layer components {
  .btn-primary { background: #2874f0; border-radius: 6px; }
}
@layer utilities {
  .u-w-full { width: 100%; }
}
body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; padding: 16px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>

<button class="btn btn-primary u-w-full">Proceed to Pay Rs. 7499</button>

</body>
</html>

expert.content:
4. Advantages

• Long term caching. A content hashed filename such as app.9f3c1a.css can be cached for a year.
• Parallel download. Several link tags fetch in parallel, unlike @import chains which are serial.
• Layer control at import. Vendor CSS can be permanently subordinated without touching its source.
• Independent deploys. Teams can ship their own bundle without rebuilding the whole app.

5. Disadvantages

• Render blocking by default, so a slow stylesheet delays the first paint entirely.
• @import waterfalls add a full round trip per level of nesting.
• Global namespace. Without layers or CSS Modules, one team's selector can override another's.
• Cache invalidation mistakes. Serving style.css without a hash means users see stale styles after a deploy.

1. Definition

• The cascade is the process the browser uses to decide which style wins when several rules target the same element and the same property.
• The word Cascading in Cascading Style Sheets comes from this process.
• Simplified order of checks: importance, then origin, then specificity, then source order (the last rule wins).

2. Purpose of this topic

• To explain why your rule is not applying even though it looks correct.
• To let you override library styles such as Bootstrap in a controlled way.
• To stop you from reaching for !important as the first solution.

3. Need of this topic

• Every developer hits the moment when a colour refuses to change. The cascade is always the answer.
• Without it, large stylesheets become unpredictable.
• It is one of the most asked topics in front end interviews.
codeExamples:
